11 October 2026 — A test function that is nonnegative on the whole strip cannot separate a point from the zeros near it: a certificate excluding \(1/2+\delta+i\gamma_0\) needs the weighted count of actual zeros near \(\gamma_0\) to be below \(4/\cos(\pi\delta)\)

Working proof of an elementary obstruction, with a numerical control; it limits a method and proves nothing about zeta zeros. Strip positivity obstruction. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Chosen. This entry takes the second review's picked lead, positivity certificates, ahead of the queue's head, as that review's Decisive test requires. It bears on off-line exclusion: the certificate was the one formulation found in which a single off-line zero violates an inequality with no hypothesis on the others. At the goal's parameters the test could only tell whether that formulation can work at fixed distance from the line; a no gives nothing toward the goal and removes a class of methods.

Architecture test. The second review asked to prove or break its reviewer's proposed obstruction. Outcome: it holds, with explicit constants and without the explicit formula. For a test function with nonnegative real part on the closed strip, \(\Re h(\gamma+iy)\ge\cos(\pi y)\cos(\pi\delta)e^{-\pi|\gamma-\gamma_0|}\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\); so any sound upper bound for the sum of \(\Re h\) over the actual zeros is at least \(\cos(\pi\delta)D(\gamma_0)\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\), with \(D\) a weighted count of actual zeros near \(\gamma_0\), and a certificate needs \(\cos(\pi\delta)D(\gamma_0)<4\). The case the reviewer flagged, neighbours that are themselves off the line, is covered by the factor \(\cos(\pi y)\) in \(D\): the obstruction weakens as the nearby zeros approach the edge of the strip.

Question. The missing implication is an estimate excluding one off-line zero. Can a test function \(g\) with \(\Re\widehat g\ge0\) on \(|\Im z|\le1/2\) certify, through an upper bound for the sum over zeros, that \(1/2+\delta+i\gamma_0\) is not a zero, at fixed \(\delta<1/2\) and large height?

New mathematics. One lemma and its corollary. The lemma is Harnack's inequality in the strip with the constant written out; the corollary says that the method of positivity on the whole strip can exclude a point only where \(\cos(\pi\delta)\sum_\rho\cos(\pi y_\rho)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}<4\), the sum over the actual zeros \(1/2+y_\rho+i\gamma_\rho\). The proposal came from the review's reviewer. Whether the application is in the literature I have not searched; it is Harnack's inequality in the strip, presumably folklore, and no novelty is claimed.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The one formulation the review found that needs no hypothesis on the other zeros is limited, by its own positivity, to points whose distance from the edge of the strip is at most of the order of the reciprocal of the weighted local count of zeros. If the zeros near \(\gamma_0\) are on the line and as numerous as the classical count (recalled, not read: about \(\tfrac1{2\pi}\log\gamma_0\) per unit height), this is \(1/2-\delta\lesssim4\pi/\log\gamma_0\), the shape of the classical region. So, given a lower bound of order \(\log\gamma_0\) for the number of zeros in every window of bounded length (the classical local count, recalled and not read in this cycle), the method cannot prove the goal: where the goal holds nearby, it cannot reach fixed \(\delta\). One exception is noted below: zeros near \(\gamma_0\) that have been located can be subtracted. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing; it is a limit of a method. The cycle was spent on it because the review's decision depended on it.

General statement. lem:strip-positivity-obstruction, for every continuous even real \(g\) of compact support whose transform has nonnegative real part on the lines \(\Im z=\pm1/2\), every pair of points of the open strip, and every multiset of points of the strip.

Review. The stand-in review after the route review raised five objections. (1) Three entries in a row admitted a mistake with a Prevention that changed nothing, and I declined to build the closure check instead of building and measuring it: accepted and fixed. The finisher now requires of every closure a paragraph on what the item names that was not examined; measured on all notebooks by a scratch count whose output the framework commit's message quotes, 217 of 2145 research entries close an item and 4 of those would lack only this paragraph. (2) A test of a recalled inequality in 2400 configurations distinguishes nothing and should not be recorded as passed: accepted; the committed review records that lead as falsified at its break point and does not pick it; the chat table that said passed predates the review's second stage. (3) The Stop-hook pattern was committed with three false hits among twelve read and thirty unread: fixed; the pattern now needs a noun of the kind withdrawn, and all 33 remaining matches on this machine's transcripts, read, take back a statement. (4) A source not retrieved goes to the user's request file, and none was filed: fixed; a request for three papers is filed with citations, what was tried and the defaults followed. (5) "I know of no estimate" is a belief: accepted; the Li entry as committed labels it an untested hypothesis, and the route review's assessment is stated as a summary of the entries, not a search.

Statement and proof

Let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, even, of compact support, and \(h(z)=\int g(u)e^{izu}\,du\). For real \(t\) and \(|y|\le1/2\), since \(g\) is even, \(\Re h(t+iy)=\int g(u)\cosh(yu)\cos(tu)\,du\). Put \(G(u)=g(u)\cosh(u/2)\) and \(\varphi(s)=\Re h(s\pm i/2)=\widehat G(s)\). Let \[K_y(t)={2\pi\cos(\pi y)\cosh(\pi t)\over\sinh^2(\pi t)+\cos^2(\pi y)}\qquad(|y|<1/2).\]

Lemma (strip positivity obstruction). lem:strip-positivity-obstruction. Suppose \(\varphi\ge0\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then:

  1. \(\varphi\) is integrable, and for \(|y|<1/2\), \(\Re h(t+iy)=\tfrac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(s)K_y(t-s)\,ds\); in particular \(\Re h\ge0\) on the whole closed strip.
  2. For all real \(\gamma,\gamma_0\) and \(|y|,|\delta|<1/2\): \(\Re h(\gamma+iy)\ge\cos(\pi y)\cos(\pi\delta)\,e^{-\pi|\gamma-\gamma_0|}\,\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\).
  3. Let \(Z\) be a multiset of points \(\gamma_\rho+iy_\rho\) of the open strip and \(B\) a real number with \(\sum_{\rho\in Z}\Re h(\gamma_\rho+iy_\rho)\le B\). Put \(D_Z(\gamma_0)=\sum_{\rho\in Z}\cos(\pi y_\rho)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\). If \(c\,\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)>B\) for some \(c>0\), then \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_Z(\gamma_0)<c\).

Proof. (1) \(G\) is continuous with compact support and \(\widehat G=\varphi\ge0\). For \(\epsilon>0\), \(\int\varphi(s)e^{-\epsilon s^2}ds=\int G(u)\sqrt{\pi/\epsilon}\,e^{-u^2/4\epsilon}du\), which tends to \(2\pi G(0)\) as \(\epsilon\to0\) by continuity of \(G\); by monotone convergence \(\int\varphi=2\pi G(0)<\infty\). Hence Fourier inversion holds at every point: \(G(u)=\tfrac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(s)\cos(su)\,ds\). The function \(m_y(u)=\cosh(yu)/\cosh(u/2)\) is integrable for \(|y|<1/2\), and \(\int m_y(u)\cos(tu)\,du=K_y(t)\). Proof of this: for real \(w\) let \(I(w)=\int e^{iwu}/\cosh(u/2)\,du\). Since \(\cosh((u+2\pi i)/2)=-\cosh(u/2)\), integrating over the rectangle with sides \(\Im u=0\) and \(\Im u=2\pi\) gives \(I(w)(1+e^{-2\pi w})=2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{u=i\pi}\), and the residue is \(e^{-\pi w}/(\tfrac12\sinh(i\pi/2))=-2ie^{-\pi w}\), so \(I(w)=4\pi e^{-\pi w}/(1+e^{-2\pi w})=2\pi/\cosh(\pi w)\). Both sides are analytic in \(|\Im w|<1/2\), where the integral converges absolutely, so the identity holds there. For \(w=t-iy\) the integrand is \(e^{yu}e^{itu}/\cosh(u/2)\), whose integral has real part \(\int m_y(u)\cos(tu)\,du\) (the odd parts integrate to zero); and \(\cosh(\pi t-i\pi y)=\cosh\pi t\cos\pi y-i\sinh\pi t\sin\pi y\) has squared modulus \(\sinh^2\pi t+\cos^2\pi y\), so \(\Re\,2\pi/\cosh(\pi(t-iy))=K_y(t)\). The control below checks the formula numerically as well. Then \(\Re h(t+iy)=\int G(u)m_y(u)\cos(tu)\,du=\tfrac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(s)\int m_y(u)\cos(su)\cos(tu)\,du\,ds\) by Fubini, and \(\int m_y\cos(su)\cos(tu)\,du=\tfrac12(K_y(t-s)+K_y(t+s))\); as \(\varphi\) is even the two halves agree. \(K_y>0\) gives the positivity. (2) With \(c=\cos(\pi y)\in(0,1]\): \(K_y(t)/K_0(t)=c\cosh^2(\pi t)/(\sinh^2(\pi t)+c^2)\), which is at least \(c\) because \(\sinh^2+c^2\le\cosh^2\), and at most \(1/c\) because \(c^2\cosh^2\le\sinh^2+c^2\). And \(K_0(t)=2\pi/\cosh(\pi t)\) satisfies \(K_0(t+d)\ge e^{-\pi|d|}K_0(t)\), since \(\cosh(a+b)\le e^{|b|}\cosh a\). Hence \(K_y(t+d)\ge\cos(\pi y)K_0(t+d)\ge\cos(\pi y)e^{-\pi|d|}K_0(t)\ge\cos(\pi y)\cos(\pi\delta)e^{-\pi|d|}K_\delta(t)\) for all real \(t,d\). Integrating against \(\varphi\ge0\) with \(d=\gamma-\gamma_0\) gives (2). (3) By (1) every term of the sum is nonnegative, so \(B\ge0\), hence \(\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)>0\); by (2), \(B\ge\sum_\rho\Re h(\gamma_\rho+iy_\rho)\ge\cos(\pi\delta)D_Z(\gamma_0)\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\), and dividing by \(\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\) gives \(c>\cos(\pi\delta)D_Z(\gamma_0)\). \(\square\)

Degenerate cases. \(g\equiv0\): both sides of (2) vanish and (3) has no instance. \(Z\) empty: \(D_Z=0\) and (3) is no restriction, as it should be when there are no zeros to protect. \(\delta\to1/2\): the factor \(\cos(\pi\delta)\) tends to \(0\) and the restriction disappears, consistent with the edge of the strip being reachable. \(\delta=0\): a point on the line can be certified only where \(D_Z(\gamma_0)<c\). A function \(g\) that is not even, or not real, is outside the lemma as stated, and it is not an evasion: the zero set is invariant under \(z\mapsto-z\) and \(z\mapsto\bar z\), so the sum over zeros sees only the symmetrized \(g\), whose \(\Re h\) is an average of \(\Re h\) at four points of the strip, still nonnegative, with the same value at the image quadruple. Points of \(Z\) on the boundary lines are outside the statement and would contribute nonnegative terms that only strengthen (3). Compact support is used only to make \(G\) integrable; the proof works for continuous even real \(g\) with \(g\cosh(u/2)\) integrable. The constant in (2) is sharp in each factor separately at \(y=0\) (\(\cos\pi\delta\) at \(t=d=0\); \(e^{-\pi|d|}\) as \(t\to\pm\infty\) with \(\delta=0\)) and not jointly: for \(y=\delta\), \(d=0\) the true ratio is \(1\) against the bound \(\cos^2\pi\delta\).

What it says about certificates

The method. A certificate that \(1/2+\delta+i\gamma_0\) is not a zero, of the kind the review described, consists of an admissible \(g\) and a number \(B\) such that the explicit formula, with the sign of the prime term used, proves \(\sum_\rho\Re h(z_\rho)\le B\) for the actual zeros \(z_\rho\) in the variable \(z\); a zero at the point with its three images would add \(4\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)\), and the certificate succeeds if that exceeds \(B\). (For \(\delta\ne0\) and \(\gamma_0\ne0\) the four images contribute equal real parts, \(\Re h\) being even in \(t\) and in \(y\); on the line or at \(\gamma_0=0\) there are two images, and a multiple zero would count more, so \(4\) is the case for a simple off-line zero.) Part 3 with \(c=4\) and \(Z\) the actual zeros: success requires \(\cos(\pi\delta)D(\gamma_0)<4\), where \(D(\gamma_0)=\sum_\rho\cos(\pi y_\rho)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\). The explicit formula's normalization does not enter: only that the certificate's bound is sound. The constraint on \(g\) at prime powers is not used either; it can only restrict further.

Size of the count. If the \(n\) zeros within distance \(1\) of height \(\gamma_0\) are on the line, \(D(\gamma_0)\ge ne^{-\pi}\). With the classical local count (recalled, not read) and all nearby zeros on the line, \(D(\gamma_0)\) is about \(\pi^{-2}\log(\gamma_0/2\pi)\), so success requires \(\cos(\pi\delta)\lesssim4\pi^2/\log\gamma_0\). Unconditionally the factors \(\cos(\pi y_\rho)\) can be small only for zeros near the edge of the strip; I do not derive a lower bound for \(D\) here. The structural reason is the one the reviewer named: positivity for all possible zeros is paid for by Harnack's inequality, and a positive harmonic function cannot be large at a point and small at the zeros within bounded distance of it.

What the obstruction does not cover. Test functions whose real part is allowed to be negative somewhere in the strip, with the zeros in that region controlled by other information; methods that bound the sum over zeros from both sides; and certificates for a different statement than the absence of a zero at a point. The first is the reviewer's suggested evasion and needs information about \(\zeta\) near height \(\gamma_0\). A fourth exception keeps positivity on the whole strip: if a set \(S\) of actual zeros near \(\gamma_0\) has been located, their terms can be computed and subtracted, part 3 applies to the remaining zeros, and the requirement becomes \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_{Z\setminus S}(\gamma_0)<4\); this is a device for verification at a finite height, of the kind used in numerical checks, and not a route to all heights. The linear-programming form the lead names is answered by the lemma under whole-strip positivity: it holds for every admissible \(g\), so for the optimum.

Numerical control

Nonvacuity. The script kernel_check.py checks three things that could each fail. The recalled integral: \(K_y(t)\) against quadrature of \(\int m_y(u)\cos(tu)\,du\) at sixteen points (\(y\le0.49\), \(t\le2.5\)), largest relative difference \(1.8\cdot10^{-10}\). The kernel inequality of part 2 on a grid of 147600 points: least ratio of the two sides \(1.0\), attained at the trivial point \(y=\delta=0\), \(d=0\), so this confirms the inequality and says nothing about sharpness. Part 2 end to end, computed from \(g\) without the kernel, for forty admissible functions \(g=G/\cosh(u/2)\) with \(G\) a triangle times \((1+\cos au)/2\), the hypothesis \(\varphi\ge0\) checked on a grid, at thirty random pairs of points each, all 1200 pairs used: least ratio \(1.22\) (output). The first run's quadrature was wrong (a truncated oscillatory integral, relative difference \(328\)); the Fourier-integral rule replaced it. The control is not registered as a claim.

Sub-ideas

  • Relax the positivity: require \(\Re h\ge0\) only outside a window of bounded width around \(\gamma_0\), and state what must then be known about the actual zeros inside the window for a certificate to succeed at fixed \(\delta\); decide whether that requirement is weaker than a zero-free region of the same width, or the same statement.

Follow-up. Continuing: the lead asked whether a positivity certificate at a point can exclude an off-line zero with no hypothesis on the others. With positivity on the whole strip it cannot at fixed distance from the line wherever the weighted count of actual zeros exceeds \(4/\cos(\pi\delta)\). The lead's statement also names the linear-programming form and the comparison with what a relaxed positivity needs; the relaxed form is the sub-idea and the next attempt on this lead. Record search. For it the registry was searched for explicit formula positivity certificate linear programming test function strip Odlyzko, for zero-free region explicit formula trigonometric polynomial, for Harnack Poisson kernel strip positive harmonic, and for relaxed positivity window local zero density certificate: no record on these objects.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Relaxed positivity with only a count of the window's zeros gains nothing: if \(\Re h\ge-\eta\) in the window and the input is a count bound, then \(\Re h+\eta\) is nonnegative harmonic with the same Poisson representation and the requirement \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_W<4\) returns; any evasion needs the location of the window's zeros. Record. Searched relaxed positivity window local zero density certificate: no match; it is the next entry's first step.
  • Location information that would suffice is, for the line, the goal in the window except at the point; a formal intermediate is a zero-density bound for every bounded window, which density theorems give only for most heights; the known inputs for every height (local growth of \(\zeta\), cancellation in sums over primes) reach widths tending to zero. From the reviewer's memory. Record. The same search: no match.
  • A heuristic: success needs \(h\) small on average at about \(\log\gamma_0\) actual zeros per unit height while large at the point, which suggests exponential type at least \(\tfrac12\log\gamma_0\) with unsigned prime sums. Record. The same search: no match.
  • No named theorem is known to the reviewer for this application; nearest are the extremal problems for the trigonometric-polynomial method and dual limits of linear-programming bounds. Record. Searched zero-free region explicit formula trigonometric polynomial: no match.

Suggestion check. Verified and adopted in the text: the residue derivation of the kernel (the reviewer's two-line derivation used the transform of the hyperbolic secant, which is now proved in the entry); the symmetrization remark, since for real \(g\) with even part \(g_e\) the sum over a set invariant under \(z\mapsto-z\) of \(h\) equals that of the transform of \(g_e\); and the subtraction of located zeros, which is part 3 applied to the remaining multiset. The first suggestion in the list is not verified and is the next entry's test.

Verification gate. No dependency of the record is used in the proof. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the three parts, the control and the reading, and found the lemma correct; corrections, all incorporated: the proof rested on a recalled integral checked only numerically (it is now derived by residues in the entry); the claim that the control showed the constant sharp came from a trivial grid point (replaced by the true statement: sharp in each factor separately, not jointly); "exactly" overstated a one-sided bound; the count \(c=4\) needed its cases; non-even or non-real \(g\) read as an evasion and is not one; an exception that keeps whole-strip positivity, subtracting located zeros, was missing; the conclusion that the method cannot prove the goal is conditional on a local count that is recalled, and is now stated so; compact support is not needed beyond integrability. Process assessment. The lemma was the review's reviewer's proposal and took one short cycle once the explicit formula was seen not to be needed; the control's first quadrature was wrong and its own output showed it. Prevention. The class is a numerical check whose own method is unsound. This instance showed itself by an absurd number; a subtly wrong quadrature would not. The safeguard used here is an independent cross-check: the end-to-end test computes both sides from \(g\) without the kernel formula, so a wrong kernel would not pass both, and the formula is now also proved. I know no mechanical check for the soundness of a quadrature and add none; the framework changes of this turn, the closure paragraph and the tightened hook, answer the stand-in review and are described under Review.

11 October 2026 — Relaxing the positivity to \(-\eta\) in one window, paid for by one count, returns the same condition for the window's zeros; and under two classical count statements and an on-line fraction, the window's weighted count is of order \(\log T\) at a positive proportion of heights

Working proofs of two elementary statements, the second conditional on two count statements as given in a hypothesis file and on a fraction of on-line zeros; they limit a method in one model. Relaxed positivity obstruction. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Chosen. This entry continues the second review's picked lead ahead of the queue's head, as the previous entry's next step named (the queue tool's status: one entry so far, sub-idea open). It bears on off-line exclusion by deciding whether the certificate formulation escapes its obstruction when positivity is relaxed near the point. At the goal's parameters it could show that a count of nearby zeros, which is known, suffices where their location is not; if the obstruction returns, it gives nothing toward the goal.

Owed attempt. The previous entry on this lead named the relaxed form as the next attempt: positivity required only outside a window, and what a certificate then needs. It was made here; its outcome is part 2 of the lemma for one model, with the question's second half re-filed as a sub-idea.

Best outcome. Stated in the Chosen paragraph when the cycle opened: if a count of the zeros in a window sufficed where their location is not known, a relaxed certificate could succeed at fixed \(\delta\) using only the classical local count, which would be an unconditional exclusion of points at fixed distance from the line at the heights where it applies, a result of the kind the goal needs. The outcome found is the opposite, in the one model treated.

Question. The missing implication is an estimate excluding one off-line zero. (a) If \(\Re h\) may be as low as \(-\eta\) inside a window around \(\gamma_0\) and the certificate uses only an upper bound for the number of zeros there, can it succeed where the weighted count of actual zeros in the window is large? (b) What do statements read in this cycle give for that weighted count?

New mathematics. (a) In the model of one depth \(\eta\) and one count for the window: no, the requirement \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_W(\gamma_0)<4\) returns, with \(D_W\) the weighted count over the actual zeros in the window. (b) Under the Riemann–von Mangoldt count on \([T,2T]\) and the local upper count, as assumed in the density project's hypothesis file with their attribution to Titchmarsh: if at least a fraction \(\kappa>0\) of the zeros with ordinate in \((T+1,2T-1]\) is on the line, then \(D_W(\gamma_0)\ge c_W\kappa\log T\) on a subset of \([T,2T]\) of measure at least \(c'_W\kappa T\), with explicit constants. Both are elementary; no novelty is claimed.

Goal progress. Unchanged. With (a) the certificate formulation meets the same condition in a second form; other count-only models and hypotheses on the window's zeros weaker than their location are not examined. With (b) the condition is shown to fail, for a fixed window and conditionally on a positive on-line fraction, at a positive proportion of heights in \([T,2T]\) for points with \(\cos(\pi\delta)>8/m_W(T)\); a lower bound for the count in every window is still only recalled and is not used. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing; it extends the limit of a method. The cycle was spent on it because the relaxed form was the previous entry's open sub-idea and the stand-in review asked that the count not rest on recollection.

General statement. lem:relaxed-positivity-obstruction, for every continuous even real \(g\) of compact support with integrable boundary function bounded below by \(-\eta\), every window, and every multiset of points of the strip; its second part for every \(T\) at least the source's threshold.

Review. The stand-in review after the previous entry raised five objections. (1) A recalled zero count is not evidence: accepted; part (b) below derives an averaged count from two statements read in this cycle, and what remains recalled (a lower bound in every window) is labelled and unused. (2) The review called the line without mechanism while one lead was not run and another falsified by one objection: accepted; the two leads and the unrun bridge are queued for a development cycle each, by the queue tool, in the framework commit after the previous entry. (3) The chat report of the control's wrong quadrature had no Prevention paragraph: accepted; the entry had one and the chat report did not, which the Stop hook's patterns did not catch because the sentence used none of its words; the reply after this entry carries it. (4) The fix named for leads marked passed from memory did not address that class: accepted and fixed; the finisher now requires of every passed review item a statement of its break point and what the test found there; by a scratch count whose output that framework commit's message quotes, of 612 passed items in all notebooks' reviews none had one, so the check binds every new review. (5) "So this method cannot prove the hypothesis" was stated before review, on a recalled count, and for whole-strip positivity only: accepted; the committed entry states it conditionally, and this entry replaces the recalled count, for a positive proportion of heights, by two count statements assumed in a hypothesis file together with an on-line fraction as a hypothesis, and treats one model of the relaxed form.

Statement and proof

Notation as in the strip positivity obstruction: \(g\) continuous, even, real, of compact support, \(h=\widehat g\), \(u(t+iy)=\Re h(t+iy)\), \(\varphi(s)=u(s\pm i/2)\), and \(K_y\) the kernel there, for which \(\tfrac1{2\pi}\int K_y=1\) because \(K_y\) is the transform of \(m_y\) and \(m_y(0)=1\).

Lemma (relaxed positivity obstruction). lem:relaxed-positivity-obstruction.

  1. Suppose \(\varphi\) is integrable and \(\varphi\ge-\eta\) on \(\mathbb R\) for some \(\eta\ge0\). Then \(u\ge-\eta\) on the closed strip, and for all real \(\gamma,\gamma_0\) and \(|y|,|\delta|<1/2\): \(u(\gamma+iy)+\eta\ge\cos(\pi y)\cos(\pi\delta)e^{-\pi|\gamma-\gamma_0|}\,(u(\gamma_0+i\delta)+\eta)\).
  2. In addition let \(W>0\), suppose \(u\ge0\) at every point of the open strip with \(|\Re z-\gamma_0|>W\), let \(Z\) be a multiset of points of the open strip with \(\sum_{\rho\in Z}u(z_\rho)\le B\), let \(n_W\) be the number of its points with \(|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|\le W\) and \(D_W=\sum_{|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|\le W}\cos(\pi y_\rho)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\). If \(c\,u(\gamma_0+i\delta)>B+\eta N\) for some \(c>0\) and some \(N\ge n_W\), then \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_W<c\).
  3. Let \(Z\) be a multiset of points \(\gamma_\rho+iy_\rho\) of the strip, \(N(a,b)\) the number with \(a<\gamma_\rho\le b\), and suppose \(N(t,t+1)\le A_0\log(|t|+3)\) for all real \(t\) and \(|N(T,2T)-\tfrac T{2\pi}\ell(T)|\le C\log T\) for \(T\ge T_0\), with \(\ell(T)=\log\tfrac T{2\pi}+2\log2-1\). Let \(T\ge\max(T_0,2)\), \(W>0\), \(\omega=\min(W,1)\), and suppose at least \(\kappa N(T+1,2T-1)\) of the points with \(T+1<\gamma_\rho\le2T-1\) have \(y_\rho=0\). Then, with \(D_W(\gamma_0)=\sum_{|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|\le W}\cos(\pi y_\rho)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\), \[{1\over T}\int_T^{2T}D_W(\gamma_0)\,d\gamma_0\ \ge\ m_W(T):={2(1-e^{-\pi\omega})\kappa\over\pi}\Bigl({\ell(T)\over2\pi}-{C\log T+2A_0\log(2T+3)\over T}\Bigr),\] \(D_W(\gamma_0)\le4A_0\log(2T+4)\) on \([T,2T]\), and the set of \(\gamma_0\in[T,2T]\) with \(D_W(\gamma_0)\ge m_W(T)/2\) has measure at least \(T\,m_W(T)/(8A_0\log(2T+4))\).

Proof. (1) As \(\varphi\) is integrable and \(G=g\cosh(\cdot/2)\) is continuous and integrable, inversion holds and the previous entry's computation gives \(u(t+iy)=\tfrac1{2\pi}\int\varphi(s)K_y(t-s)\,ds\) (after integrability of \(\varphi\) was established, that proof used nothing else about it). Hence \(u(t+iy)+\eta=\tfrac1{2\pi}\int(\varphi(s)+\eta)K_y(t-s)\,ds\) with \(\varphi+\eta\ge0\), which is nonnegative, and the kernel inequality of the previous entry, integrated against \(\varphi+\eta\), gives the displayed bound. On the boundary \(u=\varphi\ge-\eta\). The hypothesis that \(\varphi\) is integrable is a convenience: the reviewer notes that a bounded harmonic function continuous on the closed strip is the Poisson integral of its boundary values, which I do not prove here. (2) Points of \(Z\) outside the window contribute nonnegatively. For a point inside, by (1), \(u(z_\rho)\ge C_\rho(u_0+\eta)-\eta\) with \(u_0=u(\gamma_0+i\delta)\) and \(C_\rho=\cos(\pi y_\rho)\cos(\pi\delta)e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\). So \(B\ge\cos(\pi\delta)D_W(u_0+\eta)-\eta n_W\), and the hypothesis gives \(c\,u_0>\cos(\pi\delta)D_W(u_0+\eta)+\eta(N-n_W)\ge\cos(\pi\delta)D_Wu_0\), using \(\eta\cos(\pi\delta)D_W\ge0\) and \(N\ge n_W\). If \(u_0\le0\), the left side is at most \(0\) while the middle expression is at least \(0\) because \(u_0+\eta\ge0\), which is impossible; so \(u_0>0\) and \(c>\cos(\pi\delta)D_W\). (3) For a point with \(T+1<\gamma_\rho\le2T-1\), the set of \(\gamma_0\in[T,2T]\) with \(|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|\le\omega\) is the whole interval of radius \(\omega\le1\), so \(\int_T^{2T}1_{|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|\le W}e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}d\gamma_0\ge\int_{-\omega}^{\omega}e^{-\pi|s|}ds=2(1-e^{-\pi\omega})/\pi\). Summing over the on-line points in that range, for which \(\cos(\pi y_\rho)=1\), \(\int_T^{2T}D_W\ge\tfrac{2(1-e^{-\pi\omega})}{\pi}\kappa N(T+1,2T-1)\), and, as \(T+1\le2T-1\), \(N(T+1,2T-1)=N(T,2T)-N(T,T+1)-N(2T-1,2T)\ge\tfrac T{2\pi}\ell(T)-C\log T-2A_0\log(2T+3)\). For the upper bound, \(D_W\le D\), the sum over all points; the points with \(\gamma_0+k<\gamma_\rho\le\gamma_0+k+1\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), have \(e^{-\pi|\gamma_\rho-\gamma_0|}\le e^{-\pi j_k}\) with \(j_k=k\) for \(k\ge0\) and \(-k-1\) for \(k<0\), and number at most \(A_0\log(2T+j_k+4)\) for \(\gamma_0\in[T,2T]\); with \(\log(a+j)\le\log a+j\) for \(a\ge1\), \(j\ge0\), the sum is at most \(2A_0\sum_{j\ge0}e^{-\pi j}(\log(2T+4)+j)\le4A_0\log(2T+4)\), since \(\sum_je^{-\pi j}<1.05\) and \(\sum_jje^{-\pi j}<0.05\). Finally, if \(S\) is the set where \(D_W\ge m_W/2\), then \(Tm_W\le\int_T^{2T}D_W\le4A_0\log(2T+4)|S|+Tm_W/2\). \(\square\)

Degenerate cases. With \(\eta=0\), (2) is weaker than the previous lemma's part 3, since only the window's points are counted. A window containing no point of \(Z\) has \(D_W=0\) and (2) is no restriction. \(N\) much larger than \(n_W\) only strengthens the hypothesis. No function \(g\) with \(u\) negative somewhere in the window and nonnegative outside it is exhibited: the nonvacuity of the relaxed class is not shown, and the lemma says only what such functions could not do. In (3), \(\kappa=0\) gives \(m_W=0\); for small \(T\) the quantity \(m_W(T)\) may be negative and the statement is empty; as \(W\to0\), \(m_W\) is about \(2W\kappa\ell(T)/2\pi\), so the lemma gives no obstruction for windows shorter than about \(1/\log T\). The source's \(A_0\ge1\) is not used.

Nonvacuity. Parts 1 and 2: \(g=G/\cosh(\cdot/2)\) with \(G(u)=\max(0,1-|u|/4)\), whose transform \(\varphi(s)=4(\sin(2s)/(2s))^2\) is nonnegative and integrable; \(\eta=0\), \(W=1\), \(\gamma_0=0\), \(\delta=0\), \(Z=\{5\}\) on the real axis, \(B=u(5)\), \(N=0\), \(c=4\): then \(u(0)=\int g>0\) and \(|u(5)|\le u(0)\) because \(g\ge0\), so \(4u(0)>B\), and the conclusion \(D_W=0<4\) holds. This witness has \(\eta=0\); an input with \(u\) actually negative in the window is not exhibited, as said above. Part 3: the multiset of the points \(\gamma_n>2\pi e\) on the real axis defined by \(F(\gamma_n)=n\), \(F(t)=\tfrac t{2\pi}\log\tfrac t{2\pi}-\tfrac t{2\pi}\), has \(N(T,2T)=F(2T)-F(T)+O(1)=\tfrac T{2\pi}\ell(T)+O(1)\) and \(N(t,t+1)\le F'(t+1)+1\), so both count hypotheses hold with \(\kappa=1\).

What it says

The relaxed certificate, in one model. A certificate that allows \(\Re h\ge-\eta\) in a window of half-width \(W\) around \(\gamma_0\), with one \(\eta\) for the whole window, must pay \(\eta\) for every zero that may lie there, and to do so without knowing where they are it uses an upper bound \(N\) for their number; it succeeds if \(4\Re h(\gamma_0+i\delta)>B+\eta N\). Part 2 with \(c=4\): success requires \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_W(\gamma_0)<4\), the condition of the whole-strip form restricted to the zeros of the window. In this model the freedom gained by letting \(\Re h\) be negative is offset by Harnack's inequality applied to \(\Re h+\eta\). Other count-only models are not covered: different depths \(\eta_j\) with counts \(N_j\) in sub-regions, or paying only where \(\Re h\) is actually negative. The reviewer sketches an extension to the first (the same conclusion with the count over the region of deepest negativity), listed below and unverified.

What would escape, as far as this goes. Short windows: for \(W\) below about \(1/\log T\) part 3 gives nothing, and the reviewer's remark that the zeros outside the window then obstruct unless \(\eta\) is large and the count bounded is unverified. Information on the window's zeros beyond one count: a region known to hold few zeros, or zeros confined to a set where \(h\) is small. Whether such a hypothesis can be weaker than a zero-free window is the second half of the sub-idea and is not answered here.

The count, from two statements as given in a hypothesis file. The two hypotheses of part 3 are the fields of the structure named H-RvM in the density project's hypothesis file, where they are assumed, not proved, with the attribution "Titchmarsh, Theorems 9.4 and 9.2"; I read lines 55 to 72 of that file and neither Titchmarsh nor the file's definitions of its counting function and of \(\ell\), which I take to be as written in its docstring. With them and an on-line fraction \(\kappa\) on \((T+1,2T-1]\) (which follows from a fraction \(\kappa'\) on \((T,2T]\) with a loss of \(2A_0\log(2T+3)\) points), \(D_W\ge m_W(T)/2\) on a set of heights of measure at least a constant times \(\kappa(1-e^{-\pi\omega})T\). So, conditionally on \(\kappa>0\) and for a fixed window, at a positive proportion of heights neither form of certificate in the models above can exclude a point with \(\cos(\pi\delta)>8/m_W(T)\). The density import reports a fraction of this kind; I did not re-read its statement and nothing here is based on its value. Without a fraction part 3 is empty.

Sub-ideas

  • Extend part 2 to the general count-only model: depths \(\eta_j\) on regions \(R_j\) of the window with counts \(N_j\); prove or break the reviewer's claim that success forces \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_{R_{\max}}<c\) for the region of deepest negativity, and treat negativity confined to a narrower strip by the rescaled kernel. Exhibit one admissible \(g\) with \(\Re h\) negative in a window and nonnegative outside, or show there is none.
  • Answer the second half of the earlier sub-idea: with \(\Re h\ge0\) on the line in the window and \(\ge-\eta\) off it, state the bound on the number of off-line zeros in the window that a certificate needs, and compare it with a zero-free window (the reviewer expects a bound of order one, a pointwise local density statement).

Proved so far: with positivity on the whole strip, or relaxed to \(-\eta\) in one window with one count, success requires \(\cos(\pi\delta)D_W(\gamma_0)<4\). I drafted a closure on this and the review did not uphold it: the reason given needed the count of part 3 while saying it did not, other count-only models are open, and half of the sub-idea is unanswered. 11 October 2026 — The heat flow as a filter on methods: a strip contraction proved for polynomials with its rate, one source's statements read, and the filter stated in the form that survives review; the item stays open on which structure of the primes a premise uses

Working proof of the polynomial case of a contraction attributed to de Bruijn, whose paper is unread, with a reading of one arXiv source's statements; no result about zeta zeros. Polynomial strip contraction. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Chosen. This entry takes the queued heat-flow item ahead of the queue's head: the certificate lead has had two entries in a row without bearing (the queue tool's guidance at this cycle's start), the rule asks for a different item, and the second review left this one without the development cycle the rules require before the line is called without mechanism. It bears on off-line exclusion only as a test of proposed mechanisms.

Best outcome. Written before the work: at the goal's own parameters this item excludes no zero. Its best outcome is to say which property of \(\xi\) a proof must use because the flowed functions lack it, and so to remove from the route the recorded premises that do not use it.

Question. The missing implication is an estimate excluding one off-line zero. What do the theorems on the flow say, as stated in a source; does the contraction hold with a rate in the model of finite configurations; and is any recorded premise defined for the flowed function, so that its survival under a backward flow can be tested?

New mathematics. The polynomial case of a strip contraction, with its rate: for a real polynomial \(p\) and \(p_t=e^{-tD^2}p\), the largest imaginary part \(M(t)\) of a zero satisfies \(M(t)^2\le\max(0,M(0)^2-2t)\), and where the top zero \(x+iy\) is simple, \(\tfrac{d}{dt}y^2=-2-4y\sum_j(y-y_j)/|z-z_j|^2\) over the other zeros except the conjugate, so real zeros near the pair speed the contraction. The registry has no record of it (search below). I take it to be classical and attribute it to de Bruijn from memory, his paper unread; the read source states the dynamics for real zeros only, and that zeros are real for \(t\ge1/2\). No novelty is claimed.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The filter, in the form the review left standing: no argument of the shape "a function with property \(P\) has only real zeros" can be valid for a class of functions containing some \(H_t\) with \(t<0\), because by the read source's main theorem those have non-real zeros; so a property that \(H_0\) shares with some backward-flowed \(H_t\) cannot be the only property of \(H_0\) a proof uses. Which recorded premises are of that kind is not decided here. The read lines describe \(H_t\) by an integral and say nothing of a product over primes, from which I had concluded that prime-based premises are undefined for it; the reviewer points out that \(H_t\) keeps a sum over \(n\) and loses only multiplicativity, so the right question is whether a premise uses multiplicativity or only the sum, and that is a sub-idea. Bearing. At the goal's parameters this gives nothing, as stated before the work.

General statement. lem:polynomial-strip-contraction, for every real polynomial of degree at least one and every \(t\ge0\).

What the source states

Read in the TeX source of B. Rodgers and T. Tao, The de Bruijn–Newman constant is non-negative, arXiv 1801.05914: the abstract, the introduction's paragraph on earlier results, the main theorem, and the statement of the theorem on the dynamics of zeros. In its normalization \(H_t(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)\cos(zu)\,du\) with an explicit rapidly decaying \(\Phi\); \(H_t\) is entire, even, real on the real axis, and solves \(\partial_tH_t=-\partial_{zz}H_t\). The introduction states: by results of Pólya, if \(H_t\) has only real zeros then so has \(H_{t'}\) for \(t'>t\); de Bruijn showed the zeros are real for \(t\ge1/2\); Newman showed there is a constant \(\Lambda\le1/2\) such that \(H_t\) has only real zeros exactly when \(t\ge\Lambda\); the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to \(\Lambda\le0\). The main theorem: \(\Lambda\ge0\). The theorem on dynamics, for \(\Lambda<t\le0\) (a range that is empty by the main theorem; it is used there under the assumption to be refuted): the real zeros \(x_k\) move by \(\partial_tx_k=2\sum'_{j\ne k}1/(x_k-x_j)\), a principal-value sum, attributed to Csordas, Smith and Varga. The same passage reports later bounds: \(\Lambda<1/2\) (Ki, Kim and Lee) and, in a footnote, \(\Lambda\le0.22\). The contraction of the strip of zeros with its rate is not stated in the lines read. Not read: de Bruijn's paper, Newman's, Pólya's, those of Csordas, Smith and Varga and of Ki, Kim and Lee, and the proofs.

Statement and proof

Lemma (polynomial strip contraction). lem:polynomial-strip-contraction. Let \(p\) be a polynomial with real coefficients of degree \(n\ge1\), and for real \(t\) put \(p_t=e^{-tD^2}p=\sum_{k\ge0}(-t)^kp^{(2k)}/k!\), so that \(\partial_tp_t=-p_t''\). Let \(M(t)\) be the largest imaginary part of a zero of \(p_t\). Then for \(t\ge0\), \[M(t)^2\le\max\bigl(0,\,M(0)^2-2t\bigr).\] In particular all zeros of \(p_t\) are real for \(t\ge M(0)^2/2\), and if the zeros of \(p\) are real so are those of \(p_t\) for all \(t\ge0\). Moreover, at a time when the zeros of \(p_t\) are simple and \(z=x+iy\), \(y>0\), is a zero, \[{d\over dt}\,y^2=-2-4y\sum_{j}{y-y_j\over|z-z_j|^2},\] the sum over the zeros \(z_j=x_j+iy_j\) other than \(z\) and \(\bar z\); every term is nonnegative when \(y=M(t)\).

Proof. The degree and leading coefficient of \(p_t\) do not depend on \(t\), so the zeros of \(p_t\) are continuous in \(t\) as a multiset, and \(M\) is continuous. Collisions: with \(x=\sqrt t\,w\), \(e^{-tD_x^2}x^k=t^{k/2}e^{-D_w^2}w^k\), so \(t^{-n/2}p_t(\sqrt t\,w)\) tends, uniformly on compact sets as \(t\to\infty\), to the leading coefficient times \(e^{-D_w^2}w^n\), a rescaled Hermite polynomial, which has \(n\) simple real zeros (classical). Hence the discriminant of \(p_t\), a polynomial in \(t\), is not identically zero, and the zeros are simple except at finitely many times. On an interval free of such times each zero \(z_k(t)\) is differentiable, and differentiating \(p_t(z_k(t))=0\) gives \(p_t'(z_k)\dot z_k=p_t''(z_k)\); since \(p''/p'\) at a simple zero \(z_k\) equals \(2\sum_{j\ne k}1/(z_k-z_j)\), \[\dot z_k=2\sum_{j\ne k}{1\over z_k-z_j}.\] For \(z_k=x+iy\), \(\Im\,1/(z_k-z_j)=-(y-y_j)/|z_k-z_j|^2\), and the conjugate zero \(\bar z_k\), present because \(p_t\) is real and \(y>0\), contributes \(-2y/(2y)^2=-1/(2y)\). So \(\dot y=-1/y-2\sum_j(y-y_j)/|z_k-z_j|^2\) over the remaining zeros, which is the displayed formula after multiplying by \(2y\). If \(y=M(t)>0\), every \(y-y_j\ge0\), so \(\tfrac d{dt}y^2\le-2\). On such an interval where \(M>0\), \(M^2\) is the maximum of finitely many differentiable functions, each with derivative at most \(-2\) wherever it attains the maximum; hence \(M(t_2)^2-M(t_1)^2\le-2(t_2-t_1)\) for \(t_1<t_2\) in the interval, and by continuity of \(M\) the same holds across the finitely many collision times as long as \(M>0\) in between. If \(M(t_1)=0\) and \(M(t_2)>0\) for some \(t_2>t_1\), let \(t_*\) be the last time before \(t_2\) with \(M=0\); on \((t_*,t_2]\), \(M>0\) and \(M^2\) is nonincreasing, so \(M(t_2)^2\le M(t_*)^2=0\), a contradiction. Together these give the bound and the two consequences. \(\square\)

Degenerate cases. A constant polynomial is excluded (no zeros). Degree one: \(p_t=p\), one real zero, \(M=0\). \(p=x^2+\delta^2\): \(p_t=x^2+\delta^2-2t\), \(M(t)^2=\delta^2-2t\) exactly, so the bound is attained and the constant \(2\) cannot be improved without the sum's extra term. A polynomial with non-real coefficients is outside the statement: the conjugate zero is used. For \(t<0\) nothing is claimed; the review's saved test found non-real zeros appearing from a real configuration at \(t=-0.2\) and not at \(-0.02\), \(-0.05\), \(-0.1\) (output).

Nonvacuity. The hypotheses are satisfied by any real polynomial; with a non-real pair, \(p=(x^2+\delta^2)\prod_{j}(x-x_j)\) with real \(x_j\). The review's saved test (not rerun) computed, for \(\delta\in\{0.2,0.5,1\}\) and seven real zeros at spacing \(1\) or \(3\), the first time at which all zeros are real as \(0.32\) to \(0.97\) of \(\delta^2/2\), smaller for the denser spacing, in agreement with the bound and with the sign of the extra term (output).

What the filter says

The principle. By the read main theorem, for every \(t<0\) the function \(H_t\) has a non-real zero. So an implication "property \(P\) implies only real zeros" cannot hold on any class of functions that contains some \(H_t\), \(t<0\), with \(P\). A proof of the goal may use properties that \(H_0\) shares with the backward-flowed functions, but it must also use one that they lack. This is the content of the remark, quoted in the source from Newman, that the goal, if true, is only barely so.

Applied to the record: what is and is not decided. The item proposed the strip positivity certificate as a premise that makes sense for the flowed function. Two things must be told apart. The test function \(g\) and its sum over a configuration of zeros need no primes, and the two obstruction lemmas (lem:strip-positivity-obstruction, lem:relaxed-positivity-obstruction) hold for every configuration, so they are indifferent to the flow. The certificate's bound \(B\), however, comes from the explicit formula with the sign of \(g\) at prime powers, which is where the primes enter. Whether the certificate's inequality on the zero side survives a backward flow of a finite configuration is well posed and was not tried. For the other recorded premises (the continuation criterion's saving, a bound for the prime side of the Gram form) I do not decide whether they are defined for \(H_t\): the flow multiplies \(\Phi\), itself a sum over \(n\), by a Gaussian, so a sum over \(n\) persists and what is lost is multiplicativity; the question for each premise is which of the two it uses. The criteria equivalent to reality of the zeros (the half-plane sign, the structure-function inequality, Li's positivity) fail for \(H_t\), \(t<0\), by the theorem, provided \(H_t\) satisfies each criterion's hypotheses, which I did not check; the filter adds nothing to their being restatements. For quantitative premises with slack on a bounded range of heights, the polynomial model suggests survival for a short time, zeros moving at bounded speed away from collisions; for premises over all heights the model says nothing, the speed being unbounded over heights. This is an untested hypothesis and no conclusion rests on it.

The rate, read at the scale of the zeros. The displayed formula shows that an off-line pair among dense real zeros is absorbed faster than the bound \(\delta^2/2\): each real zero at horizontal distance \(d\) adds \(4y^2/(d^2+y^2)\) to the rate of decrease of \(y^2\). For real zeros at spacing \(g\) and \(y\) well above \(g\) the sum is of order \(y/g\), which would give a time of order \(\delta g\); this ignores the motion of the real zeros during the absorption and is not proved, for finite or infinite configurations. It is the first sub-idea.

Sub-ideas

  • Prove the absorption rate for a finite configuration: for a pair at height \(y\) over \(N\) real zeros that stay within horizontal distance \(D\), \(\tfrac d{dt}y^2\le-2-4Ny^2/(D^2+y^2)\); bound how far the real zeros move meanwhile; and read the statement of the theorem of Ki, Kim and Lee that the source cites beside the bound \(\Lambda\le0.22\) (recalled by the reviewer as: for each \(t>0\) all but finitely many zeros of \(H_t\) are real), to see whether off-line exclusion for each fixed \(t>0\) is a finite-height problem and what the limit \(t\to0\) costs.
  • For each recorded prime-side premise (the continuation criterion's probe, the Gram form's prime sum, the certificate's sign at prime powers) decide whether it uses multiplicativity or only a sum over \(n\) that persists under the Gaussian multiplier; a premise of the second kind is shared by the backward-flowed functions and cannot be the only one used. Also test, in the polynomial model, whether a certificate inequality on the zero side survives a short backward flow.

Done: the statements as given in one secondary source, and the polynomial contraction. Not done: de Bruijn's own statement, and the decision for any named premise; I drafted a disposal of the item and the review did not uphold it. The next attempt on this item is the second sub-idea. For the lemma and the sub-ideas the registry was searched for heat flow polynomial zeros imaginary part contraction strip de Bruijn, and for backward heat equation Gaussian multiplier theta sum multiplicativity Euler product: no record on these objects.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Prime-free is too coarse a line: \(H_t\) is \(H_0\) convolved with a Gaussian, \(\Phi\) is a sum over \(n\), so the flowed function keeps a sum over \(n\) and loses multiplicativity; the filter's sharper form is that a premise using only the sum survives and cannot suffice. Record. Searched backward heat equation Gaussian multiplier theta sum multiplicativity Euler product: no match; second sub-idea.
  • Forward flow as a tool: the goal holds exactly when \(H_t\) has only real zeros for every \(t>0\); with the recalled theorem of Ki, Kim and Lee each fixed \(t>0\) would be a finite-height problem. Record. Searched heat flow polynomial zeros imaginary part contraction strip de Bruijn: no match; first sub-idea.
  • A provable finite form of the rate, as written in the first sub-idea. Record. The same search: no match.

11 October 2026 — Power sums over consecutive exponents: an interpolation bound proved and applied to the off-axis sum of a cluster of \(n\) pairs over \(2n\) steps, with a loss depending on the gaps between heights; Turán's theorem itself not found in a readable source

Working proof of an elementary lower bound for power sums and its application to a model sum at lattice points; the theorem the item names is unread. Interpolation power-sum bound. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Chosen. This entry takes the queued Turán item ahead of the queue's head: it is the second of the items the second review left without a development cycle, the previous two entries developed two other items, and it bears on off-line exclusion through the cluster half of the obstacle, which is also the head item's subject.

Best outcome. Written before the work: a lower bound for the contribution of a cluster of off-line zeros over a short range of bandwidths, with a loss that is a fixed power of \(T\) at most, would settle the cluster half of the obstacle at the goal's parameters: several off-line zeros near one height could then be treated as one. It would still leave the first half, the estimate itself, untouched.

Question. The missing implication is an estimate excluding one off-line zero. For the sum \(S(s)=\sum_jm_je^{-isw_j}\) over a conjugation-closed cluster of \(n\) off-axis pairs, what lower bound holds at some point of a short range of \(s\), and how does it compare with thm:resonance-free-bandwidth?

New mathematics. An elementary bound by Lagrange interpolation: for points \(z_1,\dots,z_N\) with \(z_k\) different from the others, among any \(N\) consecutive power sums one is at least \(|b_k||z_k|^{m+1}\prod_{j\ne k}|z_k-z_j|/(1+|z_j|)\). Applied to a cluster of \(n\) pairs with heights in an interval of length \(R\ge1\): among the \(2n\) points \(s=\nu\pi/R\), \(m<\nu\le m+2n\), \(m\ge0\), one has \(|S(s)|\ge m_1e^{\delta_1s_1}\sinh(\pi\delta_1/R)\prod_{j\ge2}(0.34\,|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|/R)^2\), with \(s_1=(m+1)\pi/R\) the first point of the range. The interpolation argument is standard (I recall it as the first step of the power-sum method; no source read); no novelty is claimed.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The off-axis sum of a cluster is a power sum with \(2n\) terms, so the count of all zeros does not enter the lemma. Its loss is a product over the distances of the other heights from the leading one. For heights spread evenly over the interval the product is of the form \(c^n\), which for \(n\) of order \(\log T\) is a fixed power of \(T\), the threshold named under Best outcome; for close heights it is small without bound, and that, not the number of pairs, is where this lemma fails. The bound is pointwise at a lattice point, carries \(e^{\delta_1s}\) at the first point of the range and not at the point found, and is not connected to the Gram form's norm. So the best outcome is not reached, and I had first concluded, wrongly, that the loss is beyond any power of \(T\) for \(\log T\) pairs: an arithmetic slip the reviewer caught. The reviewer sketches a gap-free bound provable in a few lines, which would give a power-of-\(T\) loss for any cluster of \(O(\log T)\) pairs at lattice points; it is unverified and is the next attempt. Bearing. At the goal's parameters nothing is proved about the form; the cycle was spent on it because the item was owed a development cycle and the head item asks the same question.

General statement. lem:interpolation-power-sum-bound, for every \(N\ge1\), all complex \(z_1,\dots,z_N\) with \(z_k\ne z_j\) for \(j\ne k\), all complex coefficients and every integer \(m\ge0\); its application for every cluster as described.

Statement and proof

Lemma (interpolation power-sum bound). lem:interpolation-power-sum-bound. Let \(z_1,\dots,z_N\) be complex numbers, \(k\) an index with \(z_k\ne z_j\) for all \(j\ne k\), \(b_1,\dots,b_N\) complex, and \(s_\nu=\sum_jb_jz_j^{\nu}\). Then for every integer \(m\ge0\), \[\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\ \ge\ |b_k|\,|z_k|^{m+1}\prod_{j\ne k}{|z_k-z_j|\over1+|z_j|}.\]

Proof. Let \(P(z)=\prod_{j\ne k}(z-z_j)/(z_k-z_j)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_iz^i\), so \(P(z_k)=1\) and \(P(z_j)=0\) for \(j\ne k\). Then \(\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}a_is_{m+1+i}=\sum_jb_jz_j^{m+1}P(z_j)=b_kz_k^{m+1}\), so \(|b_k||z_k|^{m+1}\le\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\cdot\sum_i|a_i|\). The coefficients of \(\prod_{j\ne k}(z-z_j)\) have absolute values summing to at most \(\prod_{j\ne k}(1+|z_j|)\), hence \(\sum_i|a_i|\le\prod_{j\ne k}(1+|z_j|)/|z_k-z_j|\). \(\square\)

Application to a cluster. Let \(w_j^{\pm}=\gamma_j\pm i\delta_j\), \(j=1,\dots,n\), with real \(\gamma_j\) in an interval of length \(R\ge1\), \(\gamma_j\ne\gamma_1\) for \(j\ge2\), \(0<\delta_j<1/2\), \(\delta_1=\max_j\delta_j\), and multiplicities \(m_j\ge1\). Let \(S(s)=\sum_jm_j(e^{-isw_j^+}+e^{-isw_j^-})\). Then for every integer \(m\ge0\) there is an integer \(\nu\) with \(m<\nu\le m+2n\) and \[\bigl|S(\nu\pi/R)\bigr|\ \ge\ m_1\,e^{(m+1)\pi\delta_1/R}\,\sinh(\pi\delta_1/R)\,\prod_{j\ge2}\Bigl({2|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|\over(1+e^{\pi/2})R}\Bigr)^{2}.\] If all the \(|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|\) are at least \(g\), the product is at least \((2g/((1+e^{\pi/2})R))^{2n-2}\). As \(|S(-s)|=|S(s)|\), the same holds for negative multiples.

Proof. Put \(h=\pi/R\) and \(\zeta_j^{\pm}=e^{-ihw_j^{\pm}}\), of modulus \(e^{\pm h\delta_j}\) and argument \(-h\gamma_j\). \(S(\nu h)\) is the power sum \(s_\nu\) of these \(2n\) numbers with coefficients \(m_j\). Apply the lemma with \(z_k=\zeta_1^{+}\), of modulus \(E=e^{h\delta_1}\le e^{\pi/2}\); it differs from \(\zeta_1^-\) in modulus and from the others in argument, since \(0<h|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|\le\pi\). The partner contributes \(|\zeta_1^+-\zeta_1^-|/(1+|\zeta_1^-|)=2\sinh(h\delta_1)/(1+e^{-h\delta_1})\ge\sinh(h\delta_1)\). For \(j\ge2\), with \(|r_1e^{i\theta}-r_2|^2=(r_1-r_2)^2+4r_1r_2\sin^2(\theta/2)\), \(r_1=E\), \(r_2=e^{\pm h\delta_j}\ge1/E\) (as \(\delta_j\le\delta_1\)), and \(\theta=h(\gamma_1-\gamma_j)\), \(|\theta|\le\pi\): \(|\zeta_1^+-\zeta_j^{\pm}|\ge2|\sin(\theta/2)|\ge2|\theta|/\pi=2|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|/R\), and \(1+|\zeta_j^{\pm}|\le1+E\le1+e^{\pi/2}\). Each \(j\ge2\) gives two such factors. \(\square\)

Degenerate cases. \(N=1\): the lemma is the identity \(|s_{m+1}|=|b||z|^{m+1}\). \(z_k=0\) gives the trivial bound \(0\). A point coinciding with \(z_k\) is excluded, and the bound degenerates as a point approaches \(z_k\); the other points may coincide with each other. Two points \(\pm1\) with unit coefficients: the bound is \(1\) and the true maximum over two consecutive exponents is \(2\). In the application, \(n=1\) gives \(m_1e^{(m+1)h\delta}\sinh(h\delta)\) against the true \(2m_1\cosh(\nu h\delta)\); a height equal to \(\gamma_1\) is excluded; \(R\ge1\) and \(\delta_j<1/2\) are used only for the constant. The bound ignores the positivity of the multiplicities: for two simple pairs at heights \(\pm g/2\) with equal \(\delta\), \(S(s)=4\cosh(s\delta)\cos(sg/2)\), which is not small for small \(g\) at moderate \(s\), while the bound's factor is of order \(g^2\).

Nonvacuity. The lemma's hypotheses hold, for instance, for \(z=(2,1,1/2)\), \(b=(1,1,1)\), \(m=0\), \(k=1\): the bound is \(2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{1.5}{1.5}=1\) and \(s_1=3.5\). The application's hypotheses hold for \(n=2\), \(\gamma=(0,1)\), \(R=1\), \(\delta=(0.3,0.2)\), unit multiplicities, \(m=0\): the bound is \(e^{0.3\pi}\sinh(0.3\pi)(2/(1+e^{\pi/2}))^2\), about \(0.33\).

What it says

The loss, in the goal's parameter. The factor lost against \(m_1e^{\delta_1s_1}\) is \(\sinh(\pi\delta_1/R)\prod_{j\ge2}(0.34|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|/R)^2\). For \(n\) heights spread evenly over the interval, \(|\gamma_1-\gamma_j|/R\) runs over multiples of \(1/(n-1)\) and the product is at least \(((n-1)!/(n-1)^{n-1})^2\,0.34^{2n-2}\), which is \(c^n\) with an absolute \(c\); for \(n\) of order \(\log T\) this is a fixed power of \(T\). With only a least gap \(g\) the bound \((0.34g/R)^{2n-2}\) can be as small as \(n^{-2n}\) when \(g/R\) is about \(1/n\), which for \(n\) of order \(\log T\) is \(T^{-O(\log\log T)}\). For close heights the factor is small without bound. A further factor is hidden in the exponent: the point found may be as late as \(s_1+(2n-1)\pi/R\), so against \(e^{\delta_1s}\) at that point the bound loses up to \(e^{-(2n-1)\pi\delta_1/R}\).

Comparison with the recorded theorem. thm:resonance-free-bandwidth, as registered: for the flat window on the complete grid, off-axis points at pairwise distinct heights with least gap \(g\), total multiplicity \(M\) and largest distance \(\delta_*\) of multiplicity \(m_*\); for \(\Lambda_1\ge1/\delta_*\) and \(H\ge4M^2/(gm_*^2)\) some \(\Lambda\in[\Lambda_1,\Lambda_1+H]\) has \(\|B_\Lambda\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\ge\tfrac{\sqrt2}4m_*e^{\delta_*\Lambda}/(\delta_*\Lambda)-M\). I compared with this registered summary and did not re-read the theorem's full record in this cycle. The two statements concern different quantities, a norm of the off-axis part of the form there and \(|S|\) at one lattice point here; with that said, the theorem has no multiplicative loss and a range that grows like \(1/g\), and the lemma has a range \(2n\pi/R\) independent of the gaps and a loss that depends on them. prop:subset-sum-resonance shows that at a single bandwidth a real loss of order \(b^{-2k}\) occurs for \(2^k\) points at resonant heights; the lemma says that over \(2n\) consecutive lattice points such a loss cannot persist beyond the stated factor, and I do not compare constants.

Not connected to the form's norm. The Gram model's second moment is a mean square of \(S\); passing from one lattice point to it needs a bound for the derivative of \(S\) near the point, which is not carried out here.

The theorem the item names. I searched arXiv for a statement of Turán's second main theorem; two papers that cite it were fetched as TeX sources (math/0607238 and math/0609271) and searched for the phrase, and neither states it (the first cites it to the 1984 book, Chapter 8). A request for the book is filed. The reviewer's recollection of the statement is listed below; nothing here rests on it.

Sub-ideas

  • Prove the reviewer's gap-free bound: for points of modulus at least one, interpolate \(z^{-(m+1)}\) in Newton form, bound the coefficient sum by \(\sum_{k<N}\binom{m+k}{k}2^k\le(2e(m+N)/N)^N\), and deduce \(\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\ge(N/(2e(m+N)))^N|\sum_jb_j|\); then the cluster consequence after rescaling by \(e^{h\delta_1}\), with the extra factor \(e^{-2\delta_1s}\) it costs, and the range of \(\delta_1s\) in which that is a power of \(T\).
  • Pass from a lattice point to the mean square: bound \(|S'|\) by the multiplicities and \(e^{\delta_1s}\), deduce a lower bound for the mean square of \(S\) over a short range, and state the corollary for the off-axis part's norm beside thm:resonance-free-bandwidth, re-reading that theorem's full record.
  • When the book's statement is available, restate the application with Turán's second main theorem, whose normalization by the largest modulus avoids the extra factor.

Follow-up. Continuing: the item asked to read the theorem in a source and to apply it to the off-line zeros alone, comparing with the recorded theorem. The application and comparison are made with a proved substitute; the theorem's own statement is unread. The next attempt on this item needs no source: the first sub-idea. Record search. The registry was searched for power sum lower bound Lagrange interpolation consecutive exponents Vandermonde, and for Turan power sum lower bound window (in the review's cycle): no record on these objects; the registered results on this question are thm:resonance-free-bandwidth and prop:subset-sum-resonance.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • Turán's second main theorem, from the reviewer's memory: for \(1=|z_1|\ge\dots\ge|z_n|\), \(\max_{m<\nu\le m+n}|s_\nu|\ge2(n/(8e(m+n)))^n\min_j|b_1+\dots+b_j|\), partial sums in order of decreasing modulus, no gaps needed; constant improved to \(4e\) by later authors. Record. Searched Turan power sum lower bound window: no match; third sub-idea.
  • Its consequence for the cluster: positive coefficients make the least partial sum at least \(\min m_j\), the step is free, and some \(s\in(s_0,2s_0]\) has \(|S(s)|\ge2(16e)^{-2n}\min_jm_j\,e^{\delta_1s}\), a power-of-\(T\) loss for \(n=O(\log T)\). Suggestion check. 11 October 2026 — A gap-free bound for power sums of points of modulus at least one, proved by Newton interpolation; for a cluster it bounds the off-axis sum below only by \(e^{-\delta_1s}\), so it cannot detect an off-line cluster; the conversion to the goal's parameter is written out for this bound and, conditionally, for two others

Working proof of an elementary lower bound for power sums; its consequence for the model sum is too weak to use. Gap-free power-sum bound. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Chosen. This entry continues the queued Turán item ahead of the queue's head, as the previous entry's next step named (the queue tool's status: one entry, three sub-ideas open); it bears on off-line exclusion through the cluster half of the obstacle.

Owed attempt. The previous entry on this item named the gap-free bound by Newton interpolation as the next attempt. It is made here: the bound is proved, and its consequence for the cluster is worked out and found too weak.

Best outcome. Written before the work: a lower bound for the off-axis sum of a cluster of \(n\) pairs, at some point of a short range of \(s\), of size at least \(e^{\delta_1s}\) times a loss that is small against the gain \(e^{\delta_1s}\) itself for \(n\) up to a multiple of \(\log T\); at the goal's parameters that would let a cluster of off-line zeros near one height be treated as its leading pair.

Question. The missing implication is an estimate excluding one off-line zero. Does the reviewer's few-line route give a gap-free lower bound for power sums, and what does it give for the cluster when the loss is converted to the goal's parameter?

New mathematics. One lemma: for complex \(z_1,\dots,z_N\) of modulus at least one (not necessarily distinct), complex \(b_j\) and \(m\ge0\), \(\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\ge|\sum_jb_j|/\sum_{k<N}\binom{m+k}{k}2^k\). The reviewer recalls this as Turán's first main theorem with a constant due to Makai and de Bruijn; I have read neither, and claim no novelty.

Goal progress. Unchanged. For the cluster the lemma needs all moduli at least one, which is arranged by dividing by the smallest modulus, and the bound it returns is \(|S(s)|\ge2Me^{-\delta_1s}/A\): below the benchmark \(e^{\delta_1s}\) by the square of the gain, before the factor \(A\). Converted. In the goal's parameter: the gain of the leading pair at bandwidth \(s=\theta\log T\) is \(e^{\delta_1s}=T^{\delta_1\theta}\), at most \(T^{\theta/2}\); this lemma's bound is \(2MT^{-\delta_1\theta}/A\), which is below \(2M\), the upper bound for the same sum when every \(\delta_j=0\); it is a true statement of non-cancellation and holds equally for points on the axis, so it cannot separate an off-axis cluster from an on-axis one and is useless for detection. The previous entry's bound keeps the exponential, at the first point of its range, and loses \(c^{2n}\) for evenly spread heights; Turán's second theorem, as the reviewers recall it and with a constant \(c\) that is absolute only when the starting exponent is of the order of the number of points and the multiplicities are positive, would do so for arbitrary heights. For such a bound, a loss below the gain \(T^{\delta_1\theta}\) needs \(2n\log(1/c)<\delta_1\theta\log T\), that is fewer than \(\epsilon\log T\) pairs with \(\epsilon=\delta_1\theta/(2\log(1/c))\); this is a necessary condition for use, not a sufficient one, since nothing connects the lattice point to the form's norm yet. Statement and proof

Lemma (gap-free power-sum bound). lem:gap-free-power-sum-bound. Let \(z_1,\dots,z_N\) be complex numbers with \(|z_j|\ge1\), \(b_1,\dots,b_N\) complex, \(s_\nu=\sum_jb_jz_j^{\nu}\), and \(m\ge0\) an integer. Then \[\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\ \ge\ {|b_1+\dots+b_N|\over A(m,N)},\qquad A(m,N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\binom{m+k}{k}2^k\ \le\ 2^{N-1}\binom{m+N}{N-1}.\] For \(m\ge N-1\), \(A(m,N)\le(2e(m+N)/N)^N\).

Proof. First let the \(z_j\) be distinct. Let \(f(z)=z^{-(m+1)}\) and let \(P\) be the polynomial of degree less than \(N\) with \(P(z_j)=f(z_j)\) for all \(j\). Writing \(P(z)=\sum_{i<N}a_iz^i\), \(\sum_ia_is_{m+1+i}=\sum_jb_jz_j^{m+1}P(z_j)=\sum_jb_j\), so \(|\sum_jb_j|\le\max_{m<\nu\le m+N}|s_\nu|\sum_i|a_i|\). Newton's form is \(P(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}f[z_1,\dots,z_{k+1}]\prod_{j\le k}(z-z_j)\), and the coefficients of \(\prod_{j\le k}(z-z_j)\) have absolute sum at most \(\prod_{j\le k}(1+|z_j|)\). The divided differences: for \(g_t(z)=1/(z-t)\), \(g_t[z_1,\dots,z_{k+1}]=(-1)^k/\prod_{j\le k+1}(z_j-t)\), by induction on \(k\) from \((1/(a-t)-1/(b-t))/(a-b)=-1/((a-t)(b-t))\) and the recursion for divided differences. For \(|t|<1\le|z_j|\), \(g_t(z)=\sum_{m\ge0}t^mz^{-(m+1)}\) and \(\prod_j(z_j-t)^{-1}=\prod_jz_j^{-1}\sum_{m\ge0}h_m(1/z_1,\dots,1/z_{k+1})t^m\), with \(h_m\) the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial; divided differences being finite linear combinations of values, comparing coefficients of \(t^m\) gives \[f[z_1,\dots,z_{k+1}]=(-1)^k\prod_{j\le k+1}z_j^{-1}\;h_m(1/z_1,\dots,1/z_{k+1}).\] \(h_m\) in \(k+1\) variables has \(\binom{m+k}{k}\) monomials, each of modulus at most one here, so \(|f[z_1,\dots,z_{k+1}]|\le\binom{m+k}{k}\prod_{j\le k+1}|z_j|^{-1}\). Hence the \(k\)-th Newton term contributes at most \(\binom{m+k}{k}|z_{k+1}|^{-1}\prod_{j\le k}(1+|z_j|)/|z_j|\le\binom{m+k}{k}2^k\) to \(\sum_i|a_i|\), which gives \(\sum_i|a_i|\le A(m,N)\). If some points coincide, merge them, adding their coefficients: the power sums and \(\sum b_j\) are unchanged, the number of points drops to some \(N'\le N\), and the bound for \(N'\) implies the one for \(N\), since the maximum is over a larger set of exponents and \(A(m,N')\le A(m,N)\). The bounds for \(A\): \(2^k\le2^{N-1}\) and \(\sum_{k<N}\binom{m+k}{k}=\binom{m+N}{N-1}\); and \(\binom{m+N}{N-1}=\binom{m+N}{N}\tfrac N{m+1}\le(e(m+N)/N)^N\) when \(m+1\ge N\). \(\square\)

Degenerate cases. \(N=1\): \(A=1\) and the bound is \(|b||z|^{\nu}\ge|b|\), true as \(|z|\ge1\). \(\sum b_j=0\): the bound is trivial. All points equal: merged to one, bound \(|\sum b_j|\). A point of modulus below one is outside the statement, and the bound can fail there (one point \(z=1/2\), \(b=1\): \(s_\nu=2^{-\nu}<1\)). \(z=(1,-1)\), \(b=(1,1)\), \(m=0\): \(A=1+2=3\), bound \(2/3\), true maximum over \(\nu=1,2\) is \(2\).

Nonvacuity. \(z=(2,1,-1)\), \(b=(1,1,1)\), \(m=0\), \(N=3\): \(A=1+2+4=7\), bound \(3/7\); \(s_1=2\). All moduli are at least one.

The cluster, and the conversion

Consequence for the cluster. With the previous entry's notation, \(S(\nu h)=\sum_jm_j((\zeta_j^+)^\nu+(\zeta_j^-)^\nu)\), \(|\zeta_j^{\pm}|=e^{\pm h\delta_j}\), for any step \(h>0\) and with no condition on the heights. The numbers \(E\zeta_j^{\pm}\), \(E=e^{h\delta_1}\), have modulus at least one, and their power sums are \(E^{\nu}S(\nu h)\) with coefficient sum \(2M\), \(M=\sum_jm_j\). The lemma gives, for every \(m\ge0\), some \(\nu\in(m,m+2n]\) with \[|S(\nu h)|\ \ge\ {2M\,e^{-\nu h\delta_1}\over A(m,2n)}.\] The exponential has the wrong sign: the normalization by the smallest modulus is what the lemma's hypothesis forces, and the bound then only propagates the value \(S(0)=2M\) forward against the decay of the small terms. Against the benchmark \(m_1e^{\delta_1s}\) it loses \(e^{-2\delta_1s}\) besides \(A\). The application uses neither the positivity of the multiplicities (only \(M\ne0\)) nor \(\delta_j<1/2\), and the pairing only to identify the smallest modulus. \(A(m,2n)\) is a power of \(T\) when \(n\log((m+2n)/n)=O(\log T)\), which is moot given the sign of the exponential.

What a usable bound must have. The conversion in the Goal progress paragraph shows two requirements: the normalization must be by the largest modulus, so that the bound carries \(e^{+\delta_1s}\) (the previous entry's interpolation bound has this, at the cost of the gaps; Turán's second theorem as recalled has it without that cost); and the loss \(c^{2n}\) must be below the gain \(e^{\delta_1s}\), which for \(s=\theta\log T\) restricts \(n\) to less than \(\delta_1\theta\log T/(2\log(1/c))\). A cluster of more pairs than that, within one window, is beyond these three bounds; whether a loss \(c^{2n}\) is forced for such clusters is not shown. The reviewer's example below shows it is forced when multiplicities are unrestricted, and that the example needs total multiplicity \(2^n\), more than a window can hold.

New mathematics. The splitting of each term into a weight and a shifted factor is a property of this way of writing the series and not of \(H_t\): the factor's growth cancels the weight. General statement. lem:flowed-series-expansion, for every real \(t<0\) and every complex \(z\); and for \(t=0\), every \(z\) with \(\Im z<-1\).

What the source states

Read in the TeX source of arXiv 1801.05914, beyond the lines read in the item's previous entry: \(H_0(z)=\tfrac18\xi(\tfrac12+\tfrac{iz}2)\); \(H_0(z)=\int_0^\infty\Phi(u)\cos(zu)\,du\) with \(\Phi(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}-3\pi n^2e^{5u})\exp(-\pi n^2e^{4u})\), the sum converging absolutely for negative \(u\) also, and \(\Phi\) even by Poisson summation; and, in the section on asymptotics, "as \(\Phi\) is even" \(H_t(z)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R}e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)e^{izu}du\) and, by Fubini's theorem "which can be justified when \(t<0\)", a display of \(H_t\) as half a sum over \(n\) of two oscillatory integrals. I read these lines directly and not the proofs around them.

Statement and proof

Lemma (flowed series expansion). lem:flowed-series-expansion. Let \(\varphi_n(u)=(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}-3\pi n^2e^{5u})\exp(-\pi n^2e^{4u})\), so \(\Phi=\sum_n\varphi_n\), and for real \(t\le0\) let \(K_t(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)e^{izu}\,du\) and \(F_t(w)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{tv^2}\varphi_1(v)e^{iwv}\,dv\), which is entire for \(t<0\) and defined for \(\Im w<5\) when \(t=0\). Then: (1) \(\varphi_n(u)=n^{-1/2}\varphi_1(u+\tfrac12\log n)\). (2) For \(t<0\) and every complex \(z\), and for \(t=0\) and \(\Im z<-1\), \[K_t(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-1/2-iz/2}\,e^{t\log^2n/4}\,F_t(z+it\log n),\] the series converging absolutely. (3) For \(t\ne0\) the weights \(a_t(n)=e^{t\log^2n/4}\) are not multiplicative: \(a_t(6)\ne a_t(2)a_t(3)\).

Proof. (1) With \(v=u+\tfrac12\log n\): \(e^{9v}=n^{9/2}e^{9u}\), \(e^{5v}=n^{5/2}e^{5u}\), \(e^{4v}=n^2e^{4u}\), so \(\varphi_1(v)=n^{1/2}\varphi_n(u)\). (2) Absolute convergence. \(|\varphi_n(u)|\le(2\pi^2n^4e^{9u}+3\pi n^2e^{5u})\exp(-\pi n^2e^{4u})\), and \(\sum_nn^4e^{-\pi n^2x}\le C(1+x^{-5/2})\), \(\sum_nn^2e^{-\pi n^2x}\le C(1+x^{-3/2})\) for \(x>0\), so \(\sum_n|\varphi_n(u)|\le C'e^{9|u|}(1+e^{-10u})\), at most exponential in \(|u|\); for \(t<0\) the factor \(e^{tu^2}\) makes \(\sum_n\int e^{tu^2}|\varphi_n(u)|e^{|u||\Im z|}du\) finite for every \(z\). For \(t=0\) and \(c=-\Im z>1\), \(\int|\varphi_n(u)|e^{cu}du=n^{-1/2-c/2}\int|\varphi_1(v)|e^{cv}dv\) by (1), finite because \(\varphi_1\) decays like \(e^{5v}\) at \(-\infty\) and faster than any exponential at \(+\infty\), and \(\sum_nn^{-(1+c)/2}\) converges. So the sum and the integral may be exchanged. For the \(n\)-th term put \(u=v-\tfrac12L\), \(L=\log n\): \(\varphi_n(u)=n^{-1/2}\varphi_1(v)\), \(e^{tu^2}=e^{tv^2}e^{-tLv}e^{tL^2/4}\), \(e^{izu}=e^{izv}e^{-izL/2}\), and \(e^{-tLv}e^{izv}=e^{i(z+itL)v}\); hence the term equals \(n^{-1/2-iz/2}e^{tL^2/4}F_t(z+itL)\). (3) \(\log^26-\log^22-\log^23=2\log2\log3\ne0\). \(\square\)

Consequence, with the source's evenness. As the source states \(\Phi\) even, \(H_t=\tfrac12K_t\), which gives the formula under New mathematics. At \(t=0\), \(K_0(z)=\zeta(s)F_0(z)\) for \(\Im z<-1\), \(s=\tfrac12+\tfrac{iz}2\). Check against \(H_0=\xi(s)/8\): with \(x=\pi e^{4v}\) and \(e^{izv}=e^{(2s-1)v}\), \(F_0(z)=\tfrac12\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2+2)-\tfrac34\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2)\tfrac s2(\tfrac s4-\tfrac14)=\tfrac{s(s-1)}8\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2)\), so \(K_0/2=\zeta(s)\tfrac{s(s-1)}{16}\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2)=\xi(s)/8\), with the source's \(\xi(s)=\tfrac{s(s-1)}2\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2)\zeta(s)\). This is an independent check of the lemma and of the factor \(\tfrac12\).

The form is not canonical. The \(n\)-th factor \(F_t(z+it\log n)\) depends on \(n\), and the maximum over \(v\) of \(e^{tv^2+|t|Lv}\) is \(e^{|t|L^2/4}\), which cancels the weight \(e^{tL^2/4}\); so the non-multiplicativity of the weights is a feature of this way of writing the series and by itself says nothing about \(H_t\). The reviewer's observation.

Degenerate cases. \(t=0\) and \(-1\le\Im z<5\): the series diverges, as it must, being \(\zeta\) to the left of its abscissa; for \(\Im z\ge5\) the terms are undefined. \(n=1\): the term is \(F_t(z)\). \(t>0\) is outside the statement: the convergence argument uses the Gaussian decay of \(e^{tu^2}\) for \(t<0\), and the source justifies its own exchange for \(t<0\) only. Part 3 fails at \(t=0\), where the weights are all \(1\).

Nonvacuity. Every \(t<0\) and every \(z\) satisfy the hypotheses, for instance \(t=-1\), \(z=0\); at \(t=0\), \(z=-2i\) gives \(s=3/2\).

The three premises, by their definitions

  • The Gram form's prime side, read in the density project's definitions: \(P_X(\tau)=-\tfrac1\pi\sum_{n\le X}\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}\cos(\tau\log n)\), with \(\Lambda\) the von Mangoldt function. These are the Dirichlet coefficients of \(-\zeta'/\zeta\); they are supported on prime powers and nonnegative because \(\zeta\) is an Euler product. Uses multiplicativity.
  • The continuation criterion of the seven-eighths source, as recorded in this notebook's criterion reading: a Mellin integral of the reciprocal \(L\)-function. The reciprocal's coefficients are the Möbius function by the Euler product. Which property of them the criterion's premise uses (boundedness, multiplicativity, or only that the reciprocal is a Dirichlet series) is not determined in this cycle: I rely on the recorded reading's summary and did not re-read the record or the source.
  • The certificate's sign condition \(g(\log n)\ge0\) at prime powers (second review): it controls the sign of \(\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}g(\log n)\), again through \(\Lambda\ge0\). Uses multiplicativity.

What is and is not concluded. The first and third premises use properties of \(\Lambda\) (support on prime powers, nonnegativity) that the Euler product supplies; the second is undetermined. The flowed function, by the lemma, is a series over \(n\) which in this form has non-multiplicative weights and shifted factors, a form that is not canonical. I do not prove that its logarithmic derivative or reciprocal has no expansion that could play the same role: that would need a zero-free half-plane for it and the structure of \(F_t\), which are not examined; the reviewer's heuristic, listed below, is that the series is dominated by its first term only in a region that widens logarithmically and not in a half-plane. So the filter is not shown to remove any of the three. The Best outcome paragraph, written before the work, said that the premises would then be "of the kind a proof must use"; that goes beyond the filter, which says only that a proof must use some property failing for the backward-flowed functions, of which multiplicativity is a candidate and not shown to be the one.

Goal-level route review; no result about zeta zeros. Third exclusion review. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

New mathematics. None. Statements read in four sources supplied by the user during the previous cycle are quoted below with what was and was not read.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Bearing. This review gives nothing at the goal's parameters; it selects the next test.
