Decisive test. On the queued check entry-2026-10-11-prime-side-form:s2, under the first review's lead on Weil's positivity criterion. Setting, from the prime-side form, where it is a reviewer's unverified argument: with the weight \(\varphi*\varphi\) on the primes the tested density is \(D_L(\tau)=\sum_\rho K_L(\tau-z_\rho)\) with \(K_L\ge0\) on the real line, so it is nonnegative for all \(L\) and \(\tau\) if all zeros are on the line. An earlier draft of this test asked whether a cluster of off-line pairs can keep \(D_L\) nonnegative at particular lengths; this review's reviewer gave an argument, unverified, that it cannot (for a finite configuration the pairs of largest distance contribute a negative value of size about \(e^{\delta L}c/L\) at every large \(L\), with \(c>0\) a constant of the configuration), so that question as posed appears to have a trivial answer and is not the test. The test is quantitative, in three parts. (a) Prove or break that argument with an explicit constant: a lower bound for \(c\) in terms of the number \(n\) of pairs at the largest distance, their multiplicities and the ratio of their least gap to \(\delta\). (b) With the real zeros' positive contribution bounded above by their local count, of order \(\log T\) at height \(T\), state the threshold length \(L_0(\delta,T,c)\) beyond which an off-line pair at distance \(\delta\) forces \(D_L(\tau)<0\) somewhere near its height; the reviewer's estimate is \(L_0\) about \((\log\log T)/\delta\). (c) State the premise this leaves on the prime side: a one-sided pointwise bound \(D_L(\tau)\ge-\,C\log T\) for a prime sum of length \(e^{L_0}\), about \((\log T)^{1/\delta}\), at every \(\tau\) near \(T\); and compare it with the trivial bound for that sum and with the strip positivity obstruction. Outcomes: if \(c\) is bounded below by a quantity that does not decay faster than polynomially in \(L\) for clusters with \(O(\log T)\) points, the goal has a one-sided pointwise form at lengths that are powers of \(\log T\), a premise of a different shape from a mean square at lengths beyond \(T\); if \(c\) can be as small as \(e^{-\delta L}\) for admissible clusters, or the threshold in (b) is a power of \(T\), the one-sided form has no advantage and the lead closes with that reason. Trivial cases. At \(\delta=\tfrac12\) the trivial bound \(e^{L/2}\) for the prime sum at \(L=2\log\log T\) is \(\log T\), so the premise in (c) holds trivially there, as it must: no zero has real part \(1\); the test has content only for \(\delta<\tfrac12\), where the trivial bound \((\log T)^{1/(2\delta)}\) exceeds \(\log T\). A solitary pair has \(n=1\) and \(c\) explicit, and decides only the normalization. Replacing \(\varphi\) by a translate or dilate changes \(L\) and \(\tau\) and not the outcome. Power. The recorded results bear on (a): by prop:endpoint-moment-order a cluster's sum at one length never vanishes to all orders, and by cor:maximal-cancellation-order it can lose a factor \(b^{-(n-1)}\) for equal distances, which for \(n\) of order \(\log T\) and \(b=\delta L\) of order \(\log\log T\) is \((\log\log T)^{-c'\log T}\), smaller than any power of \(\log T\): so the recorded mechanism already threatens the first outcome for clusters as large as the local count allows, and the test must say whether the one-sided quantity inherits that loss or only a constant. The strip positivity obstruction limits certificates nonnegative on a strip; here nonnegativity is on the line alone, so it does not apply as stated, and (c) is to say whether its count \(4/\cos(\pi\delta)\) reappears. Best outcome. Written before the work, with the premise the review asked to have stated: the best outcome is a proved statement that an off-line pair at distance \(\delta\) forces \(D_L(\tau)<0\) near its height at every length \(L\) beyond a threshold of order \((\log\log T)/\delta\), with a constant that clusters cannot destroy. The goal would then follow from a one-sided pointwise bound, \(D_L(\tau)\ge-C\log T\) for all \(\tau\) near \(T\), which on the prime side is an upper bound for a smoothed sum \(\sum_{n\le e^{L}}\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}(1-\log n/L)\cos(\tau\log n)\) of length about \((\log T)^{1/\delta}\). That premise is not available by any method on record, so at the goal's own parameters the best outcome gives a reformulation at short lengths and no estimate.

Architecture test. The sixth review named three parts. (a) Prove or break, with an explicit constant in terms of the number of pairs, their multiplicities and the ratio of gap to distance, that a cluster forces a negative value of size about \(e^{\delta L}c/L\) at every large \(L\): proved in a weaker form. For finite configurations at one distance the off-line part has such a value with \(c\) bounded below through the least eigenvalue of an explicit Gram matrix, independently of \(L\), once \(L\) is beyond a threshold that depends on that eigenvalue (prop:cluster-negativity-constant); the constant in terms of \(n\), the multiplicities and the gaps, which the test asked for, is not obtained. The entry also shows that the negative part is bounded above by a multiple of (width over distance)\(^k\) where \(k\) moments vanish (prop:one-sided-inherited-loss), which answers the question the test's Power paragraph put: the one-sided quantity inherits the loss and not only a constant. The test's two outcomes, a threshold that stays a power of \(\log T\) for clusters as large as the local count allows or one that becomes a power of \(T\), are not decided. (b) The threshold: for a pair in a configuration with least gap \(8\delta\) it is \(b\ge\log(7.6+2.8\,b^2N/m)\) with \(N\) the local count of real points (prop:separated-pair-negativity), about \((\log\log T)/\delta\) if \(N\) is of order \(\log T\); for clusters none is obtained beyond the constant's lower bound. (c) The prime-side premise is stated below, conditionally on the source's explicit-formula hypothesis; the strip positivity obstruction's hypothesis does not hold for this kernel.

Question. For a finite conjugation-closed configuration, how negative must the one-sided density be, at which lengths, and what do clusters do to it?

New mathematics. A lemma and three propositions for the Fejér kernel and off-line pairs at one distance, with a numerical control. The cluster constant is far from sharp.

Setting

\(K_L(w)=2(1-\cos Lw)/(Lw^2)\) for complex \(w\), so \(K_L(t)=L\operatorname{sinc}^2(tL/2)\ge0\) for real \(t\); it is \(\widehat\varphi(w)^2/L\) for the flat window on \([-L/2,L/2]\). A finite conjugation-closed configuration: real points \(\gamma\) with multiplicities, and off-line pairs \(\gamma_j\mp i\delta\), \(1\le j\le n\), at pairwise distinct heights and one distance \(\delta>0\), multiplicities \(m_j>0\), \(M=\sum m_j\), \(S^2=\sum m_j^2\), \(b=\delta L\). The one-sided density is \[D_L(\tau)=\sum_zm_zK_L(\tau-z)=R(\tau)+D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau),\qquad R(\tau)=\sum_{\gamma\ \mathrm{real}}m_\gamma K_L(\tau-\gamma)\ge0,\quad D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)=\sum_jm_j\,2\Re K_L(\tau-\gamma_j+i\delta).\] Put \[G(\tau)=\sum_jm_j\frac{e^{-iL(\tau-\gamma_j)}}{(\tau-\gamma_j+i\delta)^2},\qquad Y(\tau)=\sum_j\frac{m_j}{(\tau-\gamma_j)^2+\delta^2},\qquad P(y)=\sum_jm_je^{-iy\gamma_j}.\] Unequal distances are outside this entry.

The decomposition

Lemma (one-sided density decomposition). lem:one-sided-density-decomposition. In the Setting, for every real \(\tau\): (i) \(D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)=-\dfrac{2e^{b}}L\Re G(\tau)+E(\tau)\) with \(|E(\tau)|\le6Y(\tau)/L\); (ii) \(G(\tau)=-\displaystyle\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}P(x-L)e^{i(x-L)\tau}dx\); (iii) \(|G(\tau)|\le Y(\tau)\le M/\delta^2\); (iv) if \(N(\ell)\) bounds the number of real points, with multiplicity, in every interval of length \(\ell\), then \(R(\tau)\le\tfrac73L\,N(2\pi/L)\).

Proof. (i) For \(w=t+i\delta\), \(\cos Lw=\tfrac12e^{b}e^{-itL}+\tfrac12e^{-b}e^{itL}\), so \(K_L(w)=(2-e^{b}e^{-itL}-e^{-b}e^{itL})/(Lw^2)\) and \(2\Re K_L(w)=-\tfrac{2e^{b}}L\Re\tfrac{e^{-itL}}{w^2}+2\Re\tfrac{2-e^{-b}e^{itL}}{Lw^2}\); the last term is at most \(6/(L|w|^2)\) in modulus. Sum over \(j\) with \(t=\tau-\gamma_j\). (ii) For \(t\) real, \(\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}e^{ixt}dx=(\delta-it)^{-2}=-(t+i\delta)^{-2}\); multiply by \(m_je^{-iLt}\) with \(t=\tau-\gamma_j\) and sum: \(e^{i(x-L)(\tau-\gamma_j)}=e^{i(x-L)\tau}e^{-i(x-L)\gamma_j}\). (iii) is the triangle inequality. (iv) \(K_L(t)\le\min(L,4/(Lt^2))\). The real points with \(|\tau-\gamma|<2\pi/L\) number at most \(2N\) and contribute at most \(L\) each; those with \(2\pi k/L\le|\tau-\gamma|<2\pi(k+1)/L\), \(k\ge1\), number at most \(2N\) and contribute at most \(4/(L(2\pi k/L)^2)=L/(\pi^2k^2)\) each. So \(R\le2NL(1+\tfrac1{\pi^2}\cdot\tfrac{\pi^2}6)=\tfrac73NL\). \(\square\)

A separated pair

Proposition (separated pair negativity). prop:separated-pair-negativity. In the Setting let \(b\ge2\pi\), let \(j\) be one of the pairs, \(m'\) the largest multiplicity among the other pairs, and suppose all gaps between consecutive heights are at least \(g\ge8\delta\max(1,\sqrt{m'/m_j})\) (no condition if \(n=1\)). Then at \(\tau_*=\gamma_j+\pi/L\) \[\Re G(\tau_*)\ge0.42\,\frac{m_j}{\delta^2},\qquad D_L(\tau_*)\le R(\tau_*)-\frac{m_j}{L\delta^2}\big(0.84\,e^{b}-6.36\big).\] With (iv) of the lemma, \(D_L(\tau_*)<0\) as soon as \(0.84\,e^{b}>6.36+\tfrac73b^2N(2\pi/L)/m_j\).

Proof. Put \(x=\pi/b\le\tfrac12\), so \(\pi/L=x\delta\). The term \(j\) of \(G(\tau_*)\) is \(m_je^{-i\pi}/(x\delta+i\delta)^2=-m_j/(\delta^2(x+i)^2)\), with real part \(m_j(1-x^2)/(\delta^2(1+x^2)^2)\ge m_j\cdot0.75/(1.5625\,\delta^2)=0.48\,m_j/\delta^2\). The \(k\)-th height on either side of \(\gamma_j\) is at distance at least \(kg\) from it, and \(|\tau_*-\gamma_l|\ge kg-\pi/L\ge kg-\delta/2\ge\tfrac{15}{16}kg\), because \(g\ge8\delta\) gives \(\delta/2\le g/16\). So \[\sum_{l\ne j}\frac{m_l}{(\tau_*-\gamma_l)^2+\delta^2}\le2m'\Big(\frac{16}{15}\Big)^2\frac{\zeta(2)}{g^2}\le\frac{3.75\,m'}{g^2}\le\frac{3.75\,m_j}{64\,\delta^2}\le0.059\,\frac{m_j}{\delta^2},\] using \(g^2\ge64\delta^2m'/m_j\). Hence \(\Re G(\tau_*)\ge(0.48-0.059)m_j/\delta^2\ge0.42\,m_j/\delta^2\), and \(Y(\tau_*)\le m_j/\delta^2+0.059\,m_j/\delta^2\le1.06\,m_j/\delta^2\), so by (i) \(D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau_*)\le-\tfrac{2e^{b}}L\cdot0.42\tfrac{m_j}{\delta^2}+\tfrac{6.36\,m_j}{L\delta^2}\). The last sentence follows from (iv): \(R\le\tfrac73LN\), and \(\tfrac73LN<\tfrac{m_j}{L\delta^2}(0.84e^{b}-6.36)\) is the stated inequality. \(\square\)

A first draft of the hypothesis asked only that the other heights be at distance \(g\) from \(\gamma_j\); that does not bound how many sit there, and the statement now asks for the least gap. The reviewer then found that the proof also needs \(g\ge8\delta\), which the hypothesis did not give when \(m'<m_j\); the maximum with \(1\) was added. Whether the statement holds without it is not decided; the control has equal multiplicities and does not test it.

A cluster

Proposition (cluster negativity constant). prop:cluster-negativity-constant. In the Setting let \(H\) be the \(n\times n\) matrix \(H_{jl}=2/(2\delta+i(\gamma_j-\gamma_l))^3\), \(W=\max\gamma_j-\min\gamma_j\), and \[J=\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-2\delta x}|P(x-L)|^2dx,\qquad A_1=\frac{\pi\delta^2J}M,\qquad\varepsilon=2\pi Le^{-b}M.\] Then \(H\) is Hermitian positive definite, \(J\ge\lambda_{\min}(H)S^2>0\) for every \(L\), and \[\sup_\tau\Re G(\tau)\ \ge\ c:=\frac{A_1/4-\varepsilon/2}{W+16M/A_1}.\] Consequently, where \(c>0\), some \(\tau\) within \(8M/A_1\) of a height has \(D_L(\tau)\le R(\tau)-\tfrac{2e^{b}}Lc+\tfrac{6M}{L\delta^2}\). The lower bound \(\lambda_{\min}(H)S^2\) for \(J\) depends on the heights and \(\delta\) only, so \(c\) is bounded below uniformly in \(L\) once \(\varepsilon\le A_1/4\): no cluster makes the off-line part of the density nonnegative at arbitrarily large lengths.

Proof. With \(a_j=m_je^{iL\gamma_j}\), \(P(x-L)=\sum_ja_je^{-ix\gamma_j}\) and \(J=\sum_{j,l}a_j\overline{a_l}\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-2\delta x}e^{-ix(\gamma_j-\gamma_l)}dx=\sum_{j,l}a_j\overline{a_l}H_{jl}\). This is the squared norm in \(L^2(0,\infty)\) of \(\sum_ja_jf_j\), \(f_j(x)=xe^{-\delta x}e^{-ix\gamma_j}\), and the \(f_j\) are linearly independent for distinct \(\gamma_j\); so their Gram matrix, the transpose of \(H\), is positive definite, with the same eigenvalues as \(H\), and \(J\ge\lambda_{\min}(H)\sum|a_j|^2=\lambda_{\min}(H)S^2\). By (ii), \(G(\tau)=-\int_0^\infty h(x)e^{i(x-L)\tau}dx\) with \(h(x)=xe^{-\delta x}P(x-L)\), continuous and integrable with \(h(0)=0\); and \(G\) is integrable and bounded by (iii). Three facts follow. Plancherel: \(\int|G|^2d\tau=2\pi\int_0^\infty|h|^2=2\pi J\). The integral of \(G^2\): \(G\) has spectrum in \([-L,\infty)\) with density \(-h(y+L)\) at frequency \(y\), and \(\overline G\) has density \(-\overline{h(L-y)}\), so \(\int G^2d\tau=\int G\,\overline{\overline G}\,d\tau=2\pi\int_{-L}^{L}h(L+y)h(L-y)dy=2\pi e^{-2b}\int_{-L}^{L}(L^2-y^2)P(y)P(-y)dy\), which is \(\ge0\) because \(P(-y)=\overline{P(y)}\), the \(m_j\) being real. And inversion at frequency \(0\): \(\int G\,d\tau=-2\pi h(L)=-2\pi Le^{-b}P(0)=-\varepsilon\). So \(\int(\Re G)^2=\tfrac12\int|G|^2+\tfrac12\Re\int G^2\ge\pi J\), and since \(|\Re G|\le M/\delta^2\), \(\int|\Re G|\ge\pi J\delta^2/M=A_1\). With \(\int\Re G=-\varepsilon\), the positive part has \(\int(\Re G)^+=\tfrac12(\int|\Re G|-\varepsilon)\ge\tfrac12(A_1-\varepsilon)\). Let \(U\) be the set of \(\tau\) within \(\varrho=8M/A_1\) of some height; it lies in an interval of length \(W+2\varrho\), and outside it \(|G|\le\sum_jm_j/(\tau-\gamma_j)^2\), so \(\int_{U^c}|G|\le2M/\varrho=A_1/4\). Hence \(\int_U(\Re G)^+\ge A_1/4-\varepsilon/2\) and \(\sup_U\Re G\ge(A_1/4-\varepsilon/2)/(W+16M/A_1)\). The consequence is (i) and (iii) of the lemma at a point of \(U\) where \(\Re G\ge c\) (the supremum of a continuous function on the closure, or use \(c\) reduced by any positive amount). \(\square\)

Proposition (one-sided inherited loss). prop:one-sided-inherited-loss. In the Setting put \(\theta_j=L(\gamma_j-\gamma_1)\), \(\nu_r=\sum_jm_je^{iL\gamma_j}\theta_j^r\), let \(k\) be the least \(r\) with \(\nu_r\ne0\) and \(c_k=\sum_jm_j|\theta_j|^k\). Then for every real \(\tau\) \[|G(\tau)|\le\frac{(k+1)\,c_k}{\delta^2\,b^{k}},\qquad D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\ \ge\ -\frac{2e^{b}}L\cdot\frac{(k+1)c_k}{\delta^2b^{k}}-\frac{6M}{L\delta^2}.\] These \(\nu_r\) are the complex conjugates of the moments of prop:endpoint-moment-order, with that entry's bandwidth \(\Lambda\) equal to the length \(L\) here (both are the length of the window's support), so \(k\) is the same number and \(k\le n-1\) by that proposition. Since \(c_k/b^k=\sum_jm_j(|\gamma_j-\gamma_1|/\delta)^k\), the bound is \(M\) times a power of the cluster's width over \(\delta\); it is a power \(b^{-k}\) of the bandwidth when the gaps are multiples of \(1/L\), as in the resonant examples, where the second moment loses \(b^{-2k}\).

Proof. \(P(x-L)=\sum_ja_je^{-ix\gamma_j}=e^{-ix\gamma_1}\sum_ja_je^{-i(x/L)\theta_j}\). By Taylor's formula \(|e^{iy}-\sum_{r<k}(iy)^r/r!|\le|y|^k/k!\) for real \(y\); summing against \(a_j\) and using \(\nu_r=0\) for \(r<k\), \(|P(x-L)|\le c_k(x/L)^k/k!\). By (ii), \(|G(\tau)|\le\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}c_kx^k/(k!L^k)dx=c_k(k+1)!/(k!L^k\delta^{k+2})\). The second inequality is (i) with (iii). \(\square\)

What it says, and the prime side

  • The decisive test. A cluster cannot make the off-line part of the density nonnegative at large lengths, and the reviewer's argument is confirmed in a quantitative form: the constant is bounded below through \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\), which depends only on the heights and the distance. But the one-sided form does not escape the cluster loss: at resonant lengths the negative part is smaller by \(b^{-k}\), the same moments deciding. The difference from the second moment is in what the premise is, not in how clusters behave.
  • How weak the cluster constant is. \(c\) is of order \(J^2\delta^4/M^3\) while the true supremum is of order \(\sqrt J\) in the examples; the control shows ratios from \(10^2\) to \(10^{10}\). For separated pairs the direct proposition replaces it. A lower bound for \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\) for a cluster of \(n\) points in a window of height about \(\delta\), with \(n\) as large as the local count allows, is not obtained; by the inherited loss it cannot be better than a power of the gaps over \(\delta\), and whether the resulting threshold stays a power of \(\log T\) or becomes a power of \(T\) is the open part of the test.
  • The prime side, conditional. For the flat window \(K_L(\tau-z)=\widehat\varphi(z-\tau)^2/L\), so \(L\,D_L(\tau_k)\) is the diagonal entry at a grid height of the zero side of the density source's form. By that source's explicit-formula hypothesis, which I have not read, and for the flat window in place of its tapered one, this equals the prime-side diagonal, which by lem:prime-side-form-bound has prime part \(-2\sum_n\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}(L-\log n)\cos(\tau_k\log n)\); the diagonal of the archimedean and polar parts is not computed in the record. Under those conditions a lower bound \(D_L(\tau)\ge-X\) is an upper bound for the smoothed prime sum \(\sum_{n\le e^{L}}\Lambda(n)n^{-1/2}(1-\log n/L)\cos(\tau\log n)\), whose trivial bound is of order \(e^{L/2}\). By prop:separated-pair-negativity a separated pair at distance \(\delta\) is excluded near \(\tau\) by \(X\) below about \(0.84\,me^{\delta L}/(L\delta^2)\): against the trivial bound this is nothing for \(\delta\ge\tfrac12\) and a saving of \(e^{(1/2-\delta)L}\) for \(\delta<\tfrac12\), at any length beyond the threshold. With \(N(2\pi/L)\) of order \(\log T\), an assumption about zeros I have not read in a source, the threshold is \(b\) about \(\log\log T+2\log b\), so the sums have length \(e^{L}\) about \((\log T)^{(1+o(1))/\delta}\). So the one-sided premise is a pointwise one-sided bound with a power saving for prime sums of length a power of \(\log T\); the premises in this notebook's standing position are at lengths that are powers of the height, and no method is on record for this one either.
  • The strip positivity obstruction. lem:strip-positivity-obstruction concerns test functions whose transform has nonnegative real part on the line at height \(\tfrac12\), the edge of the strip; the ceiling \(4/\cos(\pi\delta)\) on the count is how the route reviews summarize its consequence, not part of the registered statement. Here the kernel is nonnegative on the real line only and grows like \(e^{\delta L}/(L|w|^2)\) off it, so that hypothesis fails and no such ceiling appears: the count of real points enters only through \(R\le\tfrac73LN\), which the exponential beats at the threshold. The cost has moved to the prime side.

Degenerate cases. \(n=1\): the separated proposition has no condition, \(G(\tau)=me^{-iL(\tau-\gamma)}/(\tau-\gamma+i\delta)^2\), \(J=m^2/(4\delta^3)\), \(c=\pi^2m/(1024\delta^2)\) up to \(\varepsilon\), against the true supremum near \(m/\delta^2\). No off-line pair: \(G=0\), \(D=R\ge0\), and the propositions have no content, \(M=0\) being excluded by \(m_j>0\). \(b<2\pi\) is excluded from the separated proposition; the cluster proposition holds for all \(L\) but \(c\) is negative when \(\varepsilon>A_1/2\), which happens for small \(b\) (once in the control, at \(b=10\)). Two pairs at the same height are merged by adding multiplicities. Unused: nothing in the lemma; in the cluster proposition positivity of the \(m_j\) is used for \(P(-y)=\overline{P(y)}\) (reality suffices) and \(P(0)=M\).

Nonvacuity. The six configurations of the control satisfy the Setting; the separated one (four simple pairs at gaps \(4.3\), \(4.8\), \(5.9\) with \(\delta=\tfrac12\), so \(8\delta=4\)) satisfies the separated proposition at \(b=10\), \(18.65\) and \(30\).

Numerical control

Script, its expectations written in the header and committed before the first run, and output; \(\delta=\tfrac12\), \(L=20\), \(37.3\), \(60\), six configurations (solitary; two pairs at gap \(\pi/L\); multiplicities \(1,2,1\) and \(1,3,3,1\) at gaps \(\pi/L\); five pairs within height \(0.6\); four separated pairs). \(D_{\mathrm{off}}\) is computed from the complex cosine, \(G\) from its closed form, and \(J\) three ways. A defect of the script found by the control itself: the first run computed the matrix value of \(J\) as \(a^*Ha\) where \(a^*H^{\mathsf T}a\) is right; the two other values of \(J\) agreed with each other to \(10^{-9}\) and disagreed with it by up to \(83\) percent in the two configurations whose weights are not real up to a common phase. Question. How long can a cluster of off-line pairs with bounded multiplicities keep the one-sided density nonnegative, and what lower bound for a cluster's negative part does not depend on its gaps?

New mathematics. A lemma and three propositions. A lattice of real points contributes a constant to the density. Simple pairs on the resonant lattice, in number small against \(e^{b/2}/b\), contribute no more than about one pair's bound. A cluster of \(k+1\) pairs with binomial multiplicities, built for one length, is hidden at that length behind real points of density \(\ell/2\pi\) whenever \(\ell\) exceeds an explicit bound, which with \(k\) about \(b/\pi\) allows \(b\) up to about \(1.47\log\ell\) asymptotically, where a single pair shows from about \(\log\ell\). And the cluster's exponential sum is bounded below near the endpoint by \(M(2eb)^{-n}\), without any condition on gaps.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Converted. Nothing at the goal's parameters. Bearing. None: the statements are in the model. The cycle was spent on it because the answer decides how long the prime sums of the one-sided premise must be; what is obtained is a lower bound for that length for a test at one length, about \((\log T)^{1.47/\delta}\) in place of \((\log T)^{1/\delta}\), and no upper bound.

General statement. prop:binomial-cluster-hiding, for every \(k\ge1\), every length and every lattice spacing \(s\le2\pi/L\); prop:gap-free-cluster-sum for every finite configuration of pairs at one distance with \(b\ge3\).

Setting

As in the previous entry, re-read: \(K_L(w)=2(1-\cos Lw)/(Lw^2)\); off-line pairs \(\gamma_j\mp i\delta\) at one distance with multiplicities \(m_j>0\), \(M=\sum m_j\), \(b=\delta L\); \(D_L=R+D_{\mathrm{off}}\); \(G\), \(Y\), \(P(y)=\sum_jm_je^{-iy\gamma_j}\); and lem:one-sided-density-decomposition: \(D_{\mathrm{off}}=-\tfrac{2e^{b}}L\Re G+E\), \(|E|\le6Y/L\le6M/(L\delta^2)\), \(G(\tau)=-\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}P(x-L)e^{i(x-L)\tau}dx\), hence \(|G(\tau)|\le\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}|P(x-L)|dx\). Here the real points may be infinitely many with a bounded local count, so that \(R\) converges.

A lattice of real points

Lemma (Fejér lattice density). lem:fejer-lattice-density. For \(0<s\le2\pi/L\) and every real \(\tau\), \(\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}K_L(\tau-js)=2\pi/s\). Proof. \(K_L=\widehat\varphi^{\,2}/L\) for the indicator \(\varphi\) of \([-L/2,L/2]\), so \(\int K_L(t)e^{-itv}dt=2\pi(\varphi*\varphi)(v)/L=2\pi(1-|v|/L)_+\). \(K_L\) is continuous with \(K_L(t)\le\min(L,4/(Lt^2))\), and its transform is continuous with compact support, so the Poisson summation formula applies: \(\sum_jK_L(\tau-js)=s^{-1}\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z}2\pi(1-2\pi|q|/(sL))_+e^{2\pi iq\tau/s}\), and for \(2\pi/s\ge L\) only \(q=0\) remains. \(\square\)

So simple real points on a lattice of spacing \(s\), that is \(1/s\) points per unit height, contribute exactly \(R\equiv\ell\) with \(\ell=2\pi/s\); a density of \((\log T)/2\pi\) points per unit height corresponds to \(\ell=\log T\).

Clusters on the resonant lattice

Proposition (lattice saturation). prop:lattice-saturation. Let the off-line pairs be \(N\) simple pairs at heights \(\gamma_0+j\pi/L\), \(0\le j<N\). Then \(|P(x-L)|\le1/\cos(\pi x/(2L))\) for \(0\le x<L\), and for every \(\tau\) \[|G(\tau)|\le\frac1{\delta^2}\Big(1+\frac{3\pi^2}{2b^2}+N\big(1+\tfrac b2\big)e^{-b/2}\Big).\] So at this length \(N\) simple pairs with \(N=o(e^{b/2}/b)\) produce a negative part no larger than \(1+o(1)\) times the bound \(1/\delta^2\) for a single pair, and with \(N\le e^{b/2}/b\) no larger than \(\tfrac32+o(1)\) times it.

Proof. \(e^{-i(x-L)(\gamma_0+j\pi/L)}=e^{-i(x-L)\gamma_0}q^j\) with \(q=-e^{-i\pi x/L}\), so \(|P(x-L)|=|1-q^N|/|1-q|\le2/(2|\cos(\pi x/(2L))|)\). For \(0\le u\le\pi/4\), \(1/\cos u\le1+u^2\) (both sides equal \(1\) at \(0\), and \((1+u^2)\cos u\ge(1+u^2)(1-u^2/2)\ge1\) for \(u^2\le1\)). Split the integral at \(L/2\): on \([0,L/2]\), \(|P|\le1+\pi^2x^2/(4L^2)\), giving at most \(\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}dx+\tfrac{\pi^2}{4L^2}\int_0^\infty x^3e^{-\delta x}dx=\tfrac1{\delta^2}+\tfrac{6\pi^2}{4L^2\delta^4}\); beyond, \(|P|\le N\) and \(\int_{L/2}^\infty xe^{-\delta x}dx=e^{-b/2}(b/2+1)/\delta^2\). \(\square\)

Proposition (binomial cluster hiding). prop:binomial-cluster-hiding. Let \(k\ge1\) and let the off-line pairs be \(k+1\) pairs at heights \(\gamma_0+j\pi/L\), \(0\le j\le k\), with multiplicities \(\binom kj\) (total \(2^k\), largest at most \(2^k\)). Then \(|P(x-L)|=(2|\sin(\pi x/(2L))|)^k\le(\pi x/L)^k\), and for every \(\tau\) \[|G(\tau)|\le\frac{(k+1)!}{\delta^2}\Big(\frac\pi b\Big)^k,\qquad D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\ge-\frac{2e^{b}}{L\delta^2}(k+1)!\Big(\frac\pi b\Big)^k-\frac{6\cdot2^k}{L\delta^2}.\] If in addition the real points are the lattice \(s\mathbb Z\) with \(s\le2\pi/L\) and \(\ell=2\pi/s\), then \(D_L(\tau)\ge0\) for all real \(\tau\) as soon as \[\ell\ \ge\ \frac{2e^{b}}{L\delta^2}(k+1)!\Big(\frac\pi b\Big)^k+\frac{6\cdot2^k}{L\delta^2}.\] For \(b\ge\pi\) and \(k=\lfloor b/\pi\rfloor\) the right side is at most \(\dfrac{2e^2}{L\delta^2}\big(\tfrac b\pi+1\big)^{3/2}e^{(1-1/\pi)b}+\dfrac{6\cdot2^{b/\pi}}{L\delta^2}\).

Proof. \(P(x-L)=e^{-i(x-L)\gamma_0}\sum_j\binom kjq^j=e^{-i(x-L)\gamma_0}(1+q)^k\) with \(q=-e^{-i\pi x/L}\), and \(|1+q|=|1-e^{-i\pi x/L}|=2|\sin(\pi x/(2L))|\le\pi x/L\). So \(|G|\le\int_0^\infty xe^{-\delta x}(\pi x/L)^kdx=(k+1)!\pi^k/(L^k\delta^{k+2})\). The bound for \(D_{\mathrm{off}}\) is the decomposition with \(Y\le M/\delta^2\), \(M=2^k\); the statement with the lattice is the lemma. For the last sentence: \(k!\le e\sqrt k(k/e)^k\) for \(k\ge1\), so \((k+1)!(\pi/b)^k\le(k+1)e\sqrt k\,(k\pi/(eb))^k\le(k+1)e\sqrt k\,e^{-k}\) because \(k\pi\le b\), and \(e^{-k}\le e^{1-b/\pi}\), \((k+1)\sqrt k\le(b/\pi+1)^{3/2}\), \(2^k\le2^{b/\pi}\). \(\square\)

What the two give. Take simple real points on a lattice of spacing \(s\le2\pi/L\), so \(R\equiv\ell=2\pi/s\) with \(\ell\ge L\) (hiding needs only \(R\ge\ell\), not a lattice). A single simple pair: by prop:separated-pair-negativity, \(D_L(\tau_*)\le\ell-(0.84e^{b}-6.36)/(L\delta^2)\) for \(b\ge2\pi\), negative once \(e^{b}>(b\delta\ell+6.36)/0.84\); and by \(|G|\le1/\delta^2\) it is hidden, \(D_L\ge0\), while \(2e^{b}+6\le b\delta\ell\). So a single pair shows from \(b\) about \(\log\ell+\log(b\delta)\) and not before. The binomial cluster built for the length \(L\), with \(k=\lfloor b/\pi\rfloor\), is hidden at that length as long as \(\ell\ge\tfrac{2e^2}{b\delta}(\tfrac b\pi+1)^{3/2}e^{(1-1/\pi)b}+\tfrac{6\cdot2^{b/\pi}}{b\delta}\), which allows \(b\) up to \(\log\ell/(1-1/\pi)=1.467\log\ell\) less terms of order \(\log b\). This is asymptotic: the lower-order terms, \(-\tfrac32\log b-\log(2e^2)\) in the exponent, make the hidden range pass the single pair's threshold only for \(\log\ell\) above roughly \(20\). The cluster's multiplicities are at most \(2^{b/\pi}\), about \(\ell^{0.32}\) at the end of the range; with \(\ell=\log T\) that is within a multiplicity bound of order \(\log T\), which is the bound I take for the multiplicity of a zero without having read it in a source. What this proves is a lower bound and for a test at one length: for each single \(L\) in the range there is a cluster, built for that \(L\), that the density at length \(L\) does not show. It is not proved that one fixed cluster is hidden at all shorter lengths (a rough count of exponents by the reviewer suggests it is, unverified), so a test using several lengths at once is not covered. It is also not proved that the family shows soon after the range: the bound is an upper bound for the negative part, sharp to leading order by the control only for \(b\ge2\pi(k+1)\), and near \(k\approx b/\pi\) the control's ratios are \(0.79\) and \(0.69\); the reviewer's unverified computation with the exact sum gives a range of about \(1.5\log\ell\). And it says nothing about other families. So in the model a test of the one-sided density at a single length must use a length of at least about \(1.47(\log\log T)/\delta\) to see every cluster with multiplicities up to \(\log T\), for \(T\) large enough; whether the length needed is a multiple of \(\log\log T\) or more is not decided.

A lower bound free of gaps

Proposition (gap-free cluster sum). prop:gap-free-cluster-sum. In the Setting let \(n\ge2\) be the number of off-line pairs, \(b\ge3\), and \(W=\max\gamma_j-\min\gamma_j\). Then there is \(x_*\in[1/(2\delta),2/\delta]\) with \[|P(x_*-L)|\ \ge\ p:=\frac{M}{(2eb)^{n}},\qquad\text{and}\qquad J=\int_0^\infty x^2e^{-2\delta x}|P(x-L)|^2dx\ \ge\ \frac{0.073}{\delta^2}\cdot\frac{p^2}4\cdot\min\Big(\frac p{MW},\frac3{4\delta}\Big).\] With prop:cluster-negativity-constant this bounds \(\sup\Re G\) below by an explicit function of \(n\), \(M\), \(W\), \(\delta\) and \(b\) in which no gap appears, positive only for \(b\) large against \(n\) (below).

Proof. Apply lem:gap-free-power-sum-bound (statement and proof re-read) to \(z_j=e^{-ih\gamma_j}\), of modulus \(1\), \(b_j=m_j\), \(N=n\), \(h=1/(n\delta)\) and \(m=\lceil n(b-2)\rceil\): then \(s_\nu=P(\nu h)\), \(\sum b_j=M\), and \(m\ge n-1\) since \(b\ge3\), so \(\max_{m<\nu\le m+n}|P(\nu h)|\ge M/(2e(m+n)/n)^n\ge M/(2eb)^n\), because \(m+n\le n(b-2)+1+n\le nb\). For these \(\nu\), \(\nu h>mh\ge L-2/\delta\) and \(\nu h\le(m+n)h<L-1/\delta+1/(n\delta)\le L-1/(2\delta)\). As the \(m_j\) are real, \(|P(-y)|=|P(y)|\), so with \(x=L-\nu h\) the maximum is attained at some \(x_*\in[1/(2\delta),2/\delta)\). For the integral: with \(\gamma_c\) the midpoint of the heights, \(|P(y)|=|\sum_jm_je^{-iy(\gamma_j-\gamma_c)}|\) and the derivative of the sum inside is at most \(MW/2\) in modulus, so \(|P(x-L)|\ge p/2\) for \(|x-x_*|\le p/(MW)\). The interval \([1/(2\delta),2/\delta]\) has length \(3/(2\delta)\), so on one side of \(x_*\) it contains an interval of length \(\min(p/(MW),3/(4\delta))\) on which \(|P|\ge p/2\); and on \([1/(2\delta),2/\delta]\), \(x^2e^{-2\delta x}\ge\min(e^{-1}/4,4e^{-4})/\delta^2\ge0.073/\delta^2\), the function being unimodal. \(\square\)

How far this goes. The loss \((2eb)^{-n}\) is of the same kind as the binomial example's \((k+1)!(\pi/b)^k\) with \(n=k+1\): a power of \(b\) for each pair. Through \(J\) and the earlier constant \(c=(A_1/4-\varepsilon/2)/(W+16M/A_1)\), which is of order \(J^2\), the bound for \(\sup\Re G\) is of order \((2eb)^{-6n}\) and is positive only when \(A_1/4>\varepsilon/2\), which with \(A_1\) of order \((2eb)^{-3n}\) and \(\varepsilon=2\pi Le^{-b}M\) needs roughly \(b\ge3n\log(2eb)\). For the binomial family at \(n\approx b/\pi\) it is therefore vacuous: it does not show that family at any length near its hidden range. And \(n\) counts every off-line pair of the configuration, not those near one height: the bound is not local. A local version, in which pairs farther than a multiple of \(\delta\) from the height tested do not count, is not proved. If one held, the question for clusters as large as the local count allows would be whether \(n\) pairs in a window of height about \(\delta\), with \(n\) up to about \(\delta\log T\), can lose a factor \((cb)^{-n}\); that would put the threshold at lengths of order \(\log T\log\log T\), beyond powers of \(T\). The binomial family does not do this, its multiplicities being capped; whether a family with bounded multiplicities does is the open half of the review's test. The inequality of Turán and Nazarov that the previous reviewer proposed was not read or used; Turán's Theorem 8.1, which the control's first run tested, is the statement read from the book in an earlier cycle and quoted in the working context, and it is not used either.

Degenerate cases. \(N=1\) in the saturation proposition: \(|P|=1\) and the bound is \(\delta^{-2}(1+3\pi^2/(2b^2)+(1+b/2)e^{-b/2})\), above the exact \(\sup|G|=1/\delta^2\). \(k=0\) is excluded from the hiding proposition; it would be the single pair with the bound \(1/\delta^2\). \(s>2\pi/L\): the lemma fails, the lattice sum oscillating. \(n=1\) is excluded from the gap-free proposition, where \(|P|=m\) exactly. \(b<3\) is excluded there. Unused: in the gap-free proposition distinctness of the heights (the lemma used allows coinciding points); in the hiding proposition \(k\ge1\) (the bounds hold for \(k=0\)) and the lattice (only \(R\ge\ell\) is used).

Nonvacuity. The control's configurations: \(N=2,5,40\) simple pairs and \(k=1,3,6,8\) at \(b=12,20,30\) with \(\delta=\tfrac12\); for the hiding statement at \(b=30\), \(k=8\): \(s=2\pi/\ell\) with \(\ell=7.5\cdot10^{9}\) satisfies \(s\le2\pi/L\).

Numerical control

Script, its expectations written in the header and committed before the first run, and output. \(G\) and \(D_{\mathrm{off}}\) are evaluated from their definitions on a grid in \(\tau\), the lattice sum by direct summation of \(8\cdot10^5\) terms, \(P\) at the sample points directly. Between the two runs the statement tested for the sampled lower bound was changed from a published theorem's form to this notebook's lemma, which is stronger; the first run is kept and the other statements and all expectations are unchanged. Results of the second run. The saturation bound holds in all nine cases; with \(\delta=\tfrac12\) a single pair's bound is \(4\), and forty pairs give \(\sup|G|\) between \(2.09\) and \(2.14\). The binomial bound holds in all twelve cases and is nearly attained where \(b\ge2\pi(k+1)\), as expected (ratios \(0.988\), \(0.995\), \(0.960\); expected at least \(0.3\)); elsewhere the ratio falls to \(0.16\). 11 October 2026 — The single-bandwidth loss at unequal distances by complex moments, an inequality at every bandwidth whose leading term gives the order when the scaled heights and deficits are held fixed; and, by analogy with the registry lead's collision lemma, an upper bound for the least eigenvalue of a cluster's Gram matrix by the width to the power \(2(n-1)\)

Working proofs in the abstract complete-grid model; nothing is proved about actual zeta zeros. Complex moment order. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, low effort).

Question. What is the order of the cancellation at one bandwidth among off-line pairs at unequal distances, and does anything in the registry's statements on colliding roots transfer?

New mathematics. A proposition, a corollary and a lemma. The loss at one bandwidth is governed, for arbitrary distances, by the moments of the weights \(m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}e^{-i\Lambda\gamma_j}\) against the complex numbers \(\Lambda(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)-i\Lambda\eta_j\), \(\eta_j\) being the deficit of the \(j\)-th distance below the largest. Points far below the largest distance drop out, with an explicit error. And for \(n\) pairs at one distance within a width \(W\), the least eigenvalue of the normalized Gram matrix of the many-pair bound is at most \((\Lambda W)^{2(n-1)}/(n((n-1)!)^2)\).

Goal progress. Unchanged. Converted. Nothing at the goal's parameters. Bearing. None: statements in the model. The cycle was spent on it because the unequal-distance statement could have shown that only the pairs at the largest distance matter for the loss at one bandwidth, which would have simplified every statement about clusters; what is proved is that pairs whose deficit \(\eta_j\) is large against \(k\log(2b)/\Lambda\) drop out, and examples with \(\eta_j\Lambda\) of order one show nearer pairs taking part, one of them cancelling the top pair with a compensating multiplicity.

General statement. prop:complex-moment-order, for every finite configuration of off-axis points at pairwise distinct heights, flat window, every bandwidth.

Setting

As in the short resonance-free range and the endpoint moment order, both re-read. Flat window, complete grid; off-axis points \(\gamma_j-i\delta_j\), \(\delta_j>0\), at pairwise distinct heights, multiplicities \(m_j>0\), \(M=\sum m_j\), \(\delta_*=\max\delta_j\), \(\eta_j=\delta_*-\delta_j\ge0\), \(b=\delta_*\Lambda\). \(\Sigma=e^{\delta_*s}F+R\) with \(F(s)=\sum_jm_je^{-\eta_js}e^{-is\gamma_j}\), \(|R|\le M\), \(Q(\Lambda)=\int_0^\Lambda ue^{-2\delta_*u}|F(\Lambda-u)|^2du\), and \[\Big|\,\|B_\Lambda\|_{\mathrm{HS}}-\frac{\sqrt2\,e^{b}}\Lambda\sqrt{Q(\Lambda)}\,\Big|\le M.\] Fix a reference height \(\gamma_0\) and put \[\vartheta_j=\Lambda(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)-i\Lambda\eta_j,\qquad\tilde w_j=m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}e^{-i\Lambda\gamma_j},\qquad\nu_r=\sum_j\tilde w_j\vartheta_j^{\,r}.\]

Unequal distances

Proposition (complex moment order). prop:complex-moment-order. In the Setting let \(k\) be the least \(r\) with \(\nu_r\ne0\); it exists, \(k\le n-1\), and \(k\) and \(|\nu_k|\) do not depend on the reference \(\gamma_0\) (the bound below does, through the \(|\vartheta_j|\)). Then \[\Big|\,2\delta_*(2b)^k\sqrt{Q(\Lambda)}-\frac{|\nu_k|}{k!}\sqrt{\gamma(2k+2,2b)}\,\Big|\ \le\ \frac{\sqrt{(2k+3)!}}{(k+1)!\,2b}\sum_jm_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}|\vartheta_j|^{k+1}\Big(\frac{\delta_*}{\delta_j}\Big)^{k+2}.\] For equal distances this is prop:endpoint-moment-order. The inequality holds at every bandwidth; it gives the order \(b^{-k}\) of the norm against a solitary pair, with the constant \(|\nu_k|\sqrt{(2k+1)!}/k!\), as \(b\to\infty\) with the \(m_j\), the \(\Lambda(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)\) and the \(\Lambda\eta_j\) held fixed, so that \(\delta_*/\delta_j\to1\); at a finite \(b\) a small nonzero \(\nu_0\) gives \(k=0\) with a bound larger than the main term.

Proof. The \(\vartheta_j\) are distinct, the heights being distinct, so the vectors \((\vartheta_j^r)_j\), \(r\le n-1\), are independent and \(\tilde w\ne0\): some \(\nu_r\), \(r\le n-1\), is not zero. Replacing \(\gamma_0\) by \(\gamma_0-a/\Lambda\) replaces \(\vartheta_j\) by \(\vartheta_j+a\) and \(\nu_r\) by \(\sum_{q\le r}\binom rqa^{r-q}\nu_q\), which is \(0\) for \(r<k\) and \(\nu_k\) for \(r=k\). Now \(F(\Lambda-u)=\sum_jm_je^{-\eta_j(\Lambda-u)}e^{-i(\Lambda-u)\gamma_j}=\sum_j\tilde w_je^{u(\eta_j+i\gamma_j)}=e^{iu\gamma_0}\sum_j\tilde w_je^{iu\vartheta_j/\Lambda}\), because \(i\vartheta_j/\Lambda=i(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)+\eta_j\). For complex \(z\) with \(\Re z\ge0\), \(|e^{z}-\sum_{r\le k}z^r/r!|\le|z|^{k+1}e^{\Re z}/(k+1)!\) (the remainder is \(\int_0^1\tfrac{(1-t)^k}{k!}z^{k+1}e^{tz}dt\)). With \(z=iu\vartheta_j/\Lambda\), \(\Re z=\eta_ju\ge0\); summing against \(\tilde w_j\) and using \(\nu_r=0\) for \(r<k\), \[\sum_j\tilde w_je^{iu\vartheta_j/\Lambda}=\frac{\nu_k}{k!}\Big(\frac{iu}\Lambda\Big)^k+E(u),\qquad|E(u)|\le\sum_j\frac{m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}|\vartheta_j|^{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\Big(\frac u\Lambda\Big)^{k+1}e^{\eta_ju}.\] In the norm \(\|f\|_*^2=\int_0^\Lambda ue^{-2\delta_*u}|f(u)|^2du\): \(\|u^k\|_*^2=(2\delta_*)^{-2k-2}\gamma(2k+2,2b)\), and \(\|u^{k+1}e^{\eta_ju}\|_*^2=\int_0^\Lambda u^{2k+3}e^{-2\delta_ju}du\le(2k+3)!/(2\delta_j)^{2k+4}\), since \(\delta_*-\eta_j=\delta_j>0\). By the triangle inequality \[\Big|\sqrt{Q}-\frac{|\nu_k|\sqrt{\gamma(2k+2,2b)}}{k!\,\Lambda^k(2\delta_*)^{k+1}}\Big|\le\sum_j\frac{m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}|\vartheta_j|^{k+1}\sqrt{(2k+3)!}}{(k+1)!\,\Lambda^{k+1}(2\delta_j)^{k+2}},\] and multiplying by \(2\delta_*(2b)^k=(2\delta_*)^{k+1}\Lambda^k\) gives the statement, as \((2\delta_*)^{k+1}/(\Lambda(2\delta_j)^{k+2})=(\delta_*/\delta_j)^{k+2}/(2b)\). For equal distances \(\eta_j=0\), \(\vartheta_j=\theta_j\), and \(\tilde w_j\) are the weights of prop:endpoint-moment-order. \(\square\)

Corollary (top cluster order). cor:top-cluster-order. In the Setting let \(T_*\) be the set of points with \(\delta_j=\delta_*\), and let \(k\), \(\nu_k\), \(c=\sum_{j\in T_*}m_j|\theta_j|^{k+1}\) be those of prop:endpoint-moment-order for the points of \(T_*\) alone, with \(\theta_j=\Lambda(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)\). Then \[\Big|\,2\delta_*(2b)^k\sqrt{Q(\Lambda)}-\frac{|\nu_k|}{k!}\sqrt{\gamma(2k+2,2b)}\,\Big|\ \le\ \frac{c\sqrt{(2k+3)!}}{(k+1)!\,2b}+(2b)^k\sum_{j\notin T_*}m_j\frac{\delta_*}{\delta_j}e^{-\eta_j\Lambda}.\] So the points at the largest distance decide the order when \(\eta_j\Lambda\) is large against \(k\log(2b)\) for the others; this is the extension the previous entry's reviewer proposed.

Proof. \(F(\Lambda-u)=F_*(\Lambda-u)+L(u)\) with \(F_*\) the sum over \(T_*\) and \(|L(u)|\le\sum_{j\notin T_*}m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}e^{\eta_ju}\). \(\|e^{\eta_ju}\|_*^2=\int_0^\Lambda ue^{-2\delta_ju}du\le1/(4\delta_j^2)\), so \(\|L\|_*\le\sum_{j\notin T_*}m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}/(2\delta_j)\). Apply prop:endpoint-moment-order to \(F_*\), the triangle inequality, and multiply \(\|L\|_*\) by \(2\delta_*(2b)^k\). \(\square\)

What the two say together. The proposition's \(k\) and the corollary's can differ: a point slightly below the largest distance has a weight \(m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}\) that is small and not zero, so the proposition's leading moment is of order zero with a small coefficient, while the corollary treats that point as an error. Both are true; the proposition is the sharper description when \(\eta_j\Lambda\) is of order one, the corollary when it is large. A point at a smaller distance can cancel the top pair if its multiplicity compensates: one pair of multiplicity \(1\) at distance \(\delta_*\) and one of multiplicity \(e^{\eta\Lambda}\) at distance \(\delta_*-\eta\), half a period apart, have \(\nu_0=0\) and lose a factor of order \(1/b\). The multiplicity \(e^{\eta\Lambda}\) is an integer only at isolated bandwidths; whether integer multiplicities allow such a cancellation over a range of bandwidths is not examined. So distances other than the largest are not shown to drop out of the single-bandwidth loss unless they are far below.

What the registry lead's records give

Both records were read in full in the notebook that owns them. The first, lem:cube-pair-collision-valuation with its second lemma on two double roots: when two roots \(a_i,a_j\) collide, each pair of rows \(\{i,k\},\{j,k\}\) is replaced by one row and its divided difference, a row operation of determinant \(1/\varepsilon\), so every minor vanishes to order at least the number of such blocks, \(N-2\), and exactly that where the confluent minor is nonzero; with two disjoint collisions the first-order limit rows satisfy one linear relation per pair of clusters, so first-order normalization does not give the flat limit. The second, prop:cube-cluster-order-loss with the lemma before it: scalar vanishing orders on all clusters are necessary for membership in an ideal and do not determine the degree, an explicit product-sum polynomial satisfying stronger orders below the target degree.

Nothing specific to the first record transfers (its blocks, its exponent \(N-2\), its defect at two clusters). By analogy with its row operation, the full divided difference of the exponentials gives the following standard bound.

Lemma (Gram collision order). lem:gram-collision-order. Let \(n\ge2\) off-axis points \(\gamma_j-i\delta\) at one distance and pairwise distinct heights have heights of span \(W\). (a) For the matrix \(R\) of prop:many-pair-norm-bound, the Gram matrix in \(L^2(\omega\,ds)\) of the normalized exponentials \(e^{-isz_j}\), with \(\omega\ge0\) supported in \([-\Lambda,\Lambda]\): \[\lambda_{\min}(R)\le\frac{(\Lambda W)^{2(n-1)}}{n\,((n-1)!)^2}.\] (b) For \(H_{jl}=2/(2\delta+i(\gamma_j-\gamma_l))^3\), the matrix of prop:cluster-negativity-constant: \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\le\dfrac{(2n)!\,W^{2(n-1)}}{n\,((n-1)!)^2(2\delta)^{2n+1}}\).

Proof. Let \(d_j=\prod_{l\ne j}(\gamma_j-\gamma_l)^{-1}\), real, with \(|d_j|\ge W^{-(n-1)}\), so \(\sum d_j^2\ge nW^{-2(n-1)}\). For a smooth complex-valued function \(f\) of a real variable, \(\sum_jd_jf(\gamma_j)\) is the divided difference \(f[\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n]\), and by the Hermite–Genocchi formula, an integral of \(f^{(n-1)}\) over a simplex of volume \(1/(n-1)!\), \(|f[\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n]|\le\sup|f^{(n-1)}|/(n-1)!\). (a) Apply this for each \(s\) to \(\gamma\mapsto e^{-is(\gamma-i\delta)}\), whose \((n-1)\)-th derivative has modulus \(|s|^{n-1}e^{-\delta s}\): \(|\sum_jd_je^{-isz_j}|\le\Lambda^{n-1}e^{-\delta s}/(n-1)!\) on \([-\Lambda,\Lambda]\). All the exponentials have the same norm \(N_0^{1/2}\), \(N_0=\int\omega e^{-2\delta s}ds\), so \(d^{\mathsf T}Rd=N_0^{-1}\int\omega|\sum d_je^{-isz_j}|^2ds\le\Lambda^{2(n-1)}/((n-1)!)^2\), and \(\lambda_{\min}(R)\le d^{\mathsf T}Rd/\sum d_j^2\). (b) \(H\) is, up to transposition, the Gram matrix in \(L^2(0,\infty)\) of \(f_j(x)=xe^{-\delta x}e^{-ix\gamma_j}\); \(|\sum d_jf_j(x)|\le x^{n}e^{-\delta x}/(n-1)!\), of squared norm at most \((2n)!/((2\delta)^{2n+1}((n-1)!)^2)\). \(\square\)

So the counterpart here of a collision order is the exponent \(2(n-1)\) of the width in an upper bound for the least eigenvalue. It is the statement behind the remark in the many-pair bound that its constant \(\rho=\lambda_{\min}(R)\) is small for close pairs, and behind the previous reviewer's remark on \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\); in the control's equally spaced examples the exponent is attained, and exactness is not proved (the reviewer's unverified argument below gives it in terms of the least gap). \(\lambda_{\min}\) is the worst case over all coefficient vectors, and the bound uses the alternating divided-difference weights. The cluster's actual vector has positive multiplicities with phases \(e^{-i\Lambda\gamma_j}\), which for heights within \(\pi/\Lambda\) of each other do not alternate: such a cluster reinforces (cor:maximal-cancellation-order, part (b)). The item named this as its breaking point, and that is the answer: collisions of heights bound the least eigenvalue of the Gram matrix and so weaken any bound that goes through it; the loss the cluster actually suffers is described by moments of its phases, that is by resonant spacings, for unequal distances as for equal ones. From the second record nothing transfers. The counterpart of the first record's second lemma, two clusters colliding at once, is not addressed here.

Degenerate cases. \(n=1\): \(k=0\), \(\nu_0=m e^{-i\Lambda\gamma}\), \(\vartheta=0\) with \(\gamma_0\) the point's height, and the proposition is the solitary pair exactly. All distances equal: the earlier proposition. A lower point with \(\delta_j\to0\): the factor \((\delta_*/\delta_j)^{k+2}\) grows without bound and the proposition is empty, while the corollary's term \(m_j(\delta_*/\delta_j)e^{-\eta_j\Lambda}\) also grows; a point on the axis is not an off-axis point and belongs to the real part of the configuration. \(n=1\) in the lemma is excluded (no divided difference); for \(W\Lambda\ge1\) part (a) can exceed \(1\) and says nothing. Unused: positivity of the \(m_j\) in the proposition beyond \(\tilde w\ne0\); in part (a) of the lemma the value of \(\delta\) and the flatness of the window.

Nonvacuity. The control's four configurations at unequal distances, with \(k=0,0,1,2\); the corollary's configuration has two points at the largest distance with \(k=1\) and one point with \(\eta\Lambda=14\).

Numerical control

Script and output. The registered closed form of \(\|B_\Lambda\|\), which allows unequal distances and uses nothing proved here, is compared with the proposition and the corollary combined with the Setting's inequality, at \(b=30,60,120\); least eigenvalues are computed by a library routine. On the order of events: the script's expectations were written in its header before any run, but its first commit was refused for a long message line and the first run was made before the commit that followed it; I had not read the output when I committed, which only my own account supports. A check of part (a) of the lemma was then added with its expectation, committed, and the script rerun; the first run is kept and its parts are unchanged in the second. Results. The proposition's inequality holds in all 15 cases, with \(k\) as predicted for each configuration. For the lower point near the top pair the deviation is close to the band (\(0.029\) against \(0.038\) at \(b=120\)); elsewhere, where the statement is informative, it is well inside: for the point cancelling the top one, \(7.93\) against the main term \(7.88\) at \(b=120\) with a band of \(0.24\); for three distances with weights \(1,-2,1\) and \(k=2\), \(112.2\) against \(110.9\). For the point far below the top pair the proposition's main term is \(8\cdot10^{-7}\) and its band \(0.03\) at \(b=120\): true and uninformative, as said above, and the corollary takes over: \(7.694\) against \(7.695\) with a band of \(0.23\). The negative control, the cancelling configuration with the lower multiplicity set to \(1\), tested against the cancelling configuration's main term and order, fails at all three bandwidths as predicted (\(120\) against \(7.9\) at \(b=120\)); it is off by a factor of about \(2b\) and could not have passed, so it confirms only that the test distinguishes orders. The lemma's two bounds hold in all 18 cases and the least eigenvalues scale with exponents between \(1.98\) and \(6.00\) against \(2,4,6\), within the expected \(0.3\); the bounds exceed the eigenvalues by factors from \(4\) to \(10^5\), so the constants are not sharp and the bounds could not realistically fail here.

Follow-up. Developed: prop:complex-moment-order, cor:top-cluster-order and lem:gram-collision-order, with prop:endpoint-moment-order and cor:maximal-cancellation-order from the item's first entry; the item asked to translate the registry's statements on colliding roots to the Gram model and read off the exact order of the cancellation loss, and named its own breaking point, which is what the two entries establish: with the multiplicities, the scaled heights and the scaled deficits held fixed and \(b\to\infty\), the loss is of exact order \(b^{-2k}\) in the norm's square, \(k\) being the number of vanishing complex moments; at a finite bandwidth there is an inequality with an explicit error; and collisions of heights give an upper bound for the least eigenvalue and say nothing about the loss. The translation the item proposed is thereby decided, against collision order and for resonant spacings, and the item has no further question of its own: the one question its first entry left, the largest number of vanishing moments for simple pairs or bounded multiplicities, is asked by the queued check entry-2026-10-11-gap-free-power-sum-bound:s1 ("Use the multiplicity budget ... Question. Is there a lower bound for \(\sup_\tau\Re G\) that uses only the positivity of the multiplicities and the height of the window containing the cluster?

New mathematics. Two lemmas and a theorem. An upper bound \(S\) for \(\Re G\) on the line bounds the profile \(xe^{-\delta x}|P(x-L)|\) by about \(\sqrt{S}\). A sum of exponentials with positive coefficients and frequencies in an interval of length \(c\delta\) cannot be below \(Me^{-\beta b}e^{\delta x}/(\delta x)\) on all of \([1/\delta,\beta L]\) once \(-\ln(1-\beta)-\beta\) exceeds \(\pi c\) (with a correction of order \(1/b\)). Together: \(\sup\Re G\ge\tfrac{\pi^2}{100}(e^{-\beta b}-4be^{-b})^2M/\delta^2\). Nothing depends on the number of pairs, their gaps or their multiplicities.

General statement. thm:narrow-window-negativity, for every finite set of off-line pairs at one distance with heights in an interval of length \(c\delta\), \(0<c\le1\), every length with \(b>1\) and every \(\beta\in(1/b,1)\) meeting its condition.

Setting

As in the one-sided cluster negativity, re-read: off-line pairs \(\gamma_j\mp i\delta\), \(m_j>0\), \(M=\sum m_j\), \(b=\delta L\), \(P(y)=\sum_jm_je^{-iy\gamma_j}\), \(G(\tau)=\sum_jm_je^{-iL(\tau-\gamma_j)}/(\tau-\gamma_j+i\delta)^2=-\int_0^\infty h(x)e^{i(x-L)\tau}dx\) with \(h(x)=xe^{-\delta x}P(x-L)\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(h=0\) for \(x<0\); \(|G(\tau)|\le Y(\tau)=\sum_jm_j/((\tau-\gamma_j)^2+\delta^2)\); \(D_{\mathrm{off}}=-\tfrac{2e^{b}}L\Re G+E\), \(|E|\le6Y/L\). Here all heights lie in an interval \([\gamma_a,\gamma_a+c\delta]\), and \(S=\sup_\tau\Re G(\tau)\), which is nonnegative because \(\Re G\) is continuous and tends to \(0\) at infinity.

From the density to the profile

Lemma (one-sided Fourier relation). lem:one-sided-fourier-relation. In the Setting, without the window: for every real \(x\), \[\int_{\mathbb R}\Re G(\tau)e^{-i(x-L)\tau}d\tau=-\pi\big(h(x)+\overline{h(2L-x)}\big).\] With the window, for any number \(S\ge0\) with \(\Re G\le S\) on the line: for \(0<x\le L\) and every \(\rho>0\), \[xe^{-\delta x}|P(x-L)|\le\frac2\pi\Big(S(c\delta+2\rho)+\frac{2M}\rho\Big)+2Le^{-b}M+2LMe^{-2b+\delta x}.\] In particular, if \(S=\varepsilon M/\delta^2\) with \(\varepsilon>0\), then for \(0<x\le L\) \[|P(x-L)|\le M\,\frac{e^{\delta x}}{\delta x}\,B,\qquad B=\frac2\pi\big(c\varepsilon+4\sqrt\varepsilon\big)+4be^{-b}.\]

Proof. \(h\) is continuous and integrable and \(G\) is integrable, so by Fourier inversion \(\int G(\tau)e^{-iy\tau}d\tau=-2\pi h(y+L)\) and \(\int\overline{G(\tau)}e^{-iy\tau}d\tau=-2\pi\overline{h(L-y)}\); half their sum at \(y=x-L\) is the identity. Hence \(|h(x)|\le\tfrac1\pi\int|\Re G|+|h(2L-x)|\), and for \(0<x\le L\), \(|h(2L-x)|\le(2L-x)e^{-\delta(2L-x)}M\le2LMe^{-2b+\delta x}\). At \(x=L\) the identity gives \(\int\Re G=-2\pi\Re h(L)=-2\pi Le^{-b}M\), because \(P(0)=M\); so \(\int|\Re G|=2\int(\Re G)^+-\int\Re G=2\int(\Re G)^++2\pi Le^{-b}M\). Let \(U\) be the set of \(\tau\) within \(\rho\) of the interval of heights, of length \(c\delta+2\rho\); outside it \(|G|\le\sum_jm_j/(\tau-\gamma_j)^2\), so \(\int_{U^c}|G|\le2M/\rho\), and \(\int(\Re G)^+\le S(c\delta+2\rho)+2M/\rho\). This gives the second display. With \(S=\varepsilon M/\delta^2\) and \(\rho=\delta/\sqrt\varepsilon\): \(S(c\delta+2\rho)+2M/\rho=\tfrac M\delta(c\varepsilon+4\sqrt\varepsilon)\); and \(2Le^{-b}M+2LMe^{-2b+\delta x}\le4LMe^{-b}=\tfrac M\delta4be^{-b}\) for \(x\le L\). Divide by \(xe^{-\delta x}\). \(\square\)

A majorant for sums with positive coefficients

Lemma (positive sum majorant). lem:positive-sum-majorant. Let \(m_j>0\), \(M=\sum m_j\), and let the \(\gamma_j\) lie in an interval of length \(c\delta\). For \(b>1\) and \(1/b<\beta<1\) put \[\Lambda(\beta,b)=\ln\frac{1-1/b}{1-\beta}+\frac{1-\beta}{1-1/b}-1.\] If \(\Lambda(\beta,b)>\pi c\), then some \(x\in[1/\delta,\beta L]\) has \(|P(x-L)|>Me^{-\beta b}e^{\delta x}/(\delta x)\). As \(b\to\infty\), \(\Lambda(\beta,b)\to-\ln(1-\beta)-\beta\).

Proof. \(|P|\) is unchanged when all heights are shifted, so let \(\gamma_j\in[0,c\delta]\), and put \(\Phi(z)=\sum_jm_je^{iz\gamma_j}\). It is entire, \(|\Phi(z)|\le M\) for \(\Im z\ge0\), \(\Phi(iv)=\sum m_je^{-v\gamma_j}\ge Me^{-vc\delta}\) for \(v>0\), and \(\Phi(L-x)=P(x-L)\). For \(v>0\), \[\ln\frac{\Phi(iv)}M\le\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\frac v{t^2+v^2}\ln\frac{|\Phi(t)|}M\,dt.\] To see this, map the disc to the half-plane by \(w\mapsto z=iv(1+w)/(1-w)\), which sends \(0\) to \(iv\) and normalized arc length to the measure \(\tfrac1\pi\tfrac v{t^2+v^2}dt\). The function \(f(w)=\Phi(z(w))/M\) is analytic in the open disc, of modulus at most \(1\), and continuous on the closed disc except at \(w=1\). For \(r<1\), \(\ln|f(0)|\le\tfrac1{2\pi}\int\ln|f(re^{i\theta})|d\theta\) because \(\ln|f|\) is subharmonic; the integrands are at most \(0\), so by Fatou's lemma applied to their negatives \(\limsup_{r\to1}\int\ln|f(re^{i\theta})|d\theta\le\int\ln|f(e^{i\theta})|d\theta\). Now suppose \(|P(x-L)|\le Me^{-\beta b}e^{\delta x}/(\delta x)\) for all \(x\in[1/\delta,\beta L]\). For such \(x\) and \(t=L-x\), \(\ln(|\Phi(t)|/M)\le-\beta b+\delta x-\ln(\delta x)\le-\delta(\beta L-x)=-\delta(t-a)\) with \(a=(1-\beta)L\), since \(\delta x\ge1\); elsewhere \(\ln(|\Phi|/M)\le0\). So for every \(v>0\), with \(T=L-1/\delta\), \[-vc\delta\le-\frac\delta\pi\int_a^T\frac{v\,(t-a)}{t^2+v^2}dt.\] Divide by \(v\delta\) and let \(v\to0\): the integrand converges uniformly on \([a,T]\), \(a>0\), to \((t-a)/t^2\), and \(\int_a^T(t-a)t^{-2}dt=\ln(T/a)+a/T-1=\Lambda(\beta,b)\). Hence \(\Lambda(\beta,b)\le\pi c\). \(\square\)

The bound

Theorem (narrow window negativity). thm:narrow-window-negativity. In the Setting let \(b>1\) and \(1/b<\beta<1\) with \(\Lambda(\beta,b)>\pi c\), and \(c\le1\). Then \[S=\sup_\tau\Re G(\tau)\ \ge\ \frac{\pi^2}{100}\big(e^{-\beta b}-4be^{-b}\big)_+^2\,\frac M{\delta^2},\] and some \(\tau\) has \[D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\le-\frac{2M}{L\delta^2}\Big(\frac{\pi^2}{100}\,e^{b}\big(e^{-\beta b}-4be^{-b}\big)_+^2-3\Big).\] Consequently, if the real points contribute \(R\le\ell\) everywhere, the density \(D_L\) has a negative value as soon as \(\tfrac{\pi^2}{100}e^{b}(e^{-\beta b}-4be^{-b})_+^2>3+b\delta\ell/(2M)\).

Proof. \(0\le S\le M/\delta^2\), so \(S=\varepsilon M/\delta^2\) with \(0\le\varepsilon\le1\); if \(S=0\) apply the first lemma to any positive \(S'\) and let \(S'\to0\). By the first lemma \(|P(x-L)|\le MBe^{\delta x}/(\delta x)\) for \(0<x\le L\), and by the second \(B>e^{-\beta b}\). As \(c\le1\) and \(\varepsilon\le\sqrt\varepsilon\), \(\tfrac2\pi(c\varepsilon+4\sqrt\varepsilon)\le\tfrac{10}\pi\sqrt\varepsilon\), so \(\tfrac{10}\pi\sqrt\varepsilon>e^{-\beta b}-4be^{-b}\). For the second statement take \(\tau\) with \(\Re G(\tau)\) within a factor \(1-\epsilon'\) of \(S\) and use \(|E|\le6M/(L\delta^2)\), then let \(\epsilon'\to0\) (the supremum is attained, \(\Re G\) being continuous and tending to \(0\) at infinity, when \(S>0\)). The last statement: \(D_L\le\ell+D_{\mathrm{off}}\) there, and \(\ell<\tfrac{2M}{L\delta^2}(\cdots-3)\) is the stated inequality. \(\square\)

What it gives. The exponent lost is \(2\beta\), with \(\beta\) the solution of \(\Lambda(\beta,b)=\pi c\): from the control's bisection, \(\beta=0.317\) for \(c=0.02\) at \(b=200\) and \(\beta=0.466\) for \(c=0.05\) at \(b=120\); \(\beta\) is about \(\sqrt{2\pi c}\) for small \(c\), and \(\beta=\tfrac12\) in the limit of large \(b\) at \(c=(\ln2-\tfrac12)/\pi=0.0615\). That value of \(c\) is the threshold in the limit; at a finite \(b\) it is smaller, since \(\beta\) decreases to its limit (at \(c=0.05\), \(2\beta=0.936\) at \(b=80\) and \(0.931\) at \(b=120\)). Where \(2\beta<1\) the bound grows against the factor \(e^{b}\): a cluster confined to a window of height \(c\delta\), with any number of pairs, any gaps and any multiplicities, has a negative value of the off-line part of size at least a constant times \(Me^{(1-2\beta)b}/(L\delta^2)\), and against real points of density \(\ell/2\pi\) it shows from \(b\) about \((\log(b\delta\ell/M)+\mathrm{const})/(1-2\beta)\); the multiple \(1/(1-2\beta)\) of a single pair's length is about \(14\) at \(c=0.05\) and \(2.7\) at \(c=0.02\). For \(c\ge0.0615\) the bound decays against the gain and gives no negativity; it is still a lower bound for \(\sup\Re G\) free of \(n\), which prop:gap-free-cluster-sum is not. The binomial family of the previous entry occupies a window of height about \(\delta\), so \(c\) about \(1\), outside the useful range: the theorem does not bound how long that family hides. The factor \(2\) in the exponent comes from the first lemma, where a one-sided bound for \(\Re G\) is turned into a bound for its integral through the tail \(2M/\rho\); the previous reviewer's remark, without that step, would give the exponent \(\beta\) and reach \(c=1\) with \(\beta=0.984\). I did not find how to avoid the step in this cycle; I tried a positive test kernel with a modulation and an inequality of Bernstein's type for a band-limited part of \(e^{iL\tau}G\), without reaching a statement worth recording, and this entry's reviewer proposes a version of the first (below). How sharp the theorem is was not examined: the binomial family placed inside the window, with \(k=\lfloor cb/\pi\rfloor\), has by prop:binomial-cluster-hiding \(\sup|G|\le(k+1)!(\pi/b)^k/\delta^2\) at total multiplicity \(2^k\), which the reviewer evaluates, unverified, as an exponent of about \(0.075\,b\) at \(c=0.05\), far from \(2\beta=0.93\).

Degenerate cases. One pair: \(c\) can be taken arbitrarily small, \(\beta\to1/b\), and the bound tends to \(\tfrac{\pi^2}{100}(e^{-1}-4be^{-b})^2M/\delta^2\), about \(0.013\,M/\delta^2\), against a true value of about \(M/\delta^2\) (prop:separated-pair-negativity registers at least \(0.42\,M/\delta^2\)). \(b\le1\) is excluded. \(c>1\): the theorem's constant \(10/\pi\) used \(c\le1\); the two lemmas hold for every \(c\). If \(e^{-\beta b}\le4be^{-b}\) the bound is zero. Heights not distinct are allowed. Unused: in the first lemma no bound on \(\varepsilon\) is needed; positivity of the \(m_j\) is essential in the second (\(\Phi(iv)\ge Me^{-vc\delta}\)) and in the first (\(P(0)=M\)).

Nonvacuity. The control's nine configurations satisfy the hypotheses with \(c=0.05\) and \(0.02\); for instance six pairs with multiplicities between \(1\) and \(5\) in a window of height \(0.025\) at \(\delta=\tfrac12\), \(b=80\), where \(\beta=0.468\).

Numerical control

Script, committed with its expectations before its run (the launcher now refuses a results script that is not committed), and output. The Fourier relation is tested at \(L=8\) on three pairs at six values of \(x\): it holds to \(3\cdot10^{-8}\) against a truncation bound of \(2\cdot10^{-3}\). Its negative control, the right side without the conjugation, was applied at the five values of \(x\) where the altered side differs by more than ten times the truncation bound (at \(x=L\) it does not differ) and fails at all five, as predicted. The majorant inequality is tested in nine configurations at three values of \(v\): it holds in all 27 rows within the sampling tolerance, with equality to \(2.2\cdot10^{-5}\) for the two-pair and "binomial" configurations and a strict gap, up to \(0.10\), for the random six-pair ones; I expected near-equality where the sum has no zero in the upper half-plane and did not determine where that is. This check is weaker than its count suggests: the inequality does not involve \(L\), so the two-pair rows at \(b=80\) and \(b=120\) are the same check; the "binomial" configurations all have \(k=1\) at these sizes and are two equal pairs; and the tolerance \(5\cdot10^{-3}\) exceeds the left side itself in the rows with \(v=0.5\), which therefore test nothing. The theorem's two statements hold in all nine configurations with margins so large that they could not have failed: the bound is between \(10^{-57}\) and \(10^{-34}\) of \(M/\delta^2\) where the computed supremum is between \(0.016\) and \(0.98\). So the control tests the Fourier identity, with a negative control, and gives weak support to the majorant inequality; nothing that could fail tests the profile step, the limit \(v\to0\) or the formula for \(\Lambda\), and nothing tests the strength of the theorem.

The record the item names

Read in the notebook that owns it: the corollary cor:cube-neck-atomic-density with its proof, and the statement of the theorem before it. Under a hypothesis on the window's excess (\(E\le c-w+1\)), the corollary proves that a determinant's order is at least a target for every sequence \(t'\), from the same bound on sequences \(t'_m=\sum_{k\le c}\gamma_k\lambda_k^m\) of \(c\) atoms. The step from atoms to all sequences is Prony's method: over an algebraic closure a generic vector \((t'_1,\dots,t'_{2c})\), one with nonsingular Hankel matrix and squarefree Prony polynomial with nonzero roots, is the moment vector of \(c\) atoms; polynomial coefficients vanishing on all such vectors vanish identically. So the freedom used there is that of \(c\) weights and \(c\) nodes reaching a generic target in \(2c\) coordinates.

The answer from the record

  • How many constraints. In the flat-window complete-grid model, the second moment of a cluster of \(n\) off-axis points at bandwidth \(\Lambda\) is governed by the moments \(\nu_r=\sum_j\tilde w_j\vartheta_j^{\,r}\) of prop:complex-moment-order, with nodes \(\vartheta_j=\Lambda(\gamma_j-\gamma_0)-i\Lambda\eta_j\) and weights \(\tilde w_j=m_je^{-\eta_j\Lambda}e^{-i\Lambda\gamma_j}\); the order of the loss is the number \(k\) of vanishing moments \(\nu_0=\dots=\nu_{k-1}=0\). By that proposition \(k\le n-1\) always. This has nothing to do with the tie between weights and nodes: no nonzero weights on \(n\) distinct nodes, however free, annihilate \(n\) consecutive powers, the Vandermonde matrix being invertible. Prony's \(2n\) counts something else, the parameters needed to match a generic target, and the zero target is not generic (its Hankel matrix is singular). By cor:maximal-cancellation-order, whose setting is that of the endpoint moment order, one distance, \(k=n-1\) is attained exactly by gaps that are odd multiples of \(\pi/\Lambda\) with divided-difference multiplicities.
  • What a test vector must pay. The entry on the resonance-free bandwidth closed the adaptive test vector with \(\lambda_{\max}(B)\le\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\): no test vector sees more than the norm, and by part (1) of prop:many-pair-norm-bound the two differ by at most \((2n)^{3/2}\). By lem:gram-second-moment-identity the norm is given by \(Q\), and by prop:complex-moment-order it is, as \(b\to\infty\) with the scaled heights, deficits and multiplicities fixed and up to a constant depending on \(k\), of order \(b^{-k}\) times the norm of a solitary pair of the cluster's total multiplicity. So at such a bandwidth every test vector's value is below that benchmark by a factor of that order, \(k\) up to \(n-1\).
  • Which clusters are worst. For one distance, those of cor:maximal-cancellation-order; for equally spaced heights the multiplicities are binomial. Under a bound \(K\) on multiplicities the binomial family allows \(k\) up to about \(\log_2K\) (the hidden cluster length). The largest \(k\) under bounded multiplicities in general, and whether \(k=n-1\) is attainable at unequal distances, are not on record.
  • Where the tie between weight and position could matter. A pair has a height, a distance and a multiplicity; the phase of its weight is fixed by its height and the modulus by its multiplicity and distance, and the multiplicity is a positive integer. So a cluster's moment vector depends on \(2n\) continuous parameters and \(n\) integers, besides the bandwidth and the reference, where \(n\) free complex weights and nodes are \(4n\) real parameters: the image of a smooth map from fewer dimensions has measure zero, and a generic moment vector is not that of a cluster. This is a count. It does not lower the bound \(n-1\), which holds for free weights too; it is the place where an argument that bounded multiplicities force \(k\) well below \(n-1\) would have to work, and none is given here. The item's own two breaking points are a different matter: the multiplicity bound is the open question just named, and positivity of on-line atoms does not enter, the real points not being atoms of these moments.

What this does not say. The moments describe the loss in the limit of large \(b\) at fixed scaled data; at a finite bandwidth there is the inequality of the proposition and nothing sharper. Prony's count has a different analogue here, two clusters of \(n\) pairs agreeing in many moments, which is indistinguishability of two off-line configurations and not a loss; the route does not ask to tell off-line configurations apart, only to detect that one is present.
