Question. The item, a lead from the registry: lem:cube-circle-polynomial proves that a family of polynomials has all roots on the unit circle by Rolle's theorem after a trigonometric substitution, and conj:cube-far-real-interlacing is a refuted interlacing hypothesis. Does a truncation attached to the route's objects have all its zeros on the line by an interlacing argument, and what would that say; the item names the transfer from the truncation to actual zeros as the place it would break.

New mathematics. A lemma and an example. For a polynomial \(F\) with \(u\) zeros above the real line and \(l\) below, the functions \(A_\theta=F+e^{i\theta}F^\sharp\) with \(e^{i\theta}\ne-1\) have at least \(|u-l|\) distinct real zeros and at most \(2\min(u,l)\) nonreal ones. And \(A_0\) can have all its zeros real while \(F\) has zeros on both sides. A proposition for the whole family: the mean over \(\theta\) of the number of real zeros of \(A_\theta\) is \(\tfrac1\pi\int|\phi'|\), which equals \(n\) exactly when all zeros of \(F\) are on one side; so all \(A_\theta\) real-rooted forces one side, and one of them does not.

Goal progress. Unchanged. Converted. Nothing at the goal's parameters. Bearing. None: statements about polynomials. The cycle was spent on it because an interlacing argument that put all zeros of some function attached to the configuration on the line, and from which the configuration's own zeros could be read, would be a criterion of a kind the route lacks; the example shows that one sum function with all zeros on the line does not place the configuration on one side, the lemma that what one function gives is a count with an error of twice the number of zeros on the smaller side, and the proposition that the whole family does decide one-sidedness, which for a finite configuration is the zero-free statement again.

General statement. lem:sum-function-zero-count, for every polynomial without real zeros and every \(\theta\) with \(e^{i\theta}\ne-1\), and prop:sum-family-mean-count, for every such polynomial.

The two records

Read in the notebook that owns them. lem:cube-circle-polynomial, with its proof: the polynomial \(B_L(s)=(L-1)s^{L+1}+(L+1)s^L-(L+1)s-(L-1)\), \(L\) odd, has all roots on the unit circle; the proof takes the \(k\) real roots of a Chebyshev quotient, gets \(k-1\) roots of its derivative between them by Rolle's theorem, shows by a trigonometric identity that these are roots of \(B_L\) on the upper semicircle, adds their conjugates and the roots at \(\pm1\) with their multiplicities, and finds the degree exhausted. So it is a count: enough roots are exhibited on the circle to leave none elsewhere. conj:cube-far-real-interlacing, with its entry: a family conjectured real-rooted with interlacing zeros, by analogy with a Jacobi-type relative, has mostly nonreal zeros at every size computed, and no consecutive pair interlaces; the lesson recorded there is that the property did not pass from the relative to the family.

The count

Take the real line as the critical line, the variable being \(z=(s-\tfrac12)/i\) as elsewhere in this notebook. Let \(F(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n(z-z_j)\) have no real zero, \(u\) zeros with \(\Im z_j>0\) and \(l\) with \(\Im z_j<0\), counted with multiplicity; \(F^\sharp(z)=\overline{F(\bar z)}=\prod(z-\bar z_j)\); and \(A_\theta=F+e^{i\theta}F^\sharp\).

Lemma (sum function zero count). lem:sum-function-zero-count. If \(e^{i\theta}\ne-1\), then \(A_\theta\) has degree \(n\), at least \(|u-l|\) distinct real zeros, and at most \(2\min(u,l)\) nonreal zeros counted with multiplicity. If \(e^{i\theta}=-1\), then \(A_\theta=F-F^\sharp\) either vanishes identically, which happens exactly when \(F\) has real coefficients (then \(u=l\)), or has degree less than \(n\) and at least \(|u-l|-1\) distinct real zeros.

Proof. The leading coefficient of \(A_\theta\) is \(1+e^{i\theta}\). For real \(x\), \(F^\sharp(x)=\overline{F(x)}\) and \(F(x)\ne0\), so with a continuous argument \(\phi(x)=\arg F(x)=\sum_j\arg(x-z_j)\), \[A_\theta(x)=2e^{i\theta/2}|F(x)|\cos\big(\phi(x)-\theta/2\big).\] So the real zeros of \(A_\theta\) are the \(x\) with \(\phi(x)\in\tfrac\theta2+\tfrac\pi2+\pi\mathbb Z\). As \(x\) goes from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\), \(\arg(x-z_j)\) goes from \(-\pi\) to \(0\) when \(\Im z_j>0\), increasing by \(\pi\), and from \(\pi\) to \(0\) when \(\Im z_j<0\), decreasing by \(\pi\). Normalizing so that \(\phi(+\infty)=0\), \(\phi(-\infty)=\pi(l-u)\). By the intermediate value theorem \(\phi\) takes every value strictly between \(0\) and \(\pi(l-u)\). The set \(\tfrac\theta2+\tfrac\pi2+\pi\mathbb Z\) contains \(0\) exactly when \(e^{i\theta}=-1\); otherwise it has exactly \(|u-l|\) points strictly between \(0\) and \(\pi(l-u)\), each attained at some real \(x\), at distinct points for distinct values. That gives \(|u-l|\) distinct real zeros, and the degree \(n=u+l\) leaves at most \(n-|u-l|=2\min(u,l)\) others. If \(e^{i\theta}=-1\) the set contains both ends and \(|u-l|-1\) points strictly between. \(\square\)

Example (no converse). ex:sum-function-no-converse. For \(T>0\) and \(0<\varepsilon\le T^2/4\), \(F(z)=(z-i)(z-T+i\varepsilon)\) has one zero above the line and one below, and \(A_0=F+F^\sharp=2(z^2-Tz+\varepsilon)\) has two real zeros, a double one when \(\varepsilon=T^2/4\). The lower zero may be at any distance from the line: \((T,\varepsilon)=(20,100)\) gives zeros \(i\) and \(20-100i\) and \(A_0=2(z-10)^2\). Verification. \(F(z)=z^2-(T+i(1-\varepsilon))z+i(T-i\varepsilon)=z^2-Tz+\varepsilon+i((\varepsilon-1)z+T)\), and \(F^\sharp\) has the conjugate coefficients; the discriminant of \(z^2-Tz+\varepsilon\) is \(T^2-4\varepsilon\ge0\). \(\square\)

Proposition (family mean count). prop:sum-family-mean-count. Let \(N(\theta)\) be the number of distinct real zeros of \(A_\theta\), and \(a_j(x)=\Im z_j/|x-z_j|^2\), so that \(\phi'=\sum_ja_j\). Then \[\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}N(\theta)\,d\theta=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb R}|\phi'(x)|\,dx=n-\frac2\pi\int_{\mathbb R}\min\big(P(x),Q(x)\big)\,dx,\] with \(P=\sum_{\Im z_j>0}a_j\) and \(Q=\sum_{\Im z_j<0}|a_j|\). Consequently: (1) the mean equals \(n\) if \(\min(u,l)=0\) and is less than \(n\) otherwise; (2) if \(u,l\ge1\), then \(A_\theta\) has a nonreal zero for every \(\theta\) in a set of positive measure; (3) if \(A_\theta\) has only real zeros for almost every \(\theta\), all zeros of \(F\) lie on one side of the line.

Proof. For \(\theta\in(-\pi,\pi)\) the real zeros of \(A_\theta\) are the points of \(\phi^{-1}(c+\pi\mathbb Z)\) with \(c=\tfrac\theta2+\tfrac\pi2\in(0,\pi)\), by the formula in the lemma's proof. The function \(\phi\) is smooth on the line with integrable derivative, each \(|a_j|\) having integral \(\pi\); for such a function the integral of the number of preimages over all values equals the total variation (the area formula in one variable: split the line at the finitely many zeros of \(\phi'\), or note that \(\phi\) is constant if \(\phi'\equiv0\); on each piece \(\phi\) is monotone and the change of variable is elementary). So \[\int_{\mathbb R}|\phi'|\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\#\phi^{-1}(y)\,dy=\int_0^\pi\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\#\phi^{-1}(c+k\pi)\,dc=\int_0^{\pi}N(2c-\pi)\,dc=\frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}N(\theta)\,d\theta.\] That \(\phi'\) has finitely many zeros or vanishes identically: it is a rational function. For the second equality of the statement, \(|\phi'|=|P-Q|=P+Q-2\min(P,Q)\), and \(\int(P+Q)=n\pi\). (1): \(P\) and \(Q\) are positive at every \(x\) when \(u\ge1\) and \(l\ge1\) respectively, so \(\int\min(P,Q)>0\) exactly when both are; if \(l=0\) then \(Q\equiv0\). (2): \(N(\theta)\le n\) for \(\theta\in(-\pi,\pi)\), so a mean below \(n\) gives \(N(\theta)\le n-1\) on a set of positive measure; a real zero of \(A_\theta\) is multiple only where \(\phi'\) vanishes as well, at one of finitely many points, hence for finitely many \(\theta\) (if \(\phi'\equiv0\) there is no real zero at all); for the other \(\theta\) of that set the \(n\) zeros of \(A_\theta\) are not all real. (3) is the contrapositive of (2). \(\square\)

In the example the mean is below \(2\) although \(N(0)=2\): the control computes \(1.84\) at \((T,\varepsilon)=(5,0.1)\).

What it says about the item

  • A count of the circle polynomial's kind exists and proves less than the item hoped. The lemma's proof resembles that of the circle polynomial: zeros on the line are exhibited by the intermediate value theorem, here applied to the phase, and the degree bounds the rest. No interlacing is proved; for one-sided \(F\) the phase is monotone, and then the zeros of two different \(A_\theta\) alternate. It puts all zeros of \(A_\theta\) on the line exactly when the count exhausts the degree, that is when \(\min(u,l)=0\): the configuration is already on one side. For a configuration with zeros on both sides it gives a count with an error of \(2\min(u,l)\).
  • The transfer fails in the finite model. The example has all zeros of a sum function on the line and a zero of \(F\) on each side. So "the truncation has all its zeros on the line", for one sum function, does not control the zeros it was built from, while by the proposition the same for almost every member of the family does; this is the breaking point the item named, and it is not a matter of passing to infinitely many zeros. At \((T,\varepsilon)=(5,0.1)\) the lower zero is near the line and far from the upper one: its phase change of \(-\pi\) happens on a short interval, after most of the upper zero's change of \(+\pi\), and the phase crosses the same level twice. But nearness is not needed: the example's range contains lower zeros arbitrarily far from the line, so a single sum function with all zeros real says nothing about the distance of the minority zeros either.
  • What the record already has. For finite configurations the half-plane sign of the logarithmic derivative, and the modulus inequality of a structure function at a shift, are each equivalent to all zeros lying on one side (prop:log-derivative-sign-criteria and the entry on structure functions); the local phase condition does not fail for a pair farther from the line than about half the local gap. The classical theorem that \(F\) has all zeros on one side exactly when the real and imaginary parts of its coefficients give real-rooted polynomials with interlacing zeros is the theorem of Hermite and Biehler, which the Hermite–Biehler lead names and which I have not read in a source; the example is consistent with it: for \(\varepsilon\ne1\) the imaginary part's zero \(T/(1-\varepsilon)\) lies outside the interval between the two real zeros of the real part, being above \(T\) for \(\varepsilon<1\) and negative for \(\varepsilon>1\), and for \(\varepsilon=1\) the imaginary part has no zero.
  • The refuted conjecture's caution applies. There a property of a relative did not pass to the family; here the real-rootedness of a sum function does not pass to the configuration.

The lemma and the proposition bear on a sub-idea queued under the Hermite–Biehler lead, entry-2026-10-11-structure-function-criterion:s1. I read its \(A_h\) as \(\tfrac12(G+G^\sharp)\) with \(G=F(\cdot+h)\) in the variable for which the critical line is the real line, the reading under which it is this entry's \(A_0\) for \(G\); under another reading of its \(F^\sharp(s+h)\) the lemma does not apply. The sub-idea allows points on the shifted line, which the lemma excludes: if \(G=RG_0\) with \(R\) real-rooted with real coefficients and \(G_0\) without real zeros, then \(G+e^{i\theta}G^\sharp=R\,(G_0+e^{i\theta}G_0^\sharp)\), and the lemma applies to \(G_0\). It asks, for a polynomial with exactly \(k\) points to the right of the shifted line, for a bound on the zeros of the sum function off the line: at most \(2\min(k,n-k)\), by the lemma. And it asks whether all zeros of \(A_{h,\theta}\) on the line for every \(\theta\) forces \(k=0\): they force all points to one side, by part (3); which side is not determined by the family, since exchanging \(F\) and \(F^\sharp\) permutes it. The sub-idea's third part, a source's theorem to read and compare, is untouched. It belongs to another item and is not closed here.

Degenerate cases. \(l=0\): all \(n\) zeros of \(A_\theta\) are real and distinct, the classical case. \(u=l\): the lemma gives no real zero, and none need exist (\(F=(z-i)(z+i)\), \(A_0=2(z^2+1)\)). \(n=1\): \(F=z-z_1\), \(A_\theta=(1+e^{i\theta})z-(z_1+e^{i\theta}\bar z_1)\), one real zero. \(n=0\): \(F=1\), \(A_\theta=1+e^{i\theta}\), no zeros, and the statements hold with \(u=l=0\). \(F\) with real coefficients and \(e^{i\theta}=-1\): \(A_\theta\equiv0\), stated in the lemma; for other \(\theta\), \(A_\theta=(1+e^{i\theta})F\) has no real zero and the mean count is \(0\), in agreement with \(\phi'\equiv0\). A real zero of \(F\) is excluded; it would be a common zero of \(F\) and \(F^\sharp\) and of every \(A_\theta\). Unused: nothing.

Nonvacuity. The control's 4000 random configurations of degrees \(2\) to \(12\) satisfy the hypotheses; the example's parameters \((T,\varepsilon)=(5,0.1)\).

Numerical control

Script, committed with its expectations before its run, and output. Zeros are computed by a library routine from the coefficients, which uses nothing of the proof. In 4000 random configurations with random \(\theta\), none ambiguous at the tolerance, the count holds in all; \(\theta\) is drawn from \((-3,3)\), so the script's test for a degree drop could not have fired. The bound \(|u-l|\) on real zeros is attained in 2245 of them, and with it the bound on nonreal zeros; in those the statement with \(|u-l|+1\) fails, which I wrote down as the negative control and which is only a restatement of attainment, not an independent check; in the other 1755 there are more real zeros than the lemma guarantees. The example: both zeros of \(A_0\) are real at \((5,0.1)\) and \((1,0.2)\), and nonreal at \((1,0.3)\), where \(T^2<4\varepsilon\), as written beforehand. A second script, likewise committed before its run, tests the proposition's identity (output): the left side from the zeros of \(A_\theta\) on a grid of 4000 values of \(\theta\), the right side by quadrature of \(|\phi'|\), two routes that share nothing. In 24 random configurations of degrees \(2\) to \(8\) the two sides differ by at most \(2.4\cdot10^{-4}\), against a tolerance of \(0.02\) and quantities between \(1.29\) and \(6\), so every row counts as a check; one row has a share \(2.5\cdot10^{-4}\) of grid points with a zero in the ambiguous band, the others none. In the 8 one-sided configurations both sides equal \(n\); in the 16 two-sided ones the mean is below \(n\) by at least \(0.71\), and the altered statement "the mean is \(n\)" fails on all 16, which is the negative control. I had written that six configurations would be one-sided; eight are, two of the random ones having drawn one sign. Nothing in either control tests part (2)'s step from the mean to a nonreal zero, which is a deduction.

Decisive test. On the lead entry-2026-10-11-exclusion-route-review:1, sub-idea entry-2026-10-11-prime-side-form:s2. This is the third form of the test. The first asked whether a one-sided bound \(D_L(\tau)\ge-Ce^{\theta L}\) for all large \(L\) is equivalent, in the model, to all off-line distances being at most \(\theta\); the second-stage reviewer showed that it follows in a few lines (its suggestions, unverified), so it is a lemma for the next entry and not a test. The second asked whether a cluster can stay hidden on a whole range of lengths \([L_0,\kappa L_0]\); my own attempt to answer it, below, did so in a few lines when multiplicities or the number of pairs are free. What is left undecided is the same question under the constraint the goal's instances satisfy, a local count. The test: in the setting of lem:one-sided-density-decomposition, for off-line pairs at one distance \(\delta\) with heights in a window of height \(\delta\), at most \(N\) of them counted with multiplicity, and \(b_0=\delta L_0\): prove or break a bound \[\max_{L_0\le L\le2L_0}\ \sup_\tau\Re G_L(\tau)\ \ge\ \frac{M}{\delta^2}\,(b_0N)^{-A}\] with an absolute constant \(A\). Outcomes: if it holds, the one-sided premise over the lengths \([L_0,2L_0]\) with \(L_0\) about \((A+1)(\log(b_0N))/\delta\) excludes every cluster at one distance in a window of height \(\delta\), so for those clusters the premise's prime sums have length a bounded power of \(\log T\), and the lead's remaining content, apart from unequal distances and wider windows, is the prime side; if a family with loss beyond every power of \(b_0N\) on the whole range exists, the one-sided form needs lengths that depend on the cluster as the Gram form does, and the lead closes with that. Attempt. Made before posing it, a sketch that no reviewer has checked in full. With \(P(y)=\sum m_je^{-iy\gamma_j}\), \(G_L\) is governed by \(P\) on \([-L,-L+O(1/\delta)]\), so hiding on the range of lengths means \(P\) small on about \([-2L_0,-L_0]\) while \(P(0)=M\). The product \(P(y)=M\prod_{i=1}^{n}\cos(\eta_iy/2)\) with all \(\eta_i\) near \(2\pi/(3L_0)\) has positive coefficients, each factor is at most \(\cos(\pi/3)=\tfrac12\) in modulus on that interval up to the spread of the \(\eta_i\), so \(|P|\le M2^{-n}\) there: a cluster of up to \(2^n\) heights in a window of height about \(n\eta=2\pi n/(3L_0)\) that is hidden on the whole range with loss about \(2^{-n}\). Two things the reviewer added, unverified by me beyond their arithmetic: the test's window of height \(\delta\) forces \(n\le0.48\,b_0\), so in that window the family's loss is at least \(2^{-0.48b_0}\); and the integral for \(G_L\) leaves the interval at once at \(L=L_0\), which is harmless only through that constraint, \(|P|\) growing at a rate of at most \(0.87\) per unit of \(\delta x\) against the factor \(e^{-\delta x}\), giving \(|G|\) at most about \(60\,M2^{-n}/\delta^2\). With the \(\eta_i\) equal it is the binomial family at a gap tuned to \(3L_0\), with multiplicities up to \(\binom n{n/2}\); with the \(\eta_i\) distinct and generic its \(2^n\) heights are simple. So without a count the answer is that clusters hide on a range. With the count, \(2^n\le N\) gives a loss of only \(N^{-1}\), a power, consistent with the bound proposed; and the general lower bounds on record lose more: prop:gap-free-cluster-sum bounds the sum below by \(M/(2eb)^{n}\) with \(n\) the number of pairs, which under the count is \(M/(2eb)^{N}\), far beyond a power, and the loss for \(G\) is larger still. So the test is undecided between a family built by products, which loses a power of \(N\), and inequalities of Turán's type, which allow \(e^{-cN}\). Trivial cases. One pair: prop:separated-pair-negativity gives \(\Re G\ge0.42\,m/\delta^2\) for \(b\ge2\pi\), and the bound holds with \(A=0\). Doubling every multiplicity scales \(G\) and \(M\) together; multiplicities being positive integers, the count is to be taken as \(N=M\), and doubling then only weakens the bound. A pair of multiplicity two and two coincident simple pairs are one configuration. Power. Recorded bounds on the test's object: prop:binomial-cluster-hiding (hidden at one length, loss up to about \(b^{-k}\) with \(k\le\log_2\) of the largest multiplicity); prop:one-sided-inherited-loss (the negative part is at most a multiple of \(b^{-k}\) with \(k\) vanishing moments); prop:gap-free-cluster-sum (the sum is at least \(M/(2eb)^{n}\)); thm:narrow-window-negativity (no dependence on the cluster, for windows narrower than about \(0.06\,\delta\) only, and at one length); for the Gram form, thm:short-resonance-free-range (a range depending on the least gap). None uses the count except through \(n\le N\), and none decides the test. It is a proof attempt; a computation over random and product configurations with \(N\) up to about \(60\) could show a loss growing faster than a power for some family, which would break the bound, and could not prove it. Architecture test. The seventh review asked, for pairs at one distance in a window of height \(\delta\) with total multiplicity \(N=M\), to prove or break \(\max_{L_0\le L\le2L_0}\sup_\tau\Re G_L\ge(M/\delta^2)(b_0N)^{-A}\) with an absolute \(A\). Not decided. Neither of the review's two outcomes occurred: the bound is neither proved nor broken. The test's defining constraint, the count \(N\), is used nowhere in this entry, and nothing is proved for its window of height \(\delta\). What is proved instead: for windows of height \(c\delta\) and a range \([L_0,\kappa L_0]\), some length of the range has \(\sup_\tau\Re G_L\) at least about \(e^{-2\Lambda^*}M/\delta^2\) with \(\Lambda^*\le\pi c\kappa b_0/(2(\kappa-1))\), whatever the cluster (thm:range-negativity); this beats the factor \(e^{b_0}\) exactly when \(c<(\kappa-1)/(\pi\kappa)\), so for \(c\) below \(0.159\) at \(\kappa=2\) and below \(1/\pi\) for long ranges, and not for the test's window \(c=1\). The bound is exponential in \(b_0\) and does not involve \(N\); a power of \(N\) and an exponential in \(b_0\) are different bounds when \(b_0\) is large against \(\log N\), and comparable only at lengths like the one in the review's outcome clause, \(L_0\) about \((A+1)\log(b_0N)/\delta\). For the product family the mean of \(\log|P|\) over a range of ratio two is at least \(-2\) for each factor (lem:product-range-mean), so for \(P\), on ranges of ratio two, such a family does not lose more than a fixed power of its total multiplicity. Whether the off-line part of a cluster in a window of height \(\delta\) can lose more than \(e^{-b_0}\) on a whole range is open. Setting

As in lem:one-sided-density-decomposition and the narrow window negativity. \(K_L(w)=2(1-\cos Lw)/(Lw^2)=L\big(\sin(Lw/2)/(Lw/2)\big)^2\). A finite configuration has real points, contributing \(R(\tau)=\sum K_L(\tau-\gamma')\ge0\), and off-line pairs \(\gamma_j\pm i\delta_j\), \(\delta_j>0\), of multiplicity \(m_j\), contributing \(D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)=\sum_j2m_j\Re K_L(\tau-\gamma_j-i\delta_j)\); \(D_L=R+D_{\mathrm{off}}\). Writing \(u=\tau-\gamma\), \(w=u-i\delta\), \(b=\delta L\): \[2\Re K_L(w)=-\frac{2e^{b}}L\Re\frac{e^{iLu}}{(u-i\delta)^2}+E,\qquad|E|\le\frac6{L(u^2+\delta^2)},\] from \(2-2\cos Lw=2-e^{iLw}-e^{-iLw}\) and \(e^{iLw}=e^{b}e^{iLu}\). For pairs at one distance \(\delta\), \(G_L(\tau)=\sum_jm_je^{-iL(\tau-\gamma_j)}/(\tau-\gamma_j+i\delta)^2\), whose real part is that of the sum above, \(P(y)=\sum_jm_je^{-iy\gamma_j}\), \(M=\sum m_j\), and \(S_L=\sup_\tau\Re G_L(\tau)\ge0\).

The equivalence

Proposition (one-sided half-plane equivalence). prop:one-sided-half-plane-equivalence. For a finite configuration and \(L>0\):

(a) for every \(\tau\), \[D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\ \ge\ -\sum_jm_je^{\delta_jL}\min\Big(2L,\ \frac8{L((\tau-\gamma_j)^2+\delta_j^2)}\Big).\] In particular, if all \(\delta_j\le\theta\) and \(\theta L\ge2\), then \(D_L(\tau)\ge-8Me^{\theta L}/(L\theta^2)\) for all \(\tau\), with \(M\) the total multiplicity of the pairs.

(b) Let \(\delta^*\) be the largest distance, attained by the pairs \(j\in J\), whose heights are distinct (pairs at one point being one pair with their multiplicities added), and let \(\tau\) be real with \(2\tau\ne\gamma_j+\gamma_l\) for all \(j,l\in J\), which for \(j=l\) says \(\tau\ne\gamma_j\). Put \(c_j=m_j/(\tau-\gamma_j-i\delta^*)^2\) and \(q=\sum_J|c_j|^2/(2\sum_J|c_j|)>0\). Then for every \(L_1\) and every \(q'<q\) there is \(L>L_1\) with \(D_L(\tau)\le-q'e^{\delta^*L}/L\). Consequently, if for some \(\theta\), \(C\) and \(L_1\) one has \(D_L(\tau)\ge-Ce^{\theta L}\) for all \(L\ge L_1\), then \(\delta^*\le\theta\).

Proof. (a) \(\sin z/z=\int_0^1\cos(tz)\,dt\) and \(|\cos(tz)|\le\cosh(t\,\Im z)\le e^{|\Im z|}\), so \(|K_L(w)|\le Le^{b}\) for \(\Im w=-\delta\). Also \(|1-\cos Lw|\le1+\cosh b\le2e^{b}\), so \(|K_L(w)|\le4e^{b}/(L(u^2+\delta^2))\). A pair contributes \(2m\Re K_L(w)\ge-2m|K_L(w)|\). For the particular case: \(R\ge0\), and \(e^{\delta L}\min(2L,8/(L\delta^2))=2Le^{b}\min(1,4/b^2)\); the function \(e^{b}\min(1,4/b^2)\) is increasing on \((0,2]\) and on \([2,\infty)\), where its derivative has the sign of \(b-2\), so for \(\delta\le\theta\) and \(\theta L\ge2\) it is at most \(4e^{\theta L}/(\theta L)^2\).

(b) By the display in the Setting, \[Le^{-\delta^*L}D_L(\tau)=Q(L)+r(L),\qquad Q(L)=-2\Re\sum_{j\in J}c_je^{iL(\tau-\gamma_j)},\] where \(r\) collects \(Le^{-\delta^*L}\) times the real points' part, the error terms \(E\) of the pairs in \(J\) and the pairs at smaller distances. The real points' part is at most \(L\) times their number, since \(0\le K_L\le L\) on the line; the terms \(E\) are bounded by \(6M/(L\min\delta_j^2)\); the other pairs are bounded by part (a) by \(2LMe^{\delta'L}\) with \(\delta'<\delta^*\) the next distance. So \(r(L)\to0\). \(Q\) is a real trigonometric polynomial with frequencies \(\pm(\tau-\gamma_j)\), \(j\in J\), which by the conditions on \(\tau\) are nonzero and pairwise distinct. Hence its mean value is \(0\), the mean of \(Q^2\) is \(2\sum|c_j|^2\), and \(|Q|\le2\sum|c_j|\); means over windows \([L_1,L_1+X]\) converge as \(X\to\infty\), uniformly in \(L_1\). The mean of the negative part \(Q^-\) is half the mean of \(|Q|\), which is at least the mean of \(Q^2\) divided by \(\sup|Q|\); so the mean of \(Q^-\) is at least \(q\), and \(\sup_{L>L_1}Q^-(L)\ge q\) for every \(L_1\). Take \(L_1\) so large that \(|r|\le(q-q')/2\) beyond it and \(L>L_1\) with \(Q(L)\le-(q+q')/2\). For the consequence: if \(\delta^*>\theta\), then \(-q'e^{\delta^*L}/L<-Ce^{\theta L}\) for all large \(L\). \(\square\)

So in the model the one-sided premise with exponent \(\theta\), for all large lengths, holds exactly when no pair is farther than \(\theta\) from the line, up to the factor \(8M/(L\theta^2)\); and one generic \(\tau\) suffices for the converse. The lengths at which the negative value occurs in (b) are those at which a trigonometric polynomial with the cluster's frequencies is negative: they recur, and how soon depends on the cluster. That is where a finite range of lengths differs from all lengths.

What saving on the prime side this is. Not derived here. If the density equals a prime sum of length \(e^{L}\) plus smooth terms, as the explicit formula would give under the density source's hypothesis, and if that sum's trivial bound is of order \(e^{L/2}\) as the review's reviewer estimates, then the premise with \(\theta<\tfrac12\) is a saving of \(e^{-(1/2-\theta)L}\) over the trivial bound in one direction, and by the proposition it is, in the model, the statement that no zero is farther than \(\theta\) from the line. Both conditionals are unverified in this record; the proposition is about finite configurations.

A family hidden on a range

Lemma (product range mean). lem:product-range-mean. For \(a>0\) let \(I(a)=\tfrac1a\int_a^{2a}\ln|2\cos u|\,du\). Then \(I(a)\ge-2\) for every \(a>0\). Consequently, for \(P(y)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1+e^{-iy\eta_i})\) with any \(\eta_i>0\), which has nonnegative integer coefficients with sum \(M=2^n\), and every \(L_0>0\): \[\frac1{L_0}\int_{L_0}^{2L_0}\ln|P(y)|\,dy\ge-2n,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\sup_{L_0\le y\le2L_0}\frac{|P(y)|}{M}\ge M^{-1-2/\ln2}.\]

Proof. Let \(\nu=(\ln|2\cos u|)^-\). It has period \(\pi\) and is supported, in each period, on the interval of length \(\pi/3\) centred at the zero of the cosine, where \(|2\cos u|<1\); these supports are \((\pi/3+k\pi,2\pi/3+k\pi)\). Its integral over one support is \(C_1=2\int_0^{\pi/6}-\ln(2\sin v)\,dv\), the Clausen value \(\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi/3)=1.0149\ldots\), half of it on each side of the zero. Since \(\int_a^{2a}\ln|2\cos u|\,du\ge-\int_a^{2a}\nu\): if \(a<\pi/6\), the interval \([a,2a]\) lies in \((0,\pi/3)\), where \(\nu=0\), and \(I(a)\ge0\). If \(\pi/6\le a<\pi/4\), it lies in \((0,\pi/2)\) and meets one support in at most its first half, so \(I(a)\ge-(C_1/2)/a\ge-3C_1/\pi>-1\). If \(\pi/4\le a<3\pi/4\), it lies in \((0,3\pi/2)\) and meets at most one support and the first half of the next, so \(I(a)\ge-(3C_1/2)/a\ge-6C_1/\pi>-2\). If \(a\ge3\pi/4\), an interval of length \(a\) meets at most \(a/\pi+2\) supports, so \(I(a)\ge-C_1(1/\pi+2/a)\ge-11C_1/(3\pi)>-1.2\). The consequence: \(|1+e^{-iy\eta}|=|2\cos(\eta y/2)|\), and with \(u=\eta y/2\) the mean of \(\ln|2\cos(\eta y/2)|\) over \([L_0,2L_0]\) is \(I(\eta L_0/2)\); the supremum of \(\ln|P|\) is at least its mean, and \(e^{-2n}=M^{-2/\ln2}\). \(\square\)

In the other direction, as the review recorded from my attempt and its reviewer's additions (the latter unverified): with all \(\eta_i\) near \(2\pi/(3L_0)\) each factor is at most \(1\) in modulus on \([L_0,2L_0]\), so \(|P|/M\le2^{-n}\) there. So, for \(P\) and on a range of ratio two, a product family is hidden with a loss between \(M^{-1}\) and \(M^{-3.9}\) and no more; the control finds the least value of \(I\) on its grid to be \(-1.02\), which if it is the minimum would make the lower exponent \(-2.5\).

Range negativity

Theorem (range negativity). thm:range-negativity. Let the pairs be at one distance \(\delta\) with heights in an interval of length \(c\delta\), \(0<c\le1\). Let \(b_0=\delta L_0>1\), \(\kappa>1\), and \[\Lambda^*=\frac{\pi c}2\cdot\frac{(b_0-1)(\kappa b_0-1)}{(\kappa-1)\,b_0}\ \le\ \frac{\pi c\,\kappa}{2(\kappa-1)}\,b_0.\] Then \[\sup_{L_0\le L\le\kappa L_0}S_L\ \ge\ \frac{\pi^2}{100}\big(e^{-1-\Lambda^*}-4b_0e^{-b_0}\big)_+^2\,\frac M{\delta^2}.\] Consequently, for every \(\epsilon'>0\) some \(L\in[L_0,\kappa L_0]\) and some \(\tau\) have \[D_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\le-\frac{2M}{L\delta^2}\Big((1-\epsilon')\frac{\pi^2}{100}\,e^{b_0}\big(e^{-1-\Lambda^*}-4b_0e^{-b_0}\big)_+^2-3\Big).\]

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon=\sup_{L_0\le L\le\kappa L_0}S_L\,\delta^2/M\); \(0\le\varepsilon\le1\) because \(|G_L|\le M/\delta^2\). Suppose first \(\varepsilon>0\). For each \(L\) in the range apply lem:one-sided-fourier-relation with \(S=\varepsilon M/\delta^2\ge S_L\) at \(x=1/\delta\), which is at most \(L\) since \(b_0>1\): \(|P(1/\delta-L)|\le MeB_L\) with \(B_L=\tfrac2\pi(c\varepsilon+4\sqrt\varepsilon)+4be^{-b}\le B:=\tfrac{10}\pi\sqrt\varepsilon+4b_0e^{-b_0}\), using \(c\le1\), \(\varepsilon\le\sqrt\varepsilon\) and that \(be^{-b}\) decreases for \(b\ge1\). Shift the heights into \([0,c\delta]\) and let \(\Phi(z)=\sum m_je^{iz\gamma_j}\) as in the proof of lem:positive-sum-majorant; \(|\Phi(t)|=|P(-t)|\) and \(|\Phi(-t)|=|\Phi(t)|\) for real \(t\). So \(|\Phi(t)|\le MeB\) for \(a_1\le|t|\le a_2\), with \(a_1=L_0-1/\delta\) and \(a_2=\kappa L_0-1/\delta\), and \(|\Phi|\le M\) on the whole line. If \(eB\ge1\) then \(B\ge e^{-1}\ge e^{-1-\Lambda^*}\). Otherwise the inequality proved there, \(\ln(\Phi(iv)/M)\le\tfrac1\pi\int\tfrac v{t^2+v^2}\ln(|\Phi(t)|/M)\,dt\), with \(\Phi(iv)\ge Me^{-vc\delta}\), gives for every \(v>0\) \[-vc\delta\le\frac2\pi\ln(eB)\int_{a_1}^{a_2}\frac{v\,dt}{t^2+v^2}.\] Divide by \(v\) and let \(v\to0\): \(-c\delta\le\tfrac2\pi\ln(eB)\,(1/a_1-1/a_2)\), that is \(\ln\tfrac1{eB}\le\pi c\delta/(2(1/a_1-1/a_2))\). With \(a_1=(b_0-1)/\delta\) and \(a_2=(\kappa b_0-1)/\delta\), \(1/a_1-1/a_2=\delta(\kappa-1)b_0/((b_0-1)(\kappa b_0-1))\), so the right side is \(\Lambda^*\). In both cases \(B\ge e^{-1-\Lambda^*}\), that is \(\tfrac{10}\pi\sqrt\varepsilon\ge e^{-1-\Lambda^*}-4b_0e^{-b_0}\), which is the first statement. If \(\varepsilon=0\), apply the lemma with \(S=\varepsilon''M/\delta^2\) for every \(\varepsilon''>0\) and let \(\varepsilon''\to0\): the same argument gives \(4b_0e^{-b_0}\ge e^{-1-\Lambda^*}\) and the bound is \(0\). The inequality for \(\Lambda^*\): \((b_0-1)(\kappa b_0-1)\le\kappa b_0^2\). The consequence: take \(L\) in the range with \(S_L\ge(1-\epsilon')^{1/2}\) times the supremum and \(\tau\) with \(\Re G_L(\tau)\ge(1-\epsilon')^{1/2}S_L\), and use \(D_{\mathrm{off}}=-(2e^{b}/L)\Re G_L+E\) with \(|E|\le6M/(L\delta^2)\) and \(e^{b}\ge e^{b_0}\). \(\square\)

What it gives. The factor \(e^{b_0}\) against the loss \(e^{-2\Lambda^*}\): the exponent \(1-\pi c\kappa/(\kappa-1)\) is positive exactly when \(c<(\kappa-1)/(\pi\kappa)\), which is \(0.159\) at \(\kappa=2\), \(0.239\) at \(\kappa=4\), and tends to \(1/\pi=0.318\). The comparison with the narrow window negativity, which tests one length and has its exponent below one only for \(c\) below about \(0.06\), is confounded, as the reviewer saw: this proof uses the smallness of \(\Phi\) on the two symmetric intervals \(\pm[a_1,a_2]\), and the proof of lem:positive-sum-majorant used one. With the same symmetry that lemma's condition would read \(2\Lambda(\beta,b)>\pi c\), and the one-length threshold would be \(c<2(\ln2-\tfrac12)/\pi\), about \(0.12\); that improved one-length statement is immediate from the recorded proof and is not registered here. Against it, the range's own gain is a factor of about \(1.3\) at \(\kappa=2\) and at most \(2.6\). All of this concerns the off-line part: the theorem bounds \(D_{\mathrm{off}}\), and the real points' part \(R\ge0\) can compensate at a given length, as in prop:binomial-cluster-hiding. It is a bound for the supremum over the range; it does not say at which length the negative value occurs, and the gain is counted at the shortest length \(e^{b_0}\) although the length found may be longer. The square root of lem:one-sided-fourier-relation is still in it: without it the condition would be \(c<2(\kappa-1)/(\pi\kappa)\). For windows of height \(\delta\) nothing is proved. The product family with all \(\eta_i\) near \(2\pi/(3L_0)\) has, in such a window, at most \(3b_0/(2\pi)=0.48\,b_0\) factors and so a loss of at most \(e^{-0.33b_0}\) for \(P\); this compares a loss of \(P\) with a gain for \(G\) and covers only that choice of the \(\eta_i\), the number of factors being unbounded for general ones.

Degenerate cases. Proposition: no off-line pair, both parts are empty and \(D_L=R\ge0\); one pair, part (b) has \(q=|c|/2\) and \(Q=-2|c|\cos(L(\tau-\gamma)+\arg c)\), whose least value \(-2|c|\) is four times the bound; \(\tau\) at a height or at a midpoint of two heights of \(J\) is excluded, since a frequency then vanishes or two coincide and the mean of \(Q\) need not be zero. Lemma: \(n=0\), \(P=1\), equality; \(a\to0\), \(I\to\ln2\). Theorem: one pair, \(c\) arbitrarily small, \(\Lambda^*\to0\) and the bound tends to \(\tfrac{\pi^2}{100}(e^{-1}-4b_0e^{-b_0})^2M/\delta^2\), about \(0.013\,M/\delta^2\) for large \(b_0\), against at least \(0.42\,M/\delta^2\) registered in prop:separated-pair-negativity; \(\kappa\to1\), \(\Lambda^*\to\infty\) and the bound is \(0\): a single length gives nothing by this argument, which uses only \(x=1/\delta\), where the narrow window negativity uses all \(x\) at one length; for \(c\ge(\kappa-1)/(\pi\kappa)\) the bound's exponent \(2\Lambda^*\) can exceed \(b_0\), and then it gives no negativity. Unused: integrality of the multiplicities, every statement holding for real \(m_j>0\); the count \(N\) of the review's test; in part (b) the real points enter only through their number; \(c\le1\) is used only for \(c\varepsilon\le\sqrt\varepsilon\).

Nonvacuity. Theorem: \(c=0.1\), \(\kappa=2\), \(b_0=40\): \(\Lambda^*=\pi\cdot0.05\cdot39\cdot79/40\), about \(12.1\), \(e^{-1-\Lambda^*}\) about \(2\cdot10^{-6}\) against \(4b_0e^{-b_0}\) about \(7\cdot10^{-16}\), so the bound is about \(4\cdot10^{-13}M/\delta^2\) and \(e^{b_0}\) times it about \(10^{5}\). Proposition and lemma: the control's configurations.

Numerical control

Script, committed with its expectations before its run, and output. The density is computed from the closed form of the kernel at complex arguments, which uses none of the bounds. Part (a): in 96000 samples from 60 random configurations at four lengths the bound holds, the least value of (bound plus density) over bound being \(0.75\), so the bound is never close to attained in the sample and the check, which could have failed, was not near failing. Its negative control, the bound with half the exponent applied to single pairs with \(b\) between \(8.2\) and \(19.6\) where the script asserts that the altered bound is the stronger, fails in all 12 cases. Part (b): in 20 random configurations the least value of \(Le^{-\delta^*L}D_{\mathrm{off}}\) over a window of 400 in \(L\) is at most \(-q\) within the tolerance \(0.05q\) in all 20, the ratio to \(q\) lying between \(-11.0\) and \(-4.0\), so the check passes by a factor of at least four and could hardly have failed; the seven configurations with one top pair give \(-4.00\,q\), which is the value \(-2|c|\) predicted under Degenerate cases and a check that could have failed. So \(q\) is a weak bound, and the negative control with \(3q\) differs from the statement in none of the 20 cases and tested nothing, where I had written that I expected it to differ in some. The lemma: the least value of \(I\) on the grid is \(-1.02\), at \(a=0.95\); \(I(50)=-0.003\) and \(I(0.01)=0.693\). The script's header states the lemma with \(-1.3\), which was the constant of a first proof sketch; the proof in this entry gives \(-2\) and the computation \(-1.02\), so \(-1.3\) is true on the grid and unproved. Nothing here tests the theorem: its ingredients are the Fourier relation and the majorant inequality, controlled in the narrow window negativity, and its bound is far below any value a computation at reachable sizes would produce.

What was measured

All on this repository on 11 October 2026, from the launcher's saved outputs of this session. The branch is 879 commits ahead of the published base (git's count), whose last commit is dated 8 October. The whole check took 8.3 s and then 9.1 s, in both runs the time of its slowest step, the changed-claim contract against that base; the other five checks took between 0.9 and 2.9 s each, all six running at once. Against the latest commit the contract took 1.9 s inside the check. Its report against the published base covers 1178 claims with five review fields each, 1980 changed relationships and 682 entries. Timed in its stages without a profiler: loading the registry 0.8 s; the maintenance check 4.4 s, of which hashing cited evidence 2.2 s over 1327 distinct keys, the largest share for one source file 0.75 s; the registration of new entries in five notebooks the rest. A count of the hashing found 712 normalizations of 711 distinct texts and 806 excerpts of 793 distinct anchors, so cited evidence is not hashed twice; I have not looked for repeated work elsewhere in the step. The contract ran in one process on one CPU. Beside a job loading fourteen CPUs the contract took 22.1 s and 22.8 s, and the registry validation 5.4 s and 5.6 s against 2.8 s alone: under load every check slows by a factor of two or more, which accounts for an overrun like the earlier 15.2 s whatever its scope was.

What was built

  • The contract's registration of new entries, one notebook at a time, now runs in forked workers beside the maintenance check when several notebooks changed (tools/claim_maintenance.py). Its report against the published base is byte for byte the one from before the change. Wall time of the contract alone, three runs: 6.35, 6.80 and 6.61 s, with 8.4 to 8.7 s of CPU time; inside the whole check it now takes 7.5 s where it took 8.3 and 9.1 s. That is about one second saved, and the step still runs mostly on one CPU.
  • The check (tools/check-claims.py) holds each of its six checks to the limit by that check's own time. It reads the number of changed claims from the contract's report, prints it, and gives the contract alone a limit of 5 s plus 12 ms for each changed claim (19.1 s at 1178), the other checks keeping 5 s. It measures each check's CPU time as well as its wall time, and a check over its limit in wall time but within it in CPU time is reported as a note that the machine was busy and not as a failure.
  • The launcher (compute.sh) now ends any job that took five seconds or more and used between half and one and a half CPUs with a line saying so and asking that its independent parts be split across processes before the wait is accepted or a limit raised.

Checks. The whole framework suite passes: 923 tests, in 9.7 s and 8.9 s in two runs after the last change, against a limit of 10 s. On the real repository after the changes: against the published base the check passed with the contract at 7.5 s, printing the scope; beside the fourteen-CPU load it passed with two notes (validation 5.6 s of wall time and 4.0 s of CPU; contract 22.8 s of wall time and 13.5 s of CPU, within 19.1 s); the launcher's serial line appeared on the contract's own runs ("took 7 s and used 9 s of CPU time, about 1.2 of the 14 CPUs allowed") and not on the suite's.

Limit. The scaled limit was built before the split was tried, which is the order the new launcher line warns against; it stands for now at twice the cost measured before the split, a factor of about 2.5 above the contract's present time, so a slowdown of the contract by less than that is not noticed when much is unpublished. Under load the CPU time rises too (13.5 s against 8.5 s), so the note for a busy machine depends on the margin of the scaled limit; for the fixed limit it worked with 4.0 s against 5 s. The suite is within a second of its own limit, which the next build item concerns. The forked workers are used only where the fork start method exists.

What was built

  • In tools/claim_maintenance.py the hashes of cited evidence are computed in forked workers, one batch for each source file, the largest first, and put into the parent's cache: first those of changed files, then those of the claims found to need review.   • The registration of new entries, split in the last entry with a worker pool, now uses one plain forked process and one pipe for each notebook, so that the checking process has no thread when the hashing workers are forked; a registration worker that dies is replaced by the check in the parent.
  • In tools/claim-index.py the changed command validates the registry in a forked process beside the check instead of before it; if that process reports an invalid registry, or dies, the parent validates and fails as it did.
  • In tools/check-claims.py the contract's allowance is reset from the times after the split: 6 ms for each changed claim in place of 12.
  • In tools/finish-turn.py a review's decisive test must carry an Attempt paragraph of at least forty characters.

What was measured

So the suite's own CPU time stayed between 90 and 97 s in every condition while its wall time doubled at most; in the one run beside four CPUs it was already over. The suite is parallel: about eleven CPUs' worth of work in its eight seconds, on fourteen allowed. The archived run the item cites was opened: 864 tests in 16.0 s, "212 s in the run's own control group, 11 s by other programs; the machine's 16 processors were busy for 222 s of 256", with the three browser groups at 9.7 to 10.7 s and two tests of the two-partition kernel at 3.71 and 3.38 s among its slowest. The one caveat is that the suite's own CPU time at 864 tests was not measured. The three kernel tests take 1.1 to 1.3 s when the suite runs alone today, and no test but the browser groups takes more than 3.3 s.

What was built

  • In tools/tests/run.py: readings of the run's own control group and of the other jobs present in the computation slice before and after the run; a line giving the CPU time the run used and the time that was certainly other work (other jobs that ran throughout, and programs outside the slice), printed when the run is over its limit or on request. The launcher services that the suite's own tests start are born during the run and are not counted as other work. Work the tests cause outside the slice, in the user's service manager or the kernel, still counts as other programs: alone that was 10 to 13 s, 7 to 9%, against the 40 s that a quarter of the processors for ten seconds would need.
  • A verdict in one function with its test: within the limit; over it on a busy machine, when a quarter of the processors were busy with other work, the run's own CPU time is at most 125 s and the time is at most twice the limit; or slow. A busy overrun is named, "TOO SLOW (machine busy)", and still fails. An option lets it pass and nothing uses the option: whether it should is the user's rule to change, and the question is filed.
  • In tools/tests/test_site.py a browser case over its limit fails as before and its message carries the same line.

Checks. The whole framework suite passes alone on the final code: 929 tests in 9.1 s, with 97 s of its own and 11% elsewhere; that is the slowest of the five runs alone and within a second of the limit. Beside the loads it failed and named the run busy, as designed: with two browser cases over their limit beside four CPUs, and three beside fourteen. The verdict's test uses the figures measured above, those at 50 and 53% being of the first definition; the readings of the run's own group and of the other jobs are tested on a fixture directory. The flags are tested by nested runs whose assertions are conditional: where the nested run cannot read its control group, or takes more than twice its small limit, they assert nothing, and nothing reports that they did not.

Limit. The thresholds rest on seven runs on one day. The quarter is one measurement: 31% elsewhere with a four-CPU load put the suite at 10.4 s; nothing was measured between 9% and 31%. What the busy verdict would misname as the machine's: a slowdown that adds waiting and no CPU (a sleep, a stalled read, lost parallelism) of up to twice the limit while another job happens to run; growth of the suite's own CPU time up to 125 s, a third above today's, a figure that drifts as tests are added and is fixed in the code. Because the verdict fails by default, a misnamed run still fails; the name can mislead whoever reads it. Jobs that start or end during the run are not counted, which errs toward calling the run slow. Outside the launcher the own group may be a login session with other programs in it, which errs the same way. The browser cases' message has no verdict of its own.

The item's own measurement

The printing the item asks for was built by a framework commit of 11 October: the resemblance tool, which every entry declaring a claim must run, lists the queued items of which a draft claim's summary and assessment share 0.4 of the content words. That commit's message records the first measurement, which I did not repeat: the tool's file has no later commit, by the reviewer's check of its history, so the figure is of the code as it stands: against the queue of the commit that registered the real configuration bound, the item that lemma answers scored 0.53. The second, on the notebook's other registrations, was made today through the tool's own function: the 54 claims registered from this notebook against today's 64 queued items and sub-ideas give nine pairs at the threshold (41 at 0.3 and 265 at 0.2). I read the nine against the items' text and the claims' summaries, not their proofs. At least one bears on its item: the mean count of real zeros of the sum family against the sub-idea asking to count zeros of the sum function off the line, which the entry registering that proposition had been shown and had read. Two pair a claim with a sub-idea of the entry that registered it, a follow-up question and not an answer; at registration such a sub-idea is not yet queued, so the tool would not have shown them then. Six I judged to share vocabulary (multiplicities, ranges, pairs) and no more; the reviewer doubts one of them, the short resonance-free range against the sub-idea on a multiplicity budget, since the theorem's range depends on the multiplicities, and I did not read that pair further. So at this threshold the list is short and mostly not answers: at least one useful pair in nine.

Commits against queued builds

The queue tool has a new command that takes a commit touching the framework and lists the top-level build items, queued in any notebook as that commit left it and already queued before it, of whose content words the commit's message and file names have 0.4 or more; everything is read from the commit. Necessary target. For every hypothetical zero \(\beta+i\gamma\) with \(\beta>1/2\): a proved inequality it violates. Downstream. Through thm:range-negativity a bound for the off-line part over a range of lengths excludes clusters at one distance in a narrow window: weaker than the goal. Through prop:moment-extraction-exponents the import's extraction gives \(\tfrac12+\beta(1-\tfrac1k)/(2m)\) from a \(2m\)-th moment over \(D^\beta\) rows: weaker than the goal.

Reviewer's suggestions, unverified

  • The lemma on infinite configurations. Under the local count only finitely many points have \(|\tau-\gamma|\) bounded, so the poles of the termwise transform are finite in every bounded set and the sum is meromorphic in the whole plane; distances accumulating at an unattained supremum sit at heights going to infinity. Landau's theorem, recalled and unread by the reviewer: for a nonnegative function with finite abscissa of convergence the transform is not holomorphic at the real point of that abscissa. Residues cannot cancel: the poles at \(s=\delta+i(\tau-\gamma)\) from the pairs at heights \(\gamma\) and \(2\tau-\gamma\) have residues \(-m/w^2\) and \(-m'/w^2\) with the same \(w\). The exchange of sum and integral holds for \(\Re s>1/2\) from \(|L\,K_L(w)|\le\min(L^2,4/|w|^2)e^{L/2}\), and the integral from \(0\) to \(L_1\) is entire. The hypothesis is to be \(D_L(\tau)\ge-CL^Ae^{\theta L}\), which the same argument covers and which matches the direct bound. Record. Searched Landau theorem one-sided bound infinite configuration local count Laplace transform real singularity: no registered statement; prop:one-sided-half-plane-equivalence is the finite case. To be written and reviewed in an entry of its own.
  • With \(\tau\) at the height of a pair at distance \(d\), the real pole there has positive residue, so only pairs with \(\delta>\max(d,\theta)\) are excluded. Record. Searched one-sided density lower bound all lengths infinitely many pairs half-plane equivalence accumulating distances: prop:one-sided-half-plane-equivalence excludes such \(\tau\) and says nothing of them. Carried to the lemma's entry.
  • For the prime side, a Barner-type explicit formula, recalled and unread, whose conditions the triangle meets; and the polar term \(K_L(\tau\mp i/2)\) is about \(e^{L/2}/L\), the same exponent as the prime sum, only the archimedean term being \(O(\log(2+|\tau|))\): the whole right side has trivial exponent \(\tfrac12\). Record. No registered statement of an explicit formula in this notebook, by the same two searches; lem:prime-side-form-bound is the recorded trivial bound for the Gram form. Carried to the lemma's entry.

The rows

Read in the intermediate preprint retained with the import, by line numbers of its source. The large sieve it uses is a lemma (lines 1888 to 1912): for coefficients \(\beta\) on squarefree primary \(n\) of norm about \(U\), \[\sum^*_{N(k)\le\mathcal H}\Big|\sum_{n}\beta(n)\chi_k(n)^3\Big|^2\ll(\mathcal HU)^\varepsilon(\mathcal H+U)\sum|\beta(n)|^2,\] "the star restricts \(k\) to squarefree primary elements", which are also prime to the fixed set \(S\); its proof is a citation of the quadratic large sieve of Goldmakher and Louvel, their Theorem 1.1, with the hypotheses matched in six lines. So the inequality is for squarefree rows and squarefree columns, with the quadratic character \(\chi^3\). The cited theorem, read in this cycle in the source of its arXiv version (1112.1642, Theorem 1.1): for a quadratic Hecke family \(\{\chi_{\mathfrak a}\}\) with respect to an ideal \(\mathfrak c\) of a number field, \(\sum^*_{N\mathfrak a\le M}|\sum^*_{N\mathfrak b\le N}\lambda_{\mathfrak b}\chi_{\mathfrak b}(\mathfrak a)|^2\ll(MN)^\varepsilon(M+N)\sum^*|\lambda_{\mathfrak b}|^2\), both sums over squarefree ideals prime to \(\mathfrak c\). That is the inequality the preprint quotes. Whether the preprint's characters form a Hecke family in that paper's sense, its Definition, is what the six lines assert and what I did not check. The mean square the extraction uses is the proposition on completed sums (line 1317): \(\sum_{0<N(k)\ll\mathcal H}|T(X;k,f)|^2\ll D^\varepsilon\|W\|^2(\mathcal H+\mathcal H^2N(f)/X)\) over all nonzero rows \(k\), for \(f\) squarefree, primary and prime to \(S\), with a norm \(\|W\|_{C^J}\) of the weight and for \(1\le\mathcal H,X,N(f)\le D^{C_0}\), where \(T\) is a completed sum of cubic theta coefficients with the twist \(\chi_n(k)\chi_n(f)^4\). It is proved in two steps. First a lemma for squarefree rows \(s\) and an arbitrary nonzero auxiliary \(g\) in place of \(f\) (line 1923), with the bound \(\mathcal H+\mathcal H^2N(g)/X\). Then (lines 2189 to 2212) every row is written \(k=u_0sv^2\) with \(s\) squarefree, and since \(\chi^8=\chi^2\) for a sextic character, zero extensions included, \[\chi_n(u_0sv^2)\chi_n(f)^4=\chi_n(u_0s)\chi_n(fv^2)^4,\qquad T(X;u_0sv^2,f)=T(X;u_0s,fv^2);\] the lemma with row bound \(\mathcal H/N(v)^2\) and \(g=fv^2\) gives for each \(v\) the bound \(\mathcal H/N(v)^2+\mathcal H^2N(f)/(N(v)^2X)\), and the sum over \(v\) converges. I checked the character identity and the arithmetic of the bound: \((\mathcal H/N(v)^2)^2N(fv^2)/X=\mathcal H^2N(f)/(N(v)^2X)\).

What this does at the rows that carry the content. A sixth-power row \(k=w^6\) has \(s=1\), \(v=w^3\), and in the proof sits in the block of \(v=w^3\), the row \(s=1\) of the lemma with auxiliary \(g=fw^6\) and row bound \(\mathcal H/N(w)^6\), which is at least \(1\) because \(N(v)^2\le\mathcal H\). A corollary of mine, not a statement of the preprint: the lemma at row bound \(1\) says \(|T(X;u_0,g)|^2\ll D^\varepsilon(1+N(g)/X)\) for a single completed sum, a bound linear in \(N(g)\) and valid for \(N(g)\le D^{C_0}\), the proof passing to \(2C_0\). The single-row test examined the case \(f=1\), \(g=1\) of this numerically and did not break it; it ran no \(g\) with a cube factor. The review's comparison does transfer in form: sixth-power rows carry the trivial twist up to a coprimality condition, and the statement about them is this single-row bound, which is the real content. Its symptom in the proof is that the lemma's bound has no term independent of the row range, both terms falling like \(N(v)^{-2}\), where a mean square of sums with fixed coefficients would pay the large sieve's column term once for each \(v\). So the weight of the argument is the lemma for squarefree rows and arbitrary \(g\), whose proof the completed mean square audit read, and behind it the cited quadratic large sieve and the theta transformation; not the passage to all rows. The reviewer adds, unverified: for \(n\) prime to \(w\) the twist by \(g=fw^6\) is the twist by \(f\) with a coprimality condition, highly imprimitive, so a gap, if any, would be in whether the lemma's proof handles non-squarefree, imprimitive \(g\).

The appendix's arithmetic part

Read: lines 2690 to 2873, the proofs of the Gauss-sum identities. At a primary prime \(p\) of norm \(q\), with \(\gamma_j\) the normalized Gauss sum of \(\chi_p^j\) and \(\alpha(p)=p/|p|\): (A) \(\gamma_1\gamma_2=\overline{\chi_p(4)}\gamma_3\gamma_2^3\); (B) \(\gamma_2^3=-\alpha(p)\); (C) \(\gamma_3(p)\) equals a quadratic Gauss value depending on \(p\) modulo \(4\). Checked by hand, each step: the count \(\#\{x:4x(1-x)=y\}=1+\chi_p^3(1-y)\), whence \(\chi_p(4)J(\chi_p,\chi_p)=J(\chi_p,\chi_p^3)\); the Gauss–Jacobi relations \(J(\chi,\chi^3)=g_1g_3/g_4\) and \(J(\chi,\chi)=g_1^2/g_2\); \(\gamma_2\gamma_4=\chi_p^2(-1)=1\), a cubic character at \(-1\); these give (A). For (B): \(J(\chi_p^2,\chi_p^2)\equiv\sum x^{(q-1)/3}(1-x)^{(q-1)/3}\equiv0\) modulo \(p\), every exponent in the expansion lying strictly between \(0\) and \(q-1\); its norm is \(q\), so it is a unit times \(p\); modulo \(3\) it is \(q-2+(\omega-1)\sum j_x\equiv-1\), the sum of the exponents \(j_x\) being divisible by \(3\) because \(\prod_{x\ne0,1}x(1-x)=1\) by Wilson's theorem twice; with \(p\equiv1\) modulo \(3\) the unit is \(-1\), and \(\gamma_2^3=\gamma_2^2/\gamma_4=J/\sqrt q=-\alpha(p)\). I found no error. Together (A) and (B) give \(\gamma_1\gamma_2=-\overline{\chi_p(4)}\alpha(p)\gamma_3\), the sign being the Möbius function at a prime. Not checked: the extension to squarefree \(n\) by the Chinese remainder theorem with the reciprocity factor (lines 2771 to 2780); the evaluation of the quadratic Gauss value by Poisson summation and its dependence on a ray class (lines 2783 to 2850), beyond the control of (C) at primes; and the derivation of the paired identity (line 2288), \(a_\xi(u_1)\overline{a_\xi(u_2)}\gamma(\chi_{u_1}\overline{\chi_{u_2}})=\mu(u_1)\mu(u_2)(\xi G)(u_1u_2^{-1})\), from those, which I read as a statement only.

Numerical control

Script, committed with its expectations before its run, and output. The Gauss sums are computed from their definitions, which use none of the identities, for the 42 split primary primes \(a+b\omega\), \(b\ne0\), of norm at most \(200\) (21 norms, each with its two conjugate primes); the inert primary primes \(-5\) and \(-11\), of norms \(25\) and \(121\), which meet the appendix's hypothesis, are not tested. For (C) the script compares \(\gamma_3(p)\) with the source's formula for the quadratic Gauss value, so it tests that formula together with the identification of the two, which the source proves in two lines. (A), (B) and (C) hold with largest deviations \(1.9\cdot10^{-14}\), \(2.5\cdot10^{-14}\) and \(8.2\cdot10^{-15}\) against a tolerance of \(10^{-9}\), the quantities compared having modulus one; the script's printed line says "modulus 1 or 2", which is loose. Negative control: (B) with the non-primary generator \(\omega p\), for which the script asserts that \(\gamma_2^3\) is unchanged and \(\alpha\) is multiplied by \(\omega\), so that the altered statement differs from the true one by \(\sqrt3\): it fails in all 42 cases, which follows from (B) holding and is not independent evidence: it shows that the script's test can fail. The hand check and the computation agree. The control tests split primes only.

Nonvacuity. 42 primes and three identities, which are not independent of one another as statements but are computed separately: each of the 126 comparisons could have failed.

The review's question is answered: the passage to non-squarefree rows is a correct reduction to the lemma for squarefree rows with an arbitrary auxiliary twist, so there is no gap in that passage, conditionally on that lemma. The import is not verified by this: the lemma for squarefree rows rests on a cited large sieve and on the theta transformation of the appendix's second part, read in earlier entries; the cited sources are unread; and the appendix's arithmetic is checked at primes only. The comparison I drew in the review, that an inequality over all rows for the quadratic symbol would carry a half-plane, is not an objection to this proof, for the reason given above; whether the single-row bound at the shortest range is as strong as it reads, a bound for one completed sum uniform in the auxiliary twist, is what the single-row test probed and the place I would look next.

General statement. prop:one-sided-zero-set-equivalence, for every conjugation-closed multiset with bounded imaginary parts and \(\sum m_z/(1+(\Re z)^2)<\infty\), every \(\theta\ge0\) and every real \(\tau\) that is not a real point of it.

Setting

\(K_L(w)=2(1-\cos Lw)/(Lw^2)\), with \(K_L(0)=L\). A configuration is a multiset of complex points \(z\) with multiplicities \(m_z\ge1\), closed under conjugation with equal multiplicities, with \(|\Im z|\le\Delta\) and \[\sum_zm_z/(1+(\Re z)^2)<\infty.\qquad(\mathrm H)\] Its real points are written \(\gamma'\); its other points come in pairs \(\gamma_j\pm i\delta_j\), \(\delta_j>0\), of multiplicity \(m_j\), where pairs at one point are one pair. By (H) every bounded set contains finitely many points. \(D_L(\tau)=\sum_zm_zK_L(\tau-z)\) for real \(\tau\) and \(L>0\). For a real \(\tau\) that is not a real point put \(S(\tau)=\sum_zm_z/|\tau-z|^2\), finite by (H) since finitely many points are near \(\tau\) and none is at it; \(S_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)=\sum m_z/|\tau-z|^2\) over the points of the pairs only, which is finite for every real \(\tau\), no such point being real; a pair \(j\) contributes \(2m_j/((\tau-\gamma_j)^2+\delta_j^2)\) to it.

Landau's lemma

Lemma (nonnegative transform abscissa). lem:nonnegative-transform-abscissa. Let \(L_1\ge0\), let \(g\ge0\) be continuous on \([L_1,\infty)\) and suppose \(G(s)=\int_{L_1}^\infty g(L)e^{-sL}\,dL\) converges for \(\Re s>\sigma_1\). Let \(H\) be holomorphic on an open set \(U\) containing the real half-line \((\sigma_0,\infty)\), with \(H=G\) on \(U\cap\{\Re s>\sigma_1\}\). Then \(\int_{L_1}^\infty g(L)e^{-\sigma L}\,dL<\infty\) for every real \(\sigma>\sigma_0\).

Proof. Let \(\sigma_c\) be the infimum of the real \(\sigma\) for which the integral is finite; \(\sigma_c\le\sigma_1\), and for \(\Re s>\sigma_c\) the integral converges absolutely and \(G\) is holomorphic there, with \(G^{(k)}(s)=\int(-L)^kg(L)e^{-sL}\,dL\). Suppose \(\sigma_c>\sigma_0\). Let \(W\) be the connected component of \(U\cap\{\Re s>\sigma_c\}\) that contains the half-line \((\sigma_c,\infty)\); \(G\) and \(H\) are holomorphic on \(W\) and agree on its open subset \(W\cap\{\Re s>\sigma_1\}\), which is not empty, so \(G=H\) on \(W\). Choose \(r>0\) with the disc of radius \(3r\) about \(\sigma_c\) inside \(U\), and put \(a=\sigma_c+r\). The disc of radius \(2r\) about \(a\) lies in \(U\), so the Taylor series of \(H\) at \(a\) converges there, in particular at the real point \(b=\sigma_c-r/2\), at distance \(3r/2\) from \(a\). A neighbourhood of \(a\) lies in \(W\), so \(H^{(k)}(a)=G^{(k)}(a)\), and \[H(b)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(b-a)^k}{k!}H^{(k)}(a)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(a-b)^k}{k!}\int_{L_1}^\infty L^kg(L)e^{-aL}\,dL.\] Every term is nonnegative, since \(a>b\), \(g\ge0\) and \(L\ge L_1\ge0\), so by Tonelli's theorem the sum is \(\int g(L)e^{-aL}e^{(a-b)L}\,dL=\int g(L)e^{-bL}\,dL\), which is therefore finite, with \(b<\sigma_c\): a contradiction. \(\square\)

The equivalence

Proposition (one-sided zero-set equivalence). prop:one-sided-zero-set-equivalence. For a configuration as in the Setting:

(a) the sum defining \(D_L(\tau)\) converges absolutely for every real \(\tau\) and \(L>0\); and if every \(\delta_j\le\theta\), then for every real \(\tau\) and \(L>0\), \[L\,D_L(\tau)\ \ge\ -4\,S_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\,e^{\theta L}.\]

(b) Let \(\tau\) be real and not a real point, and let \(d\ge0\) be the largest distance of a pair at height \(\tau\), with \(d=0\) if there is none. If for some \(\theta\ge0\), \(C\), \(A\ge0\) an integer and \(L_1>0\), \[L\,D_L(\tau)\ \ge\ -C\,L^A\,e^{\theta L}\quad\text{for all }L\ge L_1,\] then \(\delta_j\le\max(\theta,d)\) for every pair. In particular, if \(\tau\) is no pair's height, the displayed bound holds for some \(C\), \(A\), \(L_1\) if and only if every \(\delta_j\le\theta\).

Proof. For complex \(x\), \(|1-\cos x|\le1+\cosh(\Im x)\le2e^{|\Im x|}\). So for \(w=\tau-z\ne0\), \[|L\,K_L(w)|=\frac{2|1-\cos Lw|}{|w|^2}\le\frac{4e^{L|\Im z|}}{|\tau-z|^2}.\qquad(1)\] (a) By (1) and (H) the sum converges absolutely, the finitely many points near \(\tau\) being finitely many terms and a real point at \(\tau\) contributing \(m\,L\). A real point contributes \(m\,K_L(\tau-\gamma')\ge0\). A pair contributes \(m_j(K_L(w)+K_L(\bar w))=2m_j\Re K_L(w)\) with \(w=\tau-\gamma_j-i\delta_j\ne0\), and by (1) \(2m_jL\,\Re K_L(w)\ge-8m_je^{\delta_jL}/|w|^2\), which is \(-4e^{\delta_jL}\) times the pair's share \(2m_j/|w|^2\) of \(S_{\mathrm{off}}\). With \(\delta_j\le\theta\) this sums to the bound.

(b) Put \(f(L)=L\,D_L(\tau)=\sum_zm_z\,2(1-\cos Lw_z)/w_z^2\), \(w_z=\tau-z\ne0\). By (1), \(|f(L)|\le4S(\tau)e^{\Delta L}\), and the series converges uniformly on bounded sets of \(L\), so \(f\) is continuous. For complex \(w\) and \(\Re s>|\Im w|\), \[\int_0^\infty\frac{2(1-\cos Lw)}{w^2}e^{-sL}\,dL=\frac2{w^2}\Big(\frac1s-\frac s{s^2+w^2}\Big)=\frac2{s(s^2+w^2)}.\qquad(2)\] For \(\Re s>\Delta\) the sum over \(z\) of \(m_z\int_0^\infty|2(1-\cos Lw_z)/w_z^2|e^{-\Re s\,L}dL\) is at most \(4S(\tau)/(\Re s-\Delta)\) by (1), so by Fubini's theorem \[F(s):=\int_0^\infty f(L)e^{-sL}\,dL=\Phi(s):=\sum_z\frac{2m_z}{s(s^2+w_z^2)}\qquad(\Re s>\Delta).\] The series \(\Phi\) defines a meromorphic function on the whole plane: on a disc \(|s|\le R\), the points with \(|w_z|\le\sqrt2R\) are finitely many, and for the others \(|s^2+w_z^2|\ge|w_z|^2/2\), so the remaining series \(\sum2m_z/(s^2+w_z^2)\) is dominated by \(4\sum m_z/|w_z|^2\) and converges uniformly there. Its poles are at \(s=0\) and at the points \(s=\pm iw_z\). For a real point these are \(\pm i(\tau-\gamma')\), on the imaginary axis. For the two points of a pair, \(w=u\mp i\delta_j\) with \(u=\tau-\gamma_j\), they are the four points \(\pm\delta_j\pm iu\). So a pole of \(\Phi\) on the positive real axis occurs exactly at \(s=\delta_j\) for a pair at height \(\tau\), and \(\Phi\) is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of every real \(s>d\), the poles in a bounded set being finitely many.

The residue. Fix a pair \(j\) not at height \(\tau\) and \(s_0=\delta_j+iu\), \(u=\tau-\gamma_j\ne0\). A term \(2m_z/(s(s^2+w_z^2))\) has a pole at \(s_0\) exactly when \(w_z^2=-s_0^2\), that is \(w_z=-is_0=u-i\delta_j\), the point \(z=\gamma_j+i\delta_j\), or \(w_z=is_0=-u+i\delta_j\), the point \(z=(2\tau-\gamma_j)-i\delta_j\), the lower point of a pair at height \(2\tau-\gamma_j\) and the same distance, of multiplicity \(m'\ge0\). The pole is simple, \(s_0\ne0\) and the two roots \(\pm s_0\) of \(s^2=-w_z^2\) being distinct, with residue \(2m_z/(s_0\cdot2s_0)=m_z/s_0^2\). So the residue of \(\Phi\) at \(s_0\) is \((m_j+m')/s_0^2\ne0\): \(\Phi\) has a pole at \(s_0\).

Now assume the bound. Put \(g(L)=f(L)+CL^Ae^{\theta L}\ge0\) on \([L_1,\infty)\), continuous. For \(\Re s>\max(\Delta,\theta)\), \[G(s)=\int_{L_1}^\infty g(L)e^{-sL}\,dL=\Phi(s)-\int_0^{L_1}f(L)e^{-sL}\,dL+\frac{C\,A!}{(s-\theta)^{A+1}}-C\int_0^{L_1}L^Ae^{(\theta-s)L}\,dL.\] The two integrals over \([0,L_1]\) are entire functions of \(s\). So the right side, \(H\), is meromorphic in the plane with poles only at \(\theta\) and at the poles of \(\Phi\), and is holomorphic on an open set containing the real half-line \((\sigma_0,\infty)\), \(\sigma_0=\max(\theta,d)\). By the lemma \(\int_{L_1}^\infty g(L)e^{-\sigma L}dL<\infty\) for every \(\sigma>\sigma_0\), so \(G\) is holomorphic on \(\Re s>\sigma_0\). The meromorphic function \(H\) agrees with \(G\) on \(\Re s>\max(\Delta,\theta)\), hence on the connected half-plane \(\Re s>\sigma_0\) away from its poles, and so has no pole there. A pair with \(\delta_j>\sigma_0\) is not at height \(\tau\), since \(\delta_j>d\), and by the residue computation gives \(\Phi\), hence \(H\), a pole at \(\delta_j+i(\tau-\gamma_j)\), of real part \(\delta_j>\sigma_0\): impossible. So every \(\delta_j\le\max(\theta,d)\). The last sentence of (b) is this with \(d=0\), together with (a), which gives the bound with \(A=0\), \(C=4S_{\mathrm{off}}(\tau)\). The hypothesis \(\theta\ge0\) is not used: \(\sigma_0\ge d\ge0\) in any case. \(\square\)

The zeros of \(\zeta\). Take the points \(z_\rho=(\rho-\tfrac12)/i\) over the nontrivial zeros, with their multiplicities. The set is closed under conjugation because the zeros are symmetric about the critical line, \(|\Im z_\rho|<\tfrac12\), and (H) holds by the classical bound \(N(T+1)-N(T)\ll\log T\); these are standard facts that I did not read in a source in this cycle. So for every real \(\tau\) that is not the ordinate of a zero: \(L\,D_L(\tau)\ge-CL^Ae^{\theta L}\) for all large \(L\) if and only if \(\zeta\) has no zero with \(\Re\rho>\tfrac12+\theta\); at \(\theta=0\) the one-sided bound is the Riemann hypothesis, and then \(D_L\ge0\) outright. No explicit formula enters: the statement is about the sum over zeros. What the sum equals on the prime side, and with what trivial exponent, is not derived here; the eighth review's reviewer notes that the polar term of the explicit formula has the same exponent \(\tfrac12\) as the prime sum.

Degenerate cases. No pair: (a) gives \(D_L\ge0\) and (b) is empty. One pair at height \(\tau\) and nothing else: \(L\,D_L(\tau)=4m(\cosh\delta L-1)/\delta^2>0\), so the bound holds for every \(\theta\) while \(\delta>\theta\) is possible; this is why (b) concludes only \(\delta_j\le\max(\theta,d)\), and the pole at the real point \(s=\delta\) has the positive residue \(2m/\delta^2\). \(\tau\) at a real point: excluded for brevity; its term is \(mL^2\) with transform \(2m/s^3\), a pole at \(0\) only, and the argument goes through. A finite configuration: the statement holds with no condition on the heights at the largest distance, where prop:one-sided-half-plane-equivalence asked that \(2\tau\ne\gamma_j+\gamma_l\); the two poles then coincide and their residues add, as computed. \(\theta\ge\Delta\): the hypothesis of (b) always holds, by \(|f|\le4Se^{\Delta L}\), and the conclusion \(\delta_j\le\theta\) is trivial. Distances accumulating at a supremum not attained: covered, each pair with \(\delta_j>\theta\) giving its own pole. Unused: integrality of multiplicities; conjugation-closure is used only to make \(D_L\) real and to pair the points; the integer \(A\) could be any real \(A\ge0\) with \(\Gamma(A+1)\) in place of \(A!\).

Nonvacuity. The lattice \(z=n\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\), with one pair \(\pm i/4\) and \(\tau=\tfrac12\): (H) holds, \(\Delta=\tfrac14\), \(\tau\) is no real point and no pair's height; the proposition says \(L\,D_L(\tfrac12)\ge-CL^Ae^{\theta L}\) for all large \(L\) exactly when \(\theta\ge\tfrac14\). The zeros of \(\zeta\) are the instance the statement is for.

Numerical control

Script, committed with its expectations before its run, and output. The identity (2) by adaptive quadrature against the closed form, which the quadrature does not use, in 8 cases of complex \(w\) and \(s\): the largest relative deviation is \(3.1\cdot10^{-13}\) against a tolerance of \(10^{-8}\), the neglected tails being below \(10^{-23}\). Negative control: the closed form with \(s^2-w^2\), which the script asserts to differ from the true one by more than \(10^{-3}\) in each case, is off by between \(5\cdot10^{-2}\) and \(2.9\) and fails in all 8. The residue at a coincident pole, in 3 configurations and 4 directions of approach at distance \(10^{-6}\): the largest relative deviation from \((m+m')/s_0^2\) is \(1.9\cdot10^{-6}\) against \(10^{-4}\), which is the size of the next term of the expansion and not a sharp check. Nothing here tests the proposition itself, whose content is the argument; a finite truncation is the registered finite case.

What it gives

For this kernel the one-sided premise at all lengths is the zero-free half-plane, for the actual zeros and at any real \(\tau\) that is not the ordinate of a zero; the case of \(\tau\) at a real point is sketched under Degenerate cases and not part of the proposition. So the one-sided form is not a weaker premise than the goal; what was learned in the lead's cluster entries concerns finite ranges of lengths only. The local version at one length does inherit the cluster cancellation: that is prop:binomial-cluster-hiding, a cluster hidden at one length, with thm:range-negativity bounding how far a narrow cluster can hide over a range.

The commit against the item

Read in its diff. The finisher refused an Owed attempt paragraph that reports the named attempt as not reached, not made, unread, or read by the reviewer, unless the paragraph has a reason word (because, since, came first, comes first, the reason); entries dated before 12 October 2026 are exempt; five tests, one on the wording of the draft that prompted it. The item's two entries are the polar term audit, whose paragraph, "the uniformity and the transfer proposition are not reached", is the wording the commit's test quotes, and the descent induction audit, identified by the reviewer: "Its own proof I did not read: I chose the induction first because it could be checked completely in one sitting ... the reviewer then read the transfer proof". The commit's check refuses the first and passes the second, by its "because". So the commit let through one of the two cases the item was written on.

What is added

This is the item's demand for its second case.
